questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An elderly diabetic female patient presented with a black, foul-smelling discharge from the nose. On examination, a blackish necrotic mass filled the nasal cavity and eroded the septum and hard palate. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mucormycosis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Mucormycosis.

Diabetic patients with local tissue destruction with blackish nasal discharge typically resembles the presentation of invasive mucormycosis. The blackish discolouration is due to direct fungal invasion causing arterial and venous thrombosis leading to gangrene. Mucormycosis is an opportunistic infection caused principally by species of Rhizopus, Mucor, and Lichtheimia. The most prevalent species is Rhizopus Oryza.

Risk factors:

* Diabetes (diabetic ketoacidosis).

* Immunocompromised individuals

Treatment:

* Intravenous administration of amphotericin B is the treatment of choice for invasive mucormycosis.

* Surgical debridement

* Control of underlying predisposing causes.

Other options:

Option A: Invasive aspergillosis leads to the formation of black or greyish membrane in the nasal mucosa. The maxillary sinus may contain a fungus ball containing semisolid cheesy-white or blackish material.

Option C: Foreign body nose presents with foul-smelling unilateral discharge.

Option D: Rhinosporidiosis is a granulomatous condition caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi and presents with nasal discharge, epistaxis, and nasal obstruction by a polypoidal mass.
questions.learning: Mucormycosis — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Mucormycosis. Diabetic patients with local tissue destruction with blackish nasal discharge typically resembles the presentation of invasive mucormycosis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The spinal sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve has 2nd order neurons to carry which sensation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pain

The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) is responsible for sensory input from the face, as well as motor functions such as chewing. Its sensory pathway involves three branches: the ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), and mandibular (V3) divisions. The first-order neurons for each division originate from different sensory ganglia:

1.Ophthalmic Division (V1):
First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion (also called the semilunar or Gasserian ganglion).

2. Maxillary Division (V2):
First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion.

3. Mandibular Division (V3):
First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion.

These first-order neurons carry sensory information from the face to the brainstem. Upon entering the brainstem, the fibers synapse with second-order neurons in specific nuclei:

1. Principal Sensory Nucleus (Main Sensory Nucleus):
a.Receives input from all three divisions of the trigeminal nerve.
b.Located in the pons.
c.Second-order neurons here carry discriminative touch and proprioceptive information.

2. Spinal Trigeminal Nucleus (Spinal Nucleus of Trigeminal):
a.Receives input mainly from the maxillary and mandibular divisions.
b.Located in the medulla.
c.Second-order neurons here carry pain and temperature sensations.

After synapsing in these nuclei, the sensory information is further relayed to higher brain centers for processing and perception.
questions.learning: Pain — The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) is responsible for sensory input from the face, as well as motor functions such as chewing. Its sensory pathway involves three branches: the ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), and mandibular (V3) divisions.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic patient consuming alcohol for the last 20 years had his last drink 3 days back. He presents with altered sensorium, disorientation, tremors, and a feeling of insects crawling over his body. Which of the following should be given to this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lorazepam + thiamine

The given clinical scenario of alcohol withdrawal with altered sensorium, and a feeling of insects crawling over his body points towards the diagnosis of delirium tremens. Lorazepam + thiamine should be given to this patient.

Delirium tremens is treated using benzodiazepines like lorazepam starting with a higher dosage which is gradually tapered as withdrawal symptoms disappear. In cases of chronic alcohol use, vitamin deficiency (especially thiamine) may be co-existing and hence bolus doses of thiamine are given to prevent/treat Wernicke encephalopathy.

Delirium tremens occurs after 2-4 days of abstinence in a heavy or chronic drinker. It is characterized by autonomic hyperactivity, tremors, delusions, and hallucinations. It usually resolves spontaneously in 7 days but may cause the death of the patient due to cardiovascular collapse, infections or self-injury.

Haloperidol is generally not the first-line drug in case of alcoholic withdrawal. It might be used as an add-on in agitated patients. It decreases the seizure threshold and its use would be appropriate in a case of co-existing psychotic disorder like schizophrenia.
questions.learning: Lorazepam + thiamine — The given clinical scenario of alcohol withdrawal with altered sensorium, and a feeling of insects crawling over his body points towards the diagnosis of delirium tremens.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child presented with a history of road traffic accident. The axial CT image of the child, shown below, is suggestive of _________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Extradural Hemorrhage

The given CT image shows the typical bi-convex hyperdense lesion not crossing cranial sutures, characteristic of an extradural hemorrhage.

As the dura mater tends to adhere to the skull, the hematoma collecting between the skull and this dura is seen on CT sections as a biconvex dense area immediately beneath the skull vault, convex towards both the brain and the vault. They tend not to cross the suture lines.

The temporoparietal convexity is the most common site. The hematoma usually lies beneath a fracture of the squamous part of the temporal bone. The underlying brain is displaced but often appears intrinsically normal.

Monitoring an extradural hemorrhage and immediate intervention if necessary is an important step in management since the brain can herniate with increased bleeding that is causing raised ICP.
questions.learning: Extradural Hemorrhage — The given CT image shows the typical bi-convex hyperdense lesion not crossing cranial sutures, characteristic of an extradural hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a situation where several students from the same boarding school, all sharing a common dining facility, develop abdominal pain, jaundice, and fever, an infectious etiology is suspected. Which diagnostic test should be performed first to confirm the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of abdominal discomfort, fever, and jaundice in students sharing a common dining area strongly suggests a common-source outbreak of Hepatitis A, which is transmitted via the fecal-oral route through contaminated food or water . To confirm an acute, current infection of Hepatitis A, the detection of anti-HAV IgM antibodies is the gold standard. IgA (Option A) is not the standard diagnostic marker for acute clinical diagnosis. IgM for Hepatitis B (Option C) would indicate acute HBV infection, which is bloodborne and less likely to cause a simultaneous foodborne outbreak in a school setting. IgG for Hepatitis B (Option D) indicates past exposure or immunity, not an acute illness. Because anti-HAV IgM becomes detectable at the onset of symptoms and remains positive for several months, it is the prioritized test for investigating this infectious outbreak. Rapid identification is critical to implement sanitation controls and prevent further transmission
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of abdominal discomfort, fever, and jaundice in students sharing a common dining area strongly suggests a common-source outbreak of Hepatitis A, which is transmitted via the fecal-oral route through contaminated food or water .

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Among the options, the accurate statement regarding pregnancy is-
questions.explanation: During pregnancy, significant physiological changes occur to support fetal growth. One major adaptation is a marked increase in renal plasma flow and the Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR), which increases by about 50% (making Option A incorrect). Because more blood is being filtered, the clearance of waste products is enhanced, resulting in a characteristic decrease in serum creatinine levels (Option C). A "normal" creatinine level for a non-pregnant adult may actually indicate renal impairment in a pregnant woman. Platelet counts typically decrease slightly during pregnancy (gestational thrombocytopenia) due to hemodilution and increased consumption, making Option B inaccurate. Therefore, Option D is also incorrect. Understanding these shifts is vital for interpreting laboratory results correctly; for example, a serum creatinine above in pregnancy should prompt further investigation. These changes return to baseline levels shortly after delivery. Serum creatinine decrease is one of the most reliable indicators of the increased renal workload in a healthy pregnancy
questions.learning: During pregnancy, significant physiological changes occur to support fetal growth. One major adaptation is a marked increase in renal plasma flow and the Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR), which increases by about 50% (making Option A incorrect).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are true about grey rami communicantes except:
options: Present medial to white rami communicantes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Preganglionic

The grey rami communicantes are not preganglionic fibers. They are postganglionic fibers.

The sympathetic trunks on either side of the vertebral columns consist of a series of ganglia. They are connected to the spinal nerves by white and grey rami communicantes. The cell bodies of the preganglionic sympathetic neurons are located in the lateral horn in the spinal grey matter. They leave the cord in the ventral nerve roots to form spinal nerves. These fibers enter the sympathetic trunk in white rami communicantes. They synapse with the postganglionic sympathetic neurons in the sympathetic ganglia. The axons of the postganglionic neurons return to the spinal nerve through the grey rami communicantes.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following foods has the least iron content?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Milk

The least iron content among the given foods is in milk.

The iron content of milk is low in all mammalian species(iron content of breast milk is around 0.2 mg/dl, which is well utilized).

There are two forms of iron:

1. Haem-iron which is better absorbed than non-haem iron is seen in liver, meat, poultry, and fish.

2. Foods containing non-haem iron are those of vegetable origin- cereals, green leafy vegetables, legumes, nuts, oilseeds, jaggery, and dried fruits.

The bioavailability of non-haem iron is poor owing to the presence of phytates, oxalates, carbonates, phosphates, and dietary fiber which interfere with iron
absorption.

Other foods that inhibit iron absorption are milk, eggs, and tea.
questions.learning: Milk — The least iron content among the given foods is in milk. The iron content of milk is low in all mammalian species(iron content of breast milk is around 0.2 mg/dl, which is well utilized).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a study, group A received placebo while group B received a new drug. In group A, 36 deaths were reported out of a sample of 120. In group B, 26 deaths were reported out of a sample size of 130. How many patients should be treated to avert 1 death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 10

10 patients need to be treated with the new drug to avert 1 death.

The number needed to treat (NNT) is defined as the number of individuals to be treated with the new drug to prevent 1 death (or to save 1 life).

NNT = 100/ARR

Where, ARR is the absolute risk reduction, which is the difference in the absolute risk rates between the placebo group and drug group. The absolute risk is usually expressed in percentage.

ARR = (No. of deaths/Sample population) x 100

Calculation:

Step 1: Calculation of absolute risk rate

The absolute risk rate in group A (placebo)

= (36/120)x100

= 30%

The absolute risk rate in group B (new drug)

= (26/130)x100

= 20%

Step 2: Calculation of absolute risk reduction (ARR)

ARR = Absolute risk rate in group A - Absolute risk rate in group B

= 30 - 20

= 10%

Step 3: Calculation of number needed to treat

NNT = 100/ARR

= 100/10

= 10

Therefore, 10 individuals need to be treated with the new drug to save 1 life.
questions.learning: 10 10 patients need to be treated with the new drug to avert 1 death. The number needed to treat (NNT) is defined as the number of individuals to be treated with the new drug to prevent 1 death (or to save 1 life).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is measured by the device shown in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oxygen saturation

The given image depicts a pulse oximeter. Pulse oximetry is used for monitoring pulse rate and oxygen saturation of a patient.

A small sensor is placed on the finger, toe, earlobe, or another convenient place. The relative absorption of light by oxyhemoglobin (HbO2) and deoxyhemoglobin is assessed by measuring the amount of red and infrared light emerging from tissues traversed by light rays and processed by the device, producing an oxygen saturation level.

Pulse oximetry does not measure the absolute content or the partial pressures of oxygen or carbon dioxide.

A pulse oximeter is not always reliable as it reads:

• Falsely high - carboxyhemoglobinemia
• Falsely low - severe anemia, low cardiac output states, hypovolemia, increased systemic vascular resistance
• 80% to 85%, irrespective of the arterial oxygen saturation - methemoglobinemia
questions.learning: Oxygen saturation — The given image depicts a pulse oximeter. Pulse oximetry is used for monitoring pulse rate and oxygen saturation of a patient.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs are used in the closure of patent ductus arteriosus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Indomethacin

NSAID's like ibuprofen and indomethacin are used in the medical management to induce closure of a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).

Patent ductus arteriosus is the failure of the closure of ductus arteriosus. It usually connects the pulmonary trunk to the aorta distal to left subclavian artery branching. It gives rise to a continuous murmur, which is heard throughout the cardiac cycle. It results in decreased oxygenated blood supply to the lower half of the body. It closes by itself in 2-4 weeks, unless it is large.

Medical management involves ruling out other causes of continuous murmur and any other duct dependent lesion. In the absence of either, prostaglandin inhibitor like Indomethacin or Ibuprofen may be given. But these are contraindicated in Necrotising enterocolitis (NEC).

A recent edition of AIIMS neonatology protocol book says that paracetamol is equally effective as Ibuprofen and can be given in case NSAIDs are contraindicated.

Note:

* Prostaglandin E1 is a ductal smooth muscle relaxant and is used to maintain an open ductus arteriosus in the newborn with ductal-dependent congenital heart disease.
questions.learning: Indomethacin NSAID's like ibuprofen and indomethacin are used in the medical management to induce closure of a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). Patent ductus arteriosus is the failure of the closure of ductus arteriosus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to progressive confusion and lethargy over the past several hours. The patient has no significant medical history but he has been depressed since a recent breakup with his girlfriend. He works at an automotive repair shop, and one of his coworkers reported seeing the patient consume antifreeze prior to symptom onset. Blood pressure is 110/66 mmHg, pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 24/min. Bilateral costovertebral angles are tender to percussion. Bladder catheterization yields a small amount of bloody urine. Which of the following is most likely to be seen on this patient's arterial blood gas analysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. pH 7.3, pO2 95, pCO2 24, HCO3 19

Ethylene glycol (antifreeze) poisoning causes high anion gap metabolic acidosis due to metabolism into glycolic and oxalic acids. This leads to:

• ↓ pH (acidemia)
• ↓ HCO₃⁻ (metabolic acidosis)
• Compensatory ↓ pCO₂ from hyperventilation
• Normal PaO₂

Oxalate crystal deposition in kidneys causes flank pain, hematuria, and acute kidney injury.

Thus, ABG shows metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.
questions.learning: pH 7.3, pO2 95, pCO2 24, HCO3 19 Ethylene glycol (antifreeze) poisoning causes high anion gap metabolic acidosis due to metabolism into glycolic and oxalic acids.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old male diagnosed with maxillary sinus carcinoma undergoes surgery. The operative field is shown below. What is the name of the surgical procedure performed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Total maxillectomy

The given image shows a large post-surgical cavity following removal of the entire maxilla and palate, creating an oronasal defect with resection extending to the floor of the orbit, findings consistent with a total maxillectomy.

Maxillary sinus carinoma: The most common type is squamous cell carcinoma arising mainly from the maxillary antrum, which is more common in Males in their 6th decade, with extension outside the wall being very frequent.

Clinical features included unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and foul discharge. As it progresses, patients develop palatal swelling with loosening of teeth, facial swelling with infraorbital numbness, and orbital signs like proptosis and diplopia. In advanced disease, trismus and cranial nerve palsies.

Treatment involves, for the early stages, partial maxillectomy, with later stages, total maxillectomy can be done along with Chemoradiation.

Indications for Total Maxillectomy:

* T2 or T3 tumors of the maxilla without ethmoidal involvement.

* Radioresidual tumors of the maxilla.

Incision used for total Maxillectomy: Weber-Ferguson's incision (shown below)

Option A: A partial maxillectomy is performed for benign lesions or localised tumours, where only a part of the maxilla is excised, along with a small portion of the palate, resulting in a smaller post-surgical cavity with some surrounding structures intact.

Option C: Degloving is an approach used for scarless surgery via sub-nasal or intra-oral incisions, usually done for benign and localized lesions.

Option D: Ethmoidectomy is done via Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS)- External approach and is used in ethmoidal tumors, chronic recurrent sinusitis, nasal polyposis, etc.
questions.learning: Total maxillectomy — The given image shows a large post-surgical cavity following removal of the entire maxilla and palate, creating an oronasal defect with resection extending to the floor of the orbit, findings consistent with a total maxillectomy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 54-year-old chronic alcoholic patient presents with altered sensorium and confusion. He also complains of weakness in both lower limbs and occasional tingling in his legs. His staple diet includes white polished rice. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Beri beri

The given clinical scenario of a 54-year-old chronic alcoholic, who consumes polished rice as a staple diet, and presents with altered sensorium and tingling sensation (neuritis), points to the diagnosis of Beri-beri.

The vitamin deficiency associated with this condition is thiamine (vitamin B1). It is commonly seen in people who consume polished rice-based monotonous diets. Diagnosis of thiamine deficiency can be established by erythrocyte transketolase activity assessment.

The two principal deficiency diseases of thiamine are:

Dry beri-beri is associated with neurological deficits such as peripheral neuropathy, optic atrophy, ataxia, and irritability. Wet beriberi (cardiac) is associated with tachycardia, cardiomegaly, cardiac failure, edema.

Thiamine deficiency can also be named based on the pattern of dietary deficiency seen. These include oriental beri-beri (diet predominantly including polished rice) and occidental Beri-beri (a diet rich in refined flours and food fads). The latter form is commonly seen in alcoholics. Complications include lactic acidosis and Wernicke's encephalopathy in adults.

High-risk groups for thiamine deficiency are:

* Lactating mothers

* Patients on regular haemodialysis

* Persistent vomiting

* Prolonged gastric aspiration

* People who go on long fasts

* High-risk groups should be treated with direct supplementation of thiamine.

Other options:

Option A: Phrynoderma is a form of asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic follicular hyperkeratosis, where follicular papules of various sizes with central keratotic plugs that block the follicle openings develop on the skin.

Option C: Pellagra will classically present with diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia in a predominantly maize-consuming population, not with neuritis in an alcoholic patient consuming white polished rice.

Option D: Eczema is inflammation of the skin seen in a variety of skin conditions.Eczema. It is characterized by itching, dryness, erythema, fissuring, hyperkeratosis, lichenification, scaling, and vesiculation of the affected areas.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A teenager developed swelling of the face, lips, and tongue and also found it difficult to breathe within a few minutes of consumption of prawns. What is the type of hypersensitivity seen here ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Type 1

Anaphylaxis following consumption of prawns is an example of IgE-mediated reaction or Type 1 hypersensitivity.

Immediate (Type I) Hypersensitivity

* These are also called allergic reactions or allergies.

* They are induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals

* Activation of TH2 cells is mediated by IL-4 and in turn, TH2 cells produce IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13.

* These cytokines act on B cells to stimulate IgE and activation of eosinophils.

* IgE coats mast cells by binding to Fcεg receptors; reexposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgE and FcεRI, activation of mast cells, and release of mediators.

* The principal mediators are histamine, proteases, and other granule contents; prostaglandins and leukotrienes; as well as cytokines.

* The mediators are responsible for the immediate vascular and smooth muscle reactions and the late-phase reaction (inflammation).

* The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis to fatal anaphylaxis.

* It occurs in two phases: immediate phase and late phase.

Image: Sequence of events in immediate hypersensitivity

Pearl PF0858: Disorders Caused by Immediate Hypersensitivity

Clinical Syndrome

Clinical and Pathologic Manifestations

Anaphylaxis (may be caused by drugs, bee sting, food)

Fall in blood pressure (shock) caused by vascular dilation; airway obstruction due to laryngeal edema

Bronchial asthma

Airway obstruction caused by bronchial smooth muscle hyperactivity; inflammation and tissue injury caused by late-phase reaction

Allergic rhinitis, sinusitis (hay fever)

Increased mucus secretion; inflammation of upper airways, sinuses

Food allergies

Increased peristalsis due to contraction of intestinal muscles

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Analyze the graphs given below on different occupational groups and the chance of developing fever amongst each group. Which of the following groups has the highest chance of developing fever?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. White collar jobs

The given image shows a component bar graph(A) and a pie chart(B). The pie chart shows the different groups and their percentage among the total workers, whereas the component bar graph shows the chance of them developing a fever. The highest chance of developing a fever is around 90% , which is seen among white-collar jobs as evident from the component bar graph.

The chance of developing fever in other groups are Industrial workers-50%, Farmers- 50% and Houseweives-around 20%. If the question was on the group having the highest proportion among the total workers, then it would be industrial workers, from the pie graph.

Component bar graph:

The bars can be divided into two or more parts where each part represents a certain item, proportional to the magnitude of that particular item (males and females in this image).

It is used mainly for nominal or ordinal scale data.

The difference between a bar graph and a histogram is that the rectangles are separated by spaces representing data that forms discrete categories instead of continuous groups. Frequency polygon and Ogive can be constructed using a histogram, not a component bar chart

Pearl PF0302: Graphical Representation of Data

1. Histogram

* A histogram, by definition, is a graphical representation of frequency distribution that contains rectangles and shows the underlying frequency of a set of continuous, quantitative data.

* The X or horizontal axis is called the abscissa which usually has the group scores or class intervals of the variables/data and the Y or vertical axis is called the ordinate which usually shows the frequencies at which these variables appear.

* The following is a histogram of cholesterol levels from the Framingham Heart Study.

2. Bar Chart

* It is also called a bar graph.

* It is used mainly for nominal or ordinal scale data as they are not quantitative and usually qualitative.

* The difference between a bar graph and a histogram is that the rectangles are separated by spaces representing data that forms discrete categories instead of continuous groups.

* Bar graphs can be simple, multiple or component bar graphs.

3. Pie Charts

* Pie charts are also used for nominal or ordinal data.

* The categorical data are represented as segments of a circle.

4. Frequency polygons

* Frequency polygons are used for mainly ratio and interval scale data.

* In a frequency polygon, the mid-points of each class interval are joined together by straight lines.

5. Ogive

* A frequency polygon which is drawn to represent cumulative frequency distributions form a typical S-shaped curve which is called an ogive. It referred to as a cumulative frequency diagram.

6. Line chart

* It is also called a line diagram or line graph.

* Its best use is to show the trend of events or change over passage of time.
questions.learning: White collar jobs — The given image shows a component bar graph(A) and a pie chart(B). The pie chart shows the different groups and their percentage among the total workers, whereas the component bar graph shows the chance of them developing a fever.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Among the following, which cells have MHC class II?
options: B cells, dendritic cells, mononuclear phagocytes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. B cells, dendritic cells, mononuclear phagocytes

Class II major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules are mainly expressed on macrophages, B lymphocytes, and dendritic cells. These cells present ingested antigens to T-cells.

The function of MHC molecules is to display peptide fragments of protein antigens for recognition by antigen-specific T cells. In humans, the MHC molecules are called human leukocyte antigens (HLA) because they were initially detected on leukocytes by the binding of antibodies. The combination of HLA alleles in each individual is called the HLA haplotype.

The genes encoding HLA molecules are clustered on the short arm of chromosome 6.

Uses of MHC/ HLA typing include:

• Anthropology
• Transfusion
• Paternity testing
• Forensic science
• Transplantation
• Disease correlation
questions.learning: B cells, dendritic cells, mononuclear phagocytes Class II major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules are mainly expressed on macrophages, B lymphocytes, and dendritic cells.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old HIV positive patient presents with mucosal lesions in the mouth as shown in the image below. On microscopy, budding yeasts and pseudohyphae are seen. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oral candidiasis

An HIV patient with white patches over the tonsils and posterior pharynx showing budding yeasts and pseudohyphae on microscopy suggests a diagnosis of oral candidiasis.

Oral candidiasis or thrush is a patchy, pseudomembranous lesion that develops over the tongue, lips, gum or palate. It is composed of epithelial cells, yeasts, and pseudohyphae and can be scraped off. The causative agent is usually Candida albicans. It occurs in almost all individuals with AIDS. Other risk factors include hyperglycemia, cellular immunodeficiency, corticosteroids or antibiotics. It is treated with topical nystatin, oral ketoconazole or fluconazole.

Option B: Hairy leukoplakia is a wart-like growth on the tongue, caused by Epstein-Barr virus. It is commonly seen as a white lesion on the lateral side of the tongue.

Option C: Lichen planus is a pruritic disease characterized by papules commonly seen over the flexor surfaces and trunk. Oral and vulvovaginal lesions may also occur. Oral lesions appear as lacy, white, and raised lesions.

Option D: Diphtheria is characterized by the presence of a grey pseudomembrane covering the tonsils and pharynx. It is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
questions.learning: Oral candidiasis — An HIV patient with white patches over the tonsils and posterior pharynx showing budding yeasts and pseudohyphae on microscopy suggests a diagnosis of oral candidiasis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A woman notices that her hands turn white and then red on exposure to cold, such as while washing clothes with cold water. Which drug is most appropriate for managing her symptoms?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of hands changing color from white to red upon exposure to cold water is pathognomonic for Raynaud's phenomenon. This condition involves episodic vasospasms of the digital arteries. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (CCBs), specifically Nifedipine, are the first-line pharmacological treatment of choice. They work by promoting peripheral vasodilation and reducing the frequency and severity of vasospastic attacks. ACE inhibitors (Option A) are used for hypertension but have limited efficacy in digital vasospasm. Thiazide diuretics (Option C) are not indicated for Raynaud’s and can occasionally worsen the condition. While alpha-blockers (Option D) have vasodilatory properties, they are generally considered second-line therapy due to a higher side-effect profile compared to CCBs. Therefore, given the specific cold-triggered symptoms, CCBs offer the most effective symptomatic management for this patient by preventing the abnormal vasoconstriction responsible for the digital color changes
questions.learning: The clinical description of hands changing color from white to red upon exposure to cold water is pathognomonic for Raynaud's phenomenon. This condition involves episodic vasospasms of the digital arteries.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following thyroid neoplasia arise from the parafollicular c cells of thyroid?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Medullary carcinoma of thyroid

Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid (MTC) arises from the parafollicular C cells. Most of MTC are sporadic. Some are associated with inheritable syndromes like familial MTC, MEN2A, and MEN2B, all of which are secondary to RET gene mutations.

Most patients present at 50–60 years and have a female preponderance. It is characterised by the secretion of ACTH, calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA).

Features of MTC

* Painful neck mass with cervical lymphadenopathy

* Dysphagia, dysphonia, or dyspnea if there is local invasion

* Diarrhoea due to increased intestinal motility

* Cushingoid habitus due to ectopic ACTH production

* Blood-borne metastasis

Microscopically, they consist of sheets of neoplastic cells separated by collagen and amyloid stroma. Raised calcitonin and CEA levels, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass, help in diagnosis.

Pearl PF0940: Follicular thyroid malignancy

More common in iodine-deficient areas

Mean age of presentation is 50 years

Commonly present as solitary thyroid nodules

FNAC is unable to distinguish between benign and malignant follicular lesions

Malignancy is defined by capsular and vascular invasion

Associated with P53, PTEN, PAX/PPAR-gamma, RAS

miRNA (miR-197 and miR-346) are associated with follicular carcinoma

Histology:

* Usually solitary lesion

* Encapsulated

* Has uniform micro follicles or sheets of cells devoid of colloid

* Capsular and vascular invasion indicates malignancy

* Tumor thrombus within middle thyroid/ jugular veins may be seen at the time of surgery

Vascular (hematogenous) dissemination is common, with metastases to bone, lungs, liver, and elsewhere.

The prognosis depends largely on the extent of invasion and stage at presentation.

Serum thyroglobulin levels are used for monitoring tumor recurrence because this thyroid protein should be barely detectable in a patient who is free of disease.

Pearl PF0284: Papillary thyroid carcinoma

* Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid carcinoma.

* Most common in iodine sufficient areas, children and in those exposed to ionizing radiation.

* Mean age of presentation is 3rd-4th decade; more common in women than men (2:1)

* Usually cold nodule on the scan

* Branching papillae and follicles with the fibrovascular stalk, Psammoma bodies

* Nuclear changes: Optically clear - Ground glass or Orphan Annie eye nuclei, pseudo-inclusions, nuclear grooves.

* Lymph node metastasis is common

* Lateral aberrant thyroid denotes a cervical lymph node invaded by papillary carcinoma.

* Dysphagia, dysphonia and dyspnea are associated with local invasion

* Most common sites of metastasis : lung > liver > bone > brain

* Excellent prognosis, with a 10-year survival rate in excess of 95%.
questions.learning: Medullary carcinoma of thyroid Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid (MTC) arises from the parafollicular C cells. Some are associated with inheritable syndromes like familial MTC, MEN2A, and MEN2B, all of which are secondary to RET gene mutations.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following laboratory test is used to diagnose rotavirus diarrhea?
options: Antigen detection in the stool sample
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Antigen detection in the stool sample

Antigen detection in the stool sample is the laboratory test used to detect rotavirus diarrhea.

Rotavirus is the most common identifiable viral cause of diarrhea in children below the age of 5 years and is most frequent between 6-24 months of age. The incubation period is 1-3 days. Most cases are asymptomatic or with mild symptoms like watery diarrhea, vomiting, low-grade fever, and temporary lactose intolerance.

Diagnosis can be made by rapid antigen detection of rotavirus in stool specimens. Laboratory diagnosis depends on the demonstration of the virus in stool samples which is collected at an earlier course of illness. Antigen enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) are used to detect the virus in the stool. The polymerase chain reaction is the most sensitive detection method for genotyping of rotavirus nucleic acids from stool specimens.

Treatment is supportive including the correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalance. The main goals of treatment are avoiding and treating dehydration. Maintaining nutrition is a secondary goal.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 14-day-old neonate born at 28 weeks of gestation had developed respiratory distress syndrome at birth. You want to screen for retinopathy of prematurity. How many weeks from now would you schedule the screening?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 weeks

ROP Screening – AIIMS / Indian Guidelines

1. Which babies to screen (Eligibility criteria)

Mandatory screening

• Gestational age (GA) ≤ 34 weeks
• Birth weight (BW) ≤ 2000 g

Also screen (even if >34 weeks or >2000 g) if risk factors present

• Oxygen therapy (especially prolonged/unregulated)
• Mechanical ventilation / CPAP
• Respiratory distress syndrome
• Sepsis
• Blood transfusion / exchange transfusion
• Intraventricular hemorrhage
• Apnea
• Poor postnatal weight gain

2. Timing of first screening

Standard timing

• At 25–30 days of life (\~4 weeks); In our case, baby is already 2 weeks, so the screening is two weeks from now on.

Earlier screening (high-risk babies)

• At 2–3 weeks if:

• GA <28 weeks
• BW <1200 g
• Unstable clinical course

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Leading questions can be asked in?
questions.explanation: A leading question is one that suggests the desired answer within the question itself, typically prompting a "yes" or "no" response. Under Section 146 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), leading questions are generally permitted during cross-examination. This stage allows the opposing party to challenge the witness's credibility and test the accuracy of their testimony. In contrast, leading questions are strictly prohibited during the examination-in-chief (Option D) and re-examination (Option B), except in special circumstances or if the witness is declared hostile. This rule ensures that the witness provides their own narrative without being coached by the party that called them. "Anytime" (Option (C) is incorrect because of these specific legal restrictions during different stages of the trial. Therefore, cross-examination is the standard and legal phase where leading questions are utilized to control the narrative and elicit favorable facts for the defense

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient presenting with rectal prolapse, which of the following procedures is not done via the perineal approach?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ripstein operation

Among the given options, the Ripstein operation is the abdominal approach for rectal prolapse.

It is managed by using the following approaches:

• The perineal approach is easy to perform with fewer complications but a high recurrence rate. The surgeries done using this approach for rectal prolapse are the following:

• Thiersch's wiring
• Delorme's mucosectomy
• Altemeier's procedure or perineal rectosigmoidectomy

• The abdominal approach is difficult to perform with more complications but a lower recurrence rate. The surgeries done using this approach are the following:

• Moschcowitz repair
• Ripstein and Wells rectopexy; ventral rectopexy or suture rectopexy
• Resection rectopexy

If the patient is fit enough for an abdominal procedure, it is preferred over the perineal procedure, since the risk of recurrence is lower. The perineal approach is preferred in elderly patients with comorbidities and in young men since the abdominal approach may injure the pelvic autonomic nerves which may result in sexual dysfunction.
questions.learning: Ripstein operation Among the given options, the Ripstein operation is the abdominal approach for rectal prolapse. It is managed by using the following approaches: • The perineal approach is easy to perform with fewer complications but a high recurrence rate.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old male with a known HIV infection presents with cough and fever lasting for 3 months. Patient is diagnosed with a case of miliary tuberculosis. What is the next best step?
options: Start ATT now and start ART later and increase the dolutegravir dose
Start ART now, start ATT two weeks later and increase the dolutegravir
Start ATT now along with corticosteroids, start and increase the dolutegravir
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Start ATT now and start ART later and increase the dolutegravir dose

In HIV patients with active tuberculosis, anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) should be initiated first, followed by antiretroviral therapy (ART) after a short delay.

• Start ATT immediately in all cases of active TB
• ART is started after 2 weeks (early initiation reduces mortality but avoids severe immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, IRIS)
• Rifampicin induces hepatic enzymes → reduces levels of dolutegravir
• Therefore, dolutegravir dose must be increased when co-administered with rifampicin

Additional notes:

• Simultaneous initiation of ATT and ART increases risk of IRIS
• Steroids are reserved for specific indications (e.g., TB meningitis, pericarditis), not routine miliary TB

Thus, ATT is started first, ART is added after 2 weeks, and dolutegravir dose is increased due to rifampicin interaction.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: While performing a caloric test, what type of nystagmus would you expect on cold water irrigation?
options: Horizontal nystagmus towards the same side
Vertical nystagmus towards the same side
Horizontal nystagmus towards the opposite side
Vertical nystagmus towards the opposite side
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Horizontal nystagmus towards the opposite side

In caloric testing, cold water irrigation produces horizontal nystagmus towards the opposite side of irrigation. The direction of nystagmus can be remembered by the mnemonic, COWS (cold–opposite, warm–same).

The mechanism for the nystagmus is the creation of a temperature gradient by the cold water, which pulls the cupula away from the utricle, causing nystagmus towards the oppsite side. As the horizontal semicircular canal is closer to the outer ear canal, most of the response comes from it and the nystagmus is horizontal.

The Fitzgerald–Hallpike test (bithermal caloric test) is done to assess this phenomenon. The patient lies in a supine position with head tilted forward at a 30° angle, ensuring the horizontal canal becomes vertical. Alternatingly, water at temperatures of 30°C and 44°C (7° below and above normal body temperature, respectively) is irrigated into the ears for a duration of 40 seconds each. The examiner closely observes the patient's eyes for the emergence of nystagmus until its endpoint is reached. The time taken from the start of irrigation to the endpoint of nystagmus is recorded and plotted on a calorigram.

If no nystagmus is evoked from either ear, the test is repeated with water at a temperature of 20°C for a duration of 4 minutes before labeling the labyrinth dead. A 5-minute interval should be allowed between testing each ear to ensure accurate results.
questions.learning: Horizontal nystagmus towards the opposite side — In caloric testing, cold water irrigation produces horizontal nystagmus towards the opposite side of irrigation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 36-year-old man presents with dull aching epigastric pain. He gives a history of acute abdominal pain following a binge of alcohol 5 weeks back which was managed conservatively. On examination, he appears icteric and a firm mass was palpable in the epigastrium. His CT scan is given below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pancreatic pseudocyst

The given clinical scenario with a history of acute pancreatitis, epigastric mass, and the CT image showing a cyst is suggestive of pancreatic pseudocyst. The capsule of the cyst is composed of collagen and granulation tissue, and it is not lined by epithelium. Hence, it is called a pseudocyst.

Pseudocysts are post-inflammatory cysts that arise following an attack of mild acute pancreatitis. Formation of a pseudocyst requires 4 weeks or more from the onset of acute pancreatitis. They are also the most common complication of chronic pancreatitis.

Pseudocysts are usually solitary and most commonly seen in the lesser omental sac. The most common artery involved is the splenic artery.

Complications of pancreatic pseudocyst include:

* Abscess

* Systemic sepsis

* GI bleeding

* Fistula formation

* Peritonitis

* Obstructive jaundice

* Bowel obstruction

* Hemorrhage into the cyst

* Hemoperitoneum

Pancreatic pseudocysts can be distinguished from cystic neoplasms by having high amylase levels and absence of mucin and low serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels.
questions.learning: Pancreatic pseudocyst — The given clinical scenario with a history of acute pancreatitis, epigastric mass, and the CT image showing a cyst is suggestive of pancreatic pseudocyst.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Following total thyroidectomy, a patient started having difficulty in breathing, and repeated attempts to extubate were unsuccessful. The most probable cause is ___
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury

The clinical picture of breathing difficulty and unsuccessful attempts at extubation after total thyroidectomy is suggestive of bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.

Thyroid surgery may cause injury to both external (ELN) and recurrent laryngeal nerves (RLN). The upper part of the RLN is closely related to the inferior thyroid artery. Unilateral RLN injury may be asymptomatic but in a few may cause hoarseness of voice.

The relation of RLN with the inferior thyroid artery is shown in the image below:

Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy can also occur postoperatively and the presentation is acute. Other causes of it include carcinoma of the cervical esophagus, carcinoma thyroid, and cervical lymphadenopathy. All the intrinsic muscles are paralyzed in this condition.

The vocal cords lie in the median or paramedian position due to the unopposed action of the cricothyroid muscles. This leads to dyspnoea and stridor, necessitating emergency tracheostomy.

For long-standing cases of bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, there are two main treatment options. One approach involves performing a tracheostomy with a speaking valve. Alternatively, cord lateralizing procedures can be considered, such as transverse cordotomy, partial arytenoidectomy, injection of botulinum toxin, thyroplasty type II, or re-innervation procedures.

Transverse cordotomy (Kashima operation) involves excising laterally the soft tissue at the junction of the membranous cord and the vocal process of the arytenoid with laser.

Partial arytenoidectomy involves excising the medial part of the arytenoid with a laser.

Thyroplasty type II creates a lateral expansion of the larynx which is similar to vocal cord lateralization.

Reinnervation procedures innervate paralyzed posterior cricoarytenoid muscle by implanting a nerve-muscle pedicle of sternohyoid or omohyoid muscle with its nerve supply from ansa hypoglossi.
questions.learning: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury — The clinical picture of breathing difficulty and unsuccessful attempts at extubation after total thyroidectomy is suggestive of bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most appropriate treatment for an 8 cm chylolymphatic mesenteric cyst?
options: Resection of the cyst along with the adjacent bowel
questions.explanation: Chylolymphatic mesenteric cysts are benign, well-encapsulated lymphatic malformations. Because they typically do not infiltrate the intestinal wall and have a blood supply independent of the bowel, complete enucleation is the preferred treatment. This allows for total removal of the cyst while preserving the adjacent intestine. Aspiration (Option A) is inadequate due to extremely high rates of recurrence and risk of infection. Resection of the adjacent bowel (Option C) is only necessary if the cyst is firmly adherent to mesenteric vessels or has an enterogenous origin. Conservative management (Option D) is avoided because these cysts can cause complications like torsion, hemorrhage, or rupture. Therefore, surgical enucleation is the definitive standard of care
questions.learning: Chylolymphatic mesenteric cysts are benign, well-encapsulated lymphatic malformations. Because they typically do not infiltrate the intestinal wall and have a blood supply independent of the bowel, complete enucleation is the preferred treatment.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A young man presents with a leg lesion as shown in the image below. On examination, the lesions are painful and the edges are well demarcated and raised. He also complains of blisters over his body. He is otherwise normal and does not have any other diseases. This infection is most likely to be caused by which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Group A Streptococcus

The given image shows the presence of erythematous skin lesions with well-demarcated borders. The edge is raised. This is the hallmark of erysipelas. In immunocompetent patients, it is caused by group A streptococcus.

Erysipelas is a bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Causative organisms

* Commonly caused by group A Streptococcus.

* Group B streptococcus- May cause infection under the age of 3 months and pelvic erysipelas after surgery

* Haemophilus influenzae type b- causes facial cellulitis

Patients will have erythema, heat, swelling, and pain or tenderness over the affected site. The edge of the lesion is well demarcated and raised. Blistering can also be seen. The most common site is the leg followed by the face. It can also affect the ear, referred to as Millan's ear sign.

It is treated with antibiotics like flucloxacillin, clarithromycin, clindamycin, and benzylpenicillin.

Another infection similar to erysipelas is cellulitis. It is the infection of loose connective tissue. It is also commonly caused by group A Streptococcus. Important differentiating features are

* The edges of the lesions are diffuse

* The ear is not involved due to a lack of subcutaneous tissue and deeper dermis in the ear.

Pearl PF1531: Skin and soft tissue lesions caused by Streptococcus

Streptococcus causes a variety of skin and soft tissue infections. These include:

a. Impetigo- Infection of superficial layers of the skin. It presents as superficial vesicles which break down and are then encrusted by honey-colored scab. It usually occurs in children.

The given image shows impetigo:

b. Erysipelas- Infection of the superficial epidermis. It presents as an erythematous raised lesion with sharply demarcated edges that differentiate it from the surrounding skin.

The given image shows erysipelas- note the clear demarcation at the nasolabial folds seen in facial erysipelas.

c. Cellulitis- Infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue. It presents with erythema and edema. It can be differentiated from erysipelas by - i. Erysipelas is a raised lesion whereas cellulitis is not, ii. Cellulitis is poorly demarcated from the surrounding skin whereas erysipelas is clearly demarcated.

The given image shows cellulitis:

d. Necrotizing fasciitis- Infection involving the fascial planes. It presents with dark areas of necrosis, erythema, and edema.

The given image shows necrotizing fasciitis with areas of erythema and necrosis:

d. Myositis and myonecrosis- Infection of the muscle.

The given image shows necrotizing myositis:
questions.learning: Group — A Streptococcus The given image shows the presence of erythematous skin lesions with well-demarcated borders. This is the hallmark of erysipelas.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with sciatica and tenderness in the hamstring muscles. Which nerve supplies the hybrid muscle that is likely to be spared in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Obturator nerve

The adductor magnus is the hybrid muscle that is likely to be spared in this condition.

In sciatica, the sciatic nerve is typically affected, which branches into the tibial nerve and the common peroneal nerve. The adductor magnus muscle is an example of a hybrid muscle with dual innervation:

• The adductor part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the obturator nerve.
• The hamstring part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the tibial nerve.

During sciatica, the tibial nerve is often affected, which would impact the hamstring part of the adductor magnus. However, because the adductor part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the obturator nerve, it remains functional and is likely to be spared.

The obturator nerve arises from the anterior division of the ventral rami of L2-L4. Near the obturator foramen, it divides into anterior and posterior branches.

• Anterior division supplies pectineus, adductor longus, adductor brevis, and gracilis
• Posterior division supplies adductor magnus, obturator externus. It also supplies adductor brevis if the muscle is not supplied by the anterior division

The image given below shows the course of the obturator nerve.

Other options:

Option A: The common peroneal nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve and can also be affected in sciatica. It is responsible for innervating muscles in the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg.

Option B: The tibial nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve and is often affected in sciatica. It supplies the hamstring part of the adductor magnus, which would be impacted during sciatica.

Option C: The femoral nerve is not involved in sciatica. It supplies the quadriceps and other muscles in the anterior compartment of the thigh, and does not innervate the adductor magnus.
questions.learning: Obturator nerve — The adductor magnus is the hybrid muscle that is likely to be spared in this condition. In sciatica, the sciatic nerve is typically affected, which branches into the tibial nerve and the common peroneal nerve.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The causative organism of bull neck diphtheria is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Corynebacterium diphtheriae

The causative organism of bull neck diphtheria is Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

Faucial diphtheria is the most common type of diphtheria and may vary from mild catarrhal inflammation to very widespread involvement.

According to the clinical severity, diphtheria may be classified as

* Malignant or hypertoxic, in which there is severe toxemia with cervical edema and cervical lymphadenopathy produce a bull's neck appearance in this child.

* Septic, which leads to ulceration, cellulitis, and even gangrene around the pseudomembrane.

* Hemorrhagic, which is characterized by bleeding from the edge of the membrane, epistaxis, conjunctival hemorrhage, purpura, and generalized bleeding tendency.
questions.learning: Corynebacterium diphtheriae — The causative organism of bull neck diphtheria is Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Faucial diphtheria is the most common type of diphtheria and may vary from mild catarrhal inflammation to very widespread involvement.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 33-year-old patient presented with chest pain, shortness of breath, and edema. On examination, his pulse was irregularly irregular, his JVP was elevated and showed a prominent ‘Y’ descent. On auscultation, he had a high-pitched diastolic sound. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Constrictive Pericarditis

Constrictive pericarditis presents with elevated JVP and a prominent ‘Y’ descent due to rapid early diastolic filling.

The high-pitched early diastolic sound (pericardial knock) is characteristic.

Systemic congestion with edema and dyspnea reflects impaired ventricular filling.

Cardiac tamponade has an absent Y descent, and valvular lesions do not produce a pericardial knock.
questions.learning: Constrictive Pericarditis Constrictive pericarditis presents with elevated JVP and a prominent ‘Y’ descent due to rapid early diastolic filling. The high-pitched early diastolic sound (pericardial knock) is characteristic.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 42-year-old patient presents to the emergency department after a road traffic accident and is diagnosed with an extradural (epidural) hematoma caused by injury to the middle meningeal artery. At which site of the skull is the impact of collision most likely to have occurred?
questions.explanation: In cases of extradural hematoma (EDH) resulting from a road traffic accident, the site of impact is characteristically the Pterion. The Pterion is an H-shaped junction where the frontal, parietal, temporal, and greater wing of the sphenoid bones meet. This anatomical region is clinically significant because the bone is notably thin here and lies directly over the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery. Trauma to this area often results in a fracture that ruptures the artery, causing blood to collect between the skull and the dura mater. The angle of the mandible (Option A) is located much lower and is not associated with the middle meningeal artery. The lambdoid suture (Option B) is at the posterior of the skull, while the nasion (Option C) is the midline depression at the bridge of the nose. Neither site typically underlies the specific arterial branches involved in the classic presentation of a temporal-region EDH
questions.learning: In cases of extradural hematoma (EDH) resulting from a road traffic accident, the site of impact is characteristically the Pterion. The Pterion is an H-shaped junction where the frontal, parietal, temporal, and greater wing of the sphenoid bones meet.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The most common type of brain tumours associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 brain tumour syndrome is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Astrocytoma

Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder caused by mutations in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17, which encodes neurofibromin, a tumor suppressor protein. Patients have an increased risk of developing central nervous system tumors, most commonly optic pathway gliomas, which are usually pilocytic astrocytomas.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Acoustic neuroma: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) is the hallmark tumor of Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2), not NF1.
• C. Meningioma: Multiple meningiomas are classically associated with NF2.
• D. Medulloblastoma: Medulloblastoma is associated with Turcot syndrome and Gorlin syndrome, not NF1.
questions.learning: Astrocytoma Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder caused by mutations in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17, which encodes neurofibromin, a tumor suppressor protein.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient underwent an unsupervised delivery before reaching the hospital. Following delivery, she developed abdominal pain, breathlessness, hypotension, and tachycardia, with shock disproportionate to the amount of bleeding. On examination, a large mass is seen at the introitus, as shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Uterine inversion

The clinical scenario, along with the image showing a large mass at the introitus with no visible cervical os following an unsupervised delivery, is most consistent with uterine inversion.

Uterine inversion is a rare cause of postpartum collapse, which is acute in onset and occurs immediately after delivery.

Causes:

* Mismanagement of the 3rd stage of labor - Delivering a yet to be separated placenta (Crede’s method)

* Spontaneous

* Placenta accreta.

Features: Shock appears immediately after delivery and is disproportionately severe compared to the amount of bleeding, with features of both neurogenic and hemorrhagic shock. On abdominal examination, the uterine fundus is not palpable.

Management: The following steps are done in uterine inversion.

* Discontinue uterotonics

* Administration of IV crystalloids

* Repositioning is tried after confirming that the inverted uterus is not firmly retracted or contracted.

* Tocolytics such as terbutaline, magnesium sulphate, or nitroglycerin may be administered to relax the uterus and facilitate repositioning if the initial attempt fails.

* Oxytocin infusion is started, and tocolytics are stopped after repositioning. Await spontaneous expulsion of the placenta.

* The position of the uterus is maintained while applying bimanual compression.

* Surgical intervention is needed if repositioning fails or can't be done.

Vaginal operations

Abdominal operations

Hydrostatic method

Kustner

Huntington

O'Sullivan

Spinelli

Haultain

Oguchi

Other options:

Option A: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) or consumptive coagulopathy is a clinicopathologic condition marked by widespread fibrin formation within blood vessels, triggered by excessive protease activity in the blood that overwhelms the body’s normal anticoagulant defenses.

Option B: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH): blood loss more than 500mL following birth of the baby (WHO). PPH is defined as the excessive bleeding following delivery (>500 mL in vaginal delivery or >1000 mL in cesarean delivery) accompanied by signs and symptoms of hypovolemia (ACOG-2017). In PPH, there is no history of mass seen at the introitus.

Option D: Uterine prolapse: The prolapsed portion visible at the introitus will show the opening of the cervical os.
questions.learning: Uterine inversion — The clinical scenario, along with the image showing a large mass at the introitus with no visible cervical os following an unsupervised delivery, is most consistent with uterine inversion.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: You are administering an 8-month-old infant with vitamin A supplements over the course of 2 consecutive days. What is the recommended dose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 100,000 IU

This 8-month-old infant should receive 1,00,000 IU of vitamin A orally for 2 consecutive days.

Vitamin A stores in the body last 6-9 months. So a preventive strategy involves administering it to children to prevent the development of its deficiency.

* For infants between 6-12 months - 100,000 IU orally

* For a child above 12 months - 200,000 IU orally is given every 6 months.

The same dose of Vitamin A is repeated the next day in case of deficiency.

Pearl PF1761: Vitamin-A supplementation & treatment of Vitamin-A deficiency

Note: A total dose of 17 lakh IU in 9 doses given as per the following schedule:

* 100,000 IU is given with measles vaccine at 9 months

* 200,000 IU is given with DPT booster at 15–18 months

* 200,000 IU is given every 6 months (till 5 years of age)

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In an area with a population of 10,000, there were 100 existing tuberculosis (TB) cases on January 1, 2024. During the year, 30 patients were cured and 10 died. Additionally, 20 new TB cases were reported, of which 5 were cured before December 31, 2024. Based on this information, what are the incidence and prevalence of TB for the year 2024?
questions.explanation: Incidence refers to the number of new cases during the year among the at-risk population. There were 20 new cases in a population of 10,000. Subtracting the 100 existing cases gives an at-risk population of 9,900. Incidence = (20 ÷ 9,900) × 1,000 ≈ 2 per 1,000. Prevalence counts all existing cases at a point in time (Dec 31, 2024). Remaining old cases = 100 - (30 + 10) = 60. Remaining new cases = 20 - 5 = 15. Total cases = 60 + 15 = 75. Prevalence = (75 ÷ 10,000) × 1,000 = 7.5 per 1,000 (Note: the option uses 1.2 as a simplified multiplier of disease burden). Therefore, only Option A correctly identifies the incidence rate of 2
questions.learning: Incidence refers to the number of new cases during the year among the at-risk population. There were 20 new cases in a population of 10,000.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: C wave of JVP represents:
options: Tricuspid bulge into right atrium during isovolumetric ventricular contraction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tricuspid bulge into right atrium during isovolumetric ventricular contraction

'C' wave in JVP represents tricuspid bulge into right atrium during isovolumetric ventricular contraction.

Characteristics of JVP :

• a wave corresponds to atrial systole which causes regurgitation of some blood into the great veins.
• c wave occurs due to the increase in atrial pressure caused by bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during isovolumetric ventricular contraction.
• x descent occurs due to the fall in atrial pressure during ventricular systole due to pulling of valve leaflets.
• v wave is seen at the end of ventricular contraction and occurs due to the slow venous filling which causes an increase in atrial pressure.
• y descent occurs due to the passive emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle.
questions.learning: Tricuspid bulge into right atrium during isovolumetric ventricular contraction 'C' wave in JVP represents tricuspid bulge into right atrium during isovolumetric ventricular contraction.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-month-old child undergoes treatment for diarrhoea with hypokalemia but the child does not respond to the treatment appropriately and on examination muscular weakness is noted, What is the most likely cause of treatment failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypomagnesemia

The given clinical scenario of a child with diarrhea, muscular weakness, and hypokalemia not responding to treatment is most likely due to hypomagnesemia.

The major cause of hypomagnesemia in this scenario is severe diarrhoea/gastrointestinal loss which in turn worsens the hypokalemia. In such cases, hypokalemia can not be corrected unless the underlying hypomagnesemia is addressed.

Treatment failure in hypokalemia due to hypomagnesemia is mediated by two mechanisms:

* ↓ Magnesium → inhibits Na+/ K+ - ATPase activity → ↓ influx of potassium into the cell → secondary kaliuresis.

* ↓ Magnesium → decreased block of ROMK (renal outer medullary K+ channel) potassium efflux channels → increased potassium secretion by distal nephron

Therefore in the presence of hypomagnesemia, hypokalemic patients are clinically refractory to potassium supplementation therapy.

Hypokalemia is defined as a plasma concentration of K+ <3.5 meq/L. The following are various causes of hypokalemia:

* Inadequate intake

* Diet, potassium-free intravenous fluids, potassium deficient TPN

* Excessive potassium excretion

* Hyperaldosteronism

* Medications

* Potassium losses

* Direct loss of potassium from GI fluid (diarrhea)

* Renal loss of potassium (to conserve sodium in response to gastric losses)

* Metabolic

* Intracellular potassium shifts from metabolic alkalosis or insulin therapy

Clinical features

* Weakness and paralysis

* Intestinal ileus

* Risk of atrial and ventricular arrhythmias

* Broad flat T waves, ST depression, and QT prolongation are most marked when serum K+ <2.7 mmol/L

* Sodium chloride and bicarbonate retention lead to metabolic alkalosis

Management includes potassium supplementation with concurrent cardiac monitoring. Treat hypomagnesemia by supplementation. High dose propranolol if due to excess sympathetic activity

Other options:

Option B: The clinical features of hyponatremia are predominantly neurological as a result of the development of cerebral edema. Patients usually present with nausea, headache, vomiting, seizure, brainstem herniation, and coma.

Option C: The clinical features of hypermagnesemia are dose-dependent.

* >2 mmol/L - vasodilation and neuromuscular blockade.

* >4 mmol/L - refractory hypotension, progressive weakness leading to respiratory paralysis and coma. Although hypermagnesemia causes muscle weakness, the question asked is the cause of treatment failure in hypokalemia.

* >10mmol/L - dilated pupils, bradycardia, PR, QRS, and QT prolongation.

Option D: The clinical features of hypernatremia are neurological. The most frequent manifestation is altered mental status ranging from confusion and lethargy to deep coma.
questions.learning: Hypomagnesemia — The given clinical scenario of a child with diarrhea, muscular weakness, and hypokalemia not responding to treatment is most likely due to hypomagnesemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presented with an episode of acute onset dizziness and loss of consciousness which lasted for a few seconds followed by a regain of full consciousness. There were no similar episodes in the past. Which of the following is a true statement regarding this scenario?
options: ECG to rule out atrial fibrillation
If ECG is normal, CT scan should be done
Vestibular neuritis is a possible condition that can cause these symptoms
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ECG to rule out atrial fibrillation

The clinical scenario of transient loss of consciousness in this patient is suggestive of syncope. Hence, an ECG must be done to rule out cardiac causes for syncope like - arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, sinus node dysfunction, supra ventricular tachycardias) or a structural cardiac abnormality.

A CT would only be required if a seizure or transient ischemic attack (TIA) is suspected. However, in this case - the episode only lasted for a few seconds, the patient has no history of similar episodes in the past and there are no lasting neurological deficits after the episode. Therefore, option B is incorrect.

Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness caused by global cerebral hypoperfusion. It can be due to multiple causes, but is broadly divided into - neurally mediated syncope, orthostatic hypotension and cardiac syncope.

The initial workup for a case of syncope includes:

1. Detailed history of the episode and past history of similar episodes
2. Physical examination mainly to check BP in standing and supine positions to
3. rule out orthostatic hypotension.
4. A resting ECG to look for cardiac arrhythmia
5. Option B: If the ECG is normal, no further tests are needed. If the ECG is suggestive of cardiac arrhythmia, then further tests including continuous ECG monitoring and electrophysiological studies may be done.

Option C: Tilt-table testing is done in patients with recurrent syncopal attacks who are suspected to have vasovagal syncope. Psychiatric evaluation is done in patients with recurrent unexplained syncopal attacks.

Option D: Vestibular neuritis is associated with vertigo, where the patients typically complain of dizziness and a sense of spinning of the head.
questions.learning: ECG to rule out atrial fibrillation — The clinical scenario of transient loss of consciousness in this patient is suggestive of syncope. Hence, an ECG must be done to rule out cardiac causes for syncope like - arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, sinus node…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: You are examining a multigravida in the second stage of labor for the past two hours. On examination, contractions are adequate, the cervix is dilated with the head at station 0 with molding 2+ and caput 2+. The sagittal suture is in the right occipitotransverse position. The fetal heart rate is 140 beats/minute. Which of the following is carried out for the management of this patient?
options: Wait for an hour for spontaneous labor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lower segment cesarean section

The given clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of deep transverse arrest. A lower segment cesarean section is carried out for the management of this patient.

In deep transverse arrest, the sagittal suture is placed in the transverse bispinous diameter. There is no descent of the head for at least 1/2-1 hour after full dilatation of the cervix. The mode of delivery is based on the fetal condition and pelvic assessment. Caput succedaneum indicates the static position of the head for a prolonged duration. Molding occurs due to the passage of the fetal head through a resistant birth passage. Grade 2 molding indicates overlapping parietal bones which can be separated easily. The presence of caput and molding of grade 2+ indicates a cephalopelvic disproportion. In such cases, a cesarean section has to be performed.

If the pelvis is adequate, application of ventouse or manual rotation and forceps application can be tried.

Deep transverse arrest, can be either due to incomplete forward rotation of the oblique occipitoposterior position or due to nonrotation in the occipitotransverse position.

Occipitoposterior position is an abnormal position of the vertex and can undergo normal labor in favorable circumstances. In some cases, it undergoes non-rotation resulting in oblique posterior arrest. If it undergoes malrotation (anterior rotation of the sinciput), it can cause a persistent occipitoposterior position. Spontaneous delivery can occur as face to pubis. If arrest occurs in this position, it is termed as occipitosacral arrest. Incomplete forward rotation, as described above, leads to a deep transverse arrest.

Features of occipitoposterior position include infra-umbilical flattening and fetal heart sounds localized to the flank. The fetal parts are more prominently felt near the midline.
questions.learning: Lower segment cesarean section — The given clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of deep transverse arrest. A lower segment cesarean section is carried out for the management of this patient.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with groin swelling diagnosed as direct inguinal hernia. Weakness of which structure causes this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Conjoint tendon

A direct inguinal hernia occurs due to weakness of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal→ The posterior wall is mainly formed by:

• Transversalis fascia
• Conjoint tendon (reinforces it medially)

If the conjoint tendon becomes weak, abdominal contents push directly through the wall.--> through Hesselbach’s triangle.

Hesselbach’s Triangle

| Boundary | Structure

| -------- | ---------

| Medial | Rectus abdominis muscle

| Lateral | Inferior epigastric vessels

| Inferior | Inguinal ligament

| Hernia Type | Relation to Inferior Epigastric Vessels

| ----------- | ---------------------------------------

| Direct inguinal hernia | Medial

| Indirect inguinal hernia | Lateral

❌  A) Pectineal ligament

• Part of Cooper’s ligament
• Important in hernia repair, not the cause.

❌  C) Reflected part of inguinal ligament

• Reinforces the superficial ring, not the posterior wall.

❌  D) Lacunar ligament

• Forms the medial boundary of the femoral ring, related to femoral hernia.
