questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Ureteric injury is most commonly observed in which population?
questions.explanation: Ureteric injury is a known complication of pelvic surgeries, especially those involving extensive dissection near the ureter. The highest risk occurs during Wertheim’s hysterectomy (radical hysterectomy), which is performed for carcinoma cervix. In this procedure: 1. The ureter is closely related to the uterine artery (“water under the bridge”) 2. Extensive dissection is done near the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments 3. The ureter is mobilized and dissected, increasing the risk of injury Because of this complex anatomy and radical nature of surgery, ureteric injury is most common in Wertheim’s hysterectomy. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Vaginal hysterectomy → Lower risk due to limited dissection (C) Abdominal hysterectomy → Moderate risk, less than radical surgery (D) Emergency C-section → Ureteric injury is rare; bladder injury more common
questions.learning: Ureteric injury is a known complication of pelvic surgeries, especially those involving extensive dissection near the ureter. The highest risk occurs during Wertheim’s hysterectomy (radical hysterectomy), which is performed for carcinoma cervix.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: GnRH deficiency with hyposmia is typically seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kallmann syndrome

Kallmann syndrome is a congenital form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism caused by failure of migration of GnRH-producing neurons and olfactory neurons during embryogenesis. It is characterized by GnRH deficiency with hyposmia/anosmia, resulting in delayed puberty, infertility, and low LH, FSH, and sex steroid levels.

Why not the other options?

• B. Bardet-Biedl syndrome: Characterized by obesity, retinal dystrophy, polydactyly, renal abnormalities, and hypogonadism, but hyposmia is not a typical feature.
• C. Prader-Willi syndrome: Presents with hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity, intellectual disability, and hypogonadism, not hyposmia.
• D. Wallenberg syndrome: A lateral medullary stroke causing dysphagia, hoarseness, ataxia, and sensory deficits; not associated with GnRH deficiency.
questions.learning: Kallmann syndrome Kallmann syndrome is a congenital form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism caused by failure of migration of GnRH-producing neurons and olfactory neurons during embryogenesis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with diarrhea and weight loss. On examination, the height and weight are lesser than expected. Laboratory investigations were positive for class II HLA-DQ2. Which of the following will you advise the child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Gluten-free diet

The clinical scenario of diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, and growth retardation, along with positive class II HLA-DQ2, is consistent with a diagnosis of celiac disease. Patients with celiac disease are advised to avoid gluten.

The dietary recommendation for celiac disease is as follows:

Diet avoided (gluten)

“BROW”

Diet Allowed

“So MRP ”

Barley
Soya bean

Rye
Maize

Oats
Rice

Wheat
Potato

Celiac disease/celiac sprue/gluten-sensitive enteropathy is an immune-mediated disorder triggered by gluten-containing foods. The presence of one of the two locus antigens HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 is necessary, but not sufficient for the development of this condition. Detection of these is not useful for the diagnosis, however, their absence helps to exclude celiac disease.

The pathogenesis involves an inflammatory response to gluten and gliadin (gluten-derived peptide). In the small intestine, gliadin is deamidated by the tissue transglutaminase (tTG), an intestinal enzyme. The deamidated gliadin is more immunogenic and is presented to helper T cells, which mediate mucosal inflammation and cause tissue damage.

Children usually present with diarrhea, weight loss, and growth failure. Other features include malabsorption, bloating, irregular bowel habits, iron deficiency anemia, osteoporosis, ataxia, and abnormal liver enzymes.

Screening for celiac disease is done by testing for serum antibodies, including tissue transglutaminase IgA, anti-endomysial, and deaminated anti-gliadin antibodies. The diagnosis in patients with positive antibodies is confirmed by biopsy of the second part of the duodenum or proximal jejunum. Microscopic findings of biopsy show intraepithelial CD8+ lymphocytes, villous atrophy, and crypt hyperplasia.

The image given below shows microscopic findings seen in celiac disease.

Other options:

Option A: Fat-free diet is advised for various disorders causing steatorrhea. These include pancreatic insufficiency, cystic fibrosis, and familial hypercholesterolemia.

Option B: Lactose-free diet is advised for lactose intolerance. It occurs due to lactase deficiency. Patients usually present with diarrhea, abdominal pain, gassiness, and bloating. A lactose tolerance test or breath hydrogen test may be used for the diagnosis.

Option C: Low-carbohydrate diet is advised for diabetes mellitus.
questions.learning: Gluten-free diet — The clinical scenario of diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, and growth retardation, along with positive class II HLA-DQ2, is consistent with a diagnosis of celiac disease.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The external validity of a screening test is related to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Generalizability

External validity of a screening test is related to generalizability.

Validity (accuracy) refers to what extent the test accurately measures which it sets out to measure. It refers to the closeness with which measured values agree with "true" values.

While assessing the validity of a research study, two kinds of validity are involved:

• External validity: If the study sample is truly representative of the population from which it was drawn, then the study is said to have external validity. Its findings can be applied to the entire population as well and therefore it is said to be generalizable.
• Internal validity: Here the results of the study are valid for the sample of patients who were actually studied.

Note: Precision (reliability or reproducibility) is a measure of the repeatability of a test. That is, the test must give consistent results when repeated more than once on the same individual or material, under the same conditions.
questions.learning: Generalizability External validity of a screening test is related to generalizability. Validity (accuracy) refers to what extent the test accurately measures which it sets out to measure.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: When assessing a patient with suspected intestinal inflammation, which biomarker is most reliable due to its high sensitivity and specificity for indicating inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract?
questions.explanation: Fecal lactoferrin is an iron-binding protein found in the secondary granules of neutrophils. When inflammation occurs in the gastrointestinal tract, neutrophils migrate to the intestinal mucosa and degranulate, releasing lactoferrin into the stool. It is a highly sensitive and specific biomarker for detecting active intestinal inflammation, particularly in differentiating Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) from non-inflammatory conditions like Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS). Fecal calprotectin is a similar, frequently tested marker. Procalcitonin (Option A) is a marker for systemic bacterial infection and sepsis. Tissue transglutaminase IgA (Option C) is a highly specific marker for Celiac disease but does not serve as a general indicator of inflammation. High-sensitivity CRP (Option D) is a marker of systemic inflammation and lacks the specificity required to localize the issue to the gut. Fecal markers like lactoferrin are valuable because they remain stable in stool for days and provide a non-invasive way to monitor disease activity and response to therapy in IBD patients
questions.learning: Fecal lactoferrin is an iron-binding protein found in the secondary granules of neutrophils. When inflammation occurs in the gastrointestinal tract, neutrophils migrate to the intestinal mucosa and degranulate, releasing lactoferrin into the stool.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 46-year-old patient presents with headache, elevated blood pressure tachycardia. Laboratory tests reveal increased creatinine, elevated renin levels. A drug is administered that inhibits the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) pathway, resulting in reduced blood pressure, improved heart rate control, and slowed renal damage. Which of the following best explains the mechanism by which RAAS inhibition exerts these effects?
options: Inhibition of aldosterone receptors to reduce sodium and water retention
Blockade of angiotensin II receptors, preventing vasodilation and aldosterone release (ARB)
Direct inhibition of renin secretion by juxtaglomerular cells
Inhibition of angiotensin-converting enzyme, reducing angiotensin II formation and decreasing vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion (ACE Inhibitor)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inhibition of angiotensin-converting enzyme, reducing angiotensin II formation and decreasing vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion (ACE Inhibitor)

The above clinical scenario of a patient presenting with headache, elevated blood pressure tachycardia. Laboratory tests reveal increased creatinine, and elevated renin levels describe a typical case where the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) is activated, with the administered drug inhibiting RAAS with reduced renal damage. accurately describes the mode of action of ACE Inhibitor drugs, which work by inhibiting angiotensin-converting enzyme, reducing angiotensin II formation, and decreasing vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion.

ACE inhibitors such as captopril or ARBs can be considered as a treatment of choice in hypertensive patients with diabetes because of the renoprotective action. It benefits diabetic patients by reducing the risk of occurrence and progression of diabetic nephropathy. They are also recommended in patients with CKD irrespective of diabetes status, as they can delay the progression of nephropathy.

The adverse effects of ACE inhibitors are:

* Hyperkalemia

* Hypotension - A sudden fall in blood pressure can occur following the first dose of ACE inhibitors.

* Cough

* Angioedema

* Teratogenicity

* Dysgeusia

* Acute renal failure can occur with ACE inhibitors in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis.

* Skin rash

* Extremely rare but reversible side effects include neutropenia.

Other Options:

Option A: ACE inhibitors do not inhibit aldosterone receptors; this is the mode of action of Mineralocorticoid (Aldosterone) Receptor Antagonists like Spironolactone.

Option B: Angiotensin Receptor Blocker does not prevent vasodilation; rather, it prevents vasoconstriction by blocking angiotensin receptors.

Option C: ACE inhibitors do not cause direct inhibition of renin secretion by juxtaglomerular cells; this is done by Renin Inhibitor drugs like Aliskiren.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following healthcare personnel does not function at the village level?
questions.explanation: The Indian public health system utilizes various workers to deliver services at the grassroots level. The Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM) is a key provider who primarily operates at the Sub-centre level, serving as a link between the village and the Primary Health Center. While she makes village visits, her official headquarters and primary work location are the Sub-centre, not the village itself. In contrast, the Anganwadi Worker (AWW) (Option B) is a village-level worker under the ICDS program focusing on nutrition. The Trained Birth Attendant (TBA) (Option C) and Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) (Option D) are strictly village-based workers who live and work within the community they serve. ASHAs, in particular, are the face of the National Health Mission at the doorstep of the rural population. Therefore, because the ANM represents the first formal link in the facility-based hierarchy rather than community-based living, she is not classified as village-level
questions.learning: The Indian public health system utilizes various workers to deliver services at the grassroots level. The Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM) is a key provider who primarily operates at the Sub-centre level, serving as a link between the village and the Primary…

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Jet-black discoloration of the tongue accompanied by tactile hallucinations is characteristic of abuse of which substance?
questions.explanation: A classic and pathognomonic presentation for chronic cocaine abuse is the combination of jet-black pigmentation of the tongue and tactile hallucinations (Option D). The tactile hallucinations are famously known as "cocaine bugs" or Magnan’s sign, where the user feels insects crawling under or on their skin (formication). The black tongue discoloration results from the chemical effects of the drug or contaminants when smoked. Heroin (Option A) and Opium (Option B) are opioids that cause miosis and respiratory depression but not these specific features. Alcohol (Option C) withdrawal can cause hallucinations but not the black tongue sign . Cocaine is a powerful stimulant that increases synaptic dopamine. The presence of formication often leads to self-excoriation as the user tries to "pick" the bugs out. Therefore, the visual sign of a black tongue combined with the sensation of crawling insects is the definitive forensic identifier for cocaine toxicity
questions.learning: A classic and pathognomonic presentation for chronic cocaine abuse is the combination of jet-black pigmentation of the tongue and tactile hallucinations (Option D).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which cells within the liver sinusoids play the primary role in removing bacterial foreign particles from the circulation?
questions.explanation: Kupffer cells are specialized, resident macrophages located within the sinusoidal lining of the liver. They constitute the largest population of tissue-resident macrophages in the body and play a vital role in the innate immune response by filtering the portal blood. Their primary function is the phagocytosis and clearance of bacterial foreign bodies, endotoxins, and cellular debris originating from the gastrointestinal tract. Hepatocytes (Option A) are the functional cells of the liver responsible for metabolism, bile production, and detoxification, but they are not primary phagocytes. Ito cells (Option B), also known as stellate cells, are located in the Space of Disse and are responsible for Vitamin A storage and, when activated, the production of collagen leading to fibrosis. Sinusoidal endothelial cells (Option C) form a fenestrated barrier but do not possess significant phagocytic capacity. The efficient scavenger function of Kupffer cells is essential for preventing systemic sepsis by intercepting pathogens before they reach the systemic circulation through the hepatic veins

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 42-year-old man had a fall followed by one episode of vomiting. When brought to the casualty, he was awake and conscious but had unrelieved anterograde amnesia. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Concussion

The given history of fall and anterograde amnesia points towards the diagnosis of concussion.

A concussion is the most common type of traumatic brain injury. It can result from vehicle accidents, falls, sports injuries, etc. Anterograde amnesia/post-traumatic amnesia is the hallmark of a concussion. In this type of amnesia, the events following the injury cannot be recalled.

Other clinical features of concussion include headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting.

Option A: Drunkenness - the patient will be drowsy or sleepy and not awake.

Option B: Diffuse axonal injury - seen in high-speed deceleration which causes disruption and shearing of axons leading to microhemorrhages. Usually results in a persistent vegetative stage.

Option D: Cerebral venous thrombosis - acute thrombosis in dural venous sinuses; manifests as headache, visual abnormalities, or seizures.
questions.learning: Concussion — The given history of fall and anterograde amnesia points towards the diagnosis of concussion. A concussion is the most common type of traumatic brain injury.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing dacryocystitis is being evaluated for surgical management. Which of the following procedures is most appropriate for her condition?
questions.explanation: Dacryocystitis is an infection of the lacrimal sac, usually due to nasolacrimal duct obstruction. For long-standing (chronic) dacryocystitis in an adult, dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) is the standard and most suitable surgical treatment. DCR creates a new permanent pathway between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity, bypassing the obstructed duct and restoring tear drainage. Dacryocystectomy (DCT) (Option B) involves the complete removal of the lacrimal sac; it is reserved for elderly patients, cases of malignancy, or where DCR is contraindicated, as it leaves the patient with permanent tearing (epiphora). Conjunctiva-cysto rhinostomy (Option C) is a more complex bypass used when the canaliculi are blocked. Balloon catheter dilation (Option D) is occasionally used for partial obstructions but is not the definitive treatment for chronic dacryocystitis. Therefore, DCR is the gold standard procedure for restoring function and preventing recurrent infection
questions.learning: Dacryocystitis is an infection of the lacrimal sac, usually due to nasolacrimal duct obstruction. For long-standing (chronic) dacryocystitis in an adult, dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) is the standard and most suitable surgical treatment.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presented to your hospital emergency with pregnancy 22 weeks, which was a result of rape. Correct statement regarding Medical Termination of Pregnancy is?
options: MTP can be done routinely after 24 weeks POG
MTP is permissible for 20-24 weeks POG in this case
MTP is permissible for 20-24 weeks POG in this case only if it threatens the life of the mother
MTP is permissible for 20-24 weeks POG in this case with 1 Doctor’s opinion only
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. MTP is permissible for 20-24 weeks POG in this case

As per the amended MTP Act (2021), termination of pregnancy is permissible between 20–24 weeks for specified categories of women, which explicitly includes survivors of rape.

In this gestational age group, opinion of two registered medical practitioners is required, and threat to the mother’s life is not mandatory for eligibility.

Termination beyond 24 weeks requires Medical Board approval and is restricted to cases of substantial fetal abnormalities.
questions.learning: MTP is permissible for 20-24 weeks POG in this case As per the amended MTP Act (2021), termination of pregnancy is permissible between 20–24 weeks for specified categories of women, which explicitly includes survivors of rape.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding bempedoic acid:
options: It is a non-competitive Inhibitor ATP citrate lyase
It inhibits the de novo synthesis of cholesterol in hepatocytes
It can be used concomitantly with statins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is a non-competitive Inhibitor ATP citrate lyase

Bempedoic acid works upstream of HMG-CoA reductase in the cholesterol synthesis pathway.

This enzyme: ATP-Citrate Lyase (ACL)

converts citrate → acetyl-CoA, which is required for cholesterol synthesis.

Bempedoic acid inhibits ATP citrate lyase, a key enzyme upstream of HMG-CoA reductase in hepatic cholesterol synthesis. Bempedoic acid blocks cholesterol synthesis earlier than statins, Less muscle toxicity compared to statins

It is a dicarboxylic acid that reduces de novo cholesterol synthesis in hepatocytes.

Statin + Bempedoic acid → synergistic LDL reduction

It can be safely used in combination with statins for additive LDL reduction.

adverse effects:

• Hyperuricemia

• Gout

• Tendon rupture (rare)

The inhibition of ATP citrate lyase is not non-competitive, making option A false.
questions.learning: It is a non-competitive Inhibitor ATP citrate lyase Bempedoic acid works upstream of HMG-CoA reductase in the cholesterol synthesis pathway. This enzyme: ATP-Citrate Lyase (ACL) converts citrate → acetyl-CoA, which is required for cholesterol synthesis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female patient presents with a hard and irregular lump in the upper outer quadrant of the breast. The histopathological slide of the mass sample is given below. What is the most likely condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lobular carcinoma

The given clinical scenario and histopathological findings of single or indian file appearance are highly suggestive of lobular carcinoma of the breast.

The histopathological image shows discohesive infiltrating tumor cells, signet-ring cells containing intracytoplasmic mucin droplets, and the Indian file appearance which is suggestive of lobular carcinoma of the breast. Tubule formation is absent in this subtype.

Lobular Carcinoma is usually bilateral, multicentric, and presents as hard irregular masses. It can have a diffuse infiltrative pattern with minimal desmoplasia. It is the most common type of breast carcinoma to present as an occult primary. Other features are

* Pathogenesis: Mutation in CDH-1 gene , which encodes for cadherin. Loss of E-cadherin leads to small, monomorphic discohesive cells arranged one after another. This arrangement is called an Indian file/single file appearance.

* Desmoplasia is minimal or absent

* They are Luminal-A type

* Excellent prognosis

Note: Mutation in CDH-1 also pose a high risk for gastric signet ring cell carcinoma.

Other options:

Option B: Papillary carcinoma consists of true papillae with a leaf-like arrangement of fibrovascular tissue, lined by the tumor cells.

Option C: Medullary carcinoma of the breast shows sheets of highly pleomorphic cells with mitotic figures, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates and a pushing border.

Option D: Colloidal carcinoma is an invasive breast carcinoma, that shows intra- and extracellular mucin deposition. Histopathological analysis of the extracellular type reveals tumour cells with faint nuclei grouped in clusters, floating in mucin pools or lakes. In the intracellular type, nuclei are pushed outward to create the appearance of a signet ring.
questions.learning: Lobular carcinoma — The given clinical scenario and histopathological findings of single or indian file appearance are highly suggestive of lobular carcinoma of the breast.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 68-year-old man with BPH underwent TURP under spinal anesthesia. During the procedure, 1.5% glycine was used as the irrigation fluid. After 45 minutes of resection, the patient developed restlessness, headache, nausea, altered sensorium, confusion, and mild hypotension. Intraoperative ABG and electrolyte analysis revealed acute dilutional electrolyte disturbance. What is the next appropriate step in intraoperative management?
options: Immediately stopping the procedure and administering hypertonic saline to correct acute symptomatic hyponatremia
Changing irrigation fluid to normal saline
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Immediately stopping the procedure and administering hypertonic saline to correct acute symptomatic hyponatremia

This patient has TURP syndrome, a complication caused by systemic absorption of large volumes of hypotonic irrigation fluid (1.5% glycine) during monopolar transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP). The diagnosis is suggested by:

• TURP under spinal anesthesia
• Use of 1.5% glycine irrigation
• Procedure lasting >45 minutes
• Restlessness, headache, nausea, confusion, altered sensorium
• Dilutional hyponatremia with mild hypotension

The first step is to stop the procedure immediately. Symptomatic acute hyponatremia requires careful administration of hypertonic (3%) saline.

Why not the other options?

• B. Fluid restriction: Appropriate only for mild, asymptomatic cases; inadequate in symptomatic patients.
• C. Change irrigation fluid to normal saline: Normal saline cannot be used with monopolar TURP and does not treat established TURP syndrome.
• D. Switch to bipolar diathermy: Bipolar TURP uses normal saline and reduces future risk but is not the immediate management once TURP syndrome has developed.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following accurately describes the composition of lactulose
questions.explanation: Lactulose is a synthetic, non-absorbable disaccharide widely used as a laxative and in the management of hepatic encephalopathy. It is composed of the monosaccharides galactose and fructose. 1. Galactose + glucose (Option A) form lactose, the natural sugar found in milk. 2. Glucose + fructose (Option B) form sucrose, commonly known as table sugar. 3. Fructose + mannose (Option D) do not form a commonly occurring or clinically relevant disaccharide. Humans lack the intestinal enzyme lactulase required to digest lactulose, so it passes unchanged into the colon. Colonic bacteria then ferment lactulose into short-chain organic acids, which lower colonic pH. This acidic environment converts toxic ammonia (NH₃) into non-absorbable ammonium ions (NH₄⁺), thereby reducing systemic ammonia levels. Additionally, lactulose exerts an osmotic laxative effect by drawing water into the colon. These combined actions explain its effectiveness in both constipation and hepatic encephalopathy management
questions.learning: Lactulose is a synthetic, non-absorbable disaccharide widely used as a laxative and in the management of hepatic encephalopathy. It is composed of the monosaccharides galactose and fructose.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 44-year-old lady presents to the hospital with a flank mass that is ballotable. On CT imaging, the mass measures 4cm. Urine examination shows malignant cells. What is the most appropriate management for her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Partial nephrectomy

Partial nephrectomy (also known as nephron-sparing surgery) is performed for renal cell carcinoma(RCC) tumors less than 4 cm in size. It is also performed for:

Indications for partial nephrectomy:

* Tumors < 4cm

* Well-selected tumors between 4-7 cm

* Bilateral tumors

* Tumor in solitary kidneys

* Patients with pre-existing renal dysfunction.

Recently, partial nephrectomy is also increasingly being performed for stage T1b tumors.

Treatment of renal cell carcinoma:

RCC is a radio and chemoresistant tumor.

Staging
Description
Management

Stage 1
Tumor <7 cm, confined to the kidney
Partial nephrectomy

Stage 2
Tumor >7 cm, confined to the kidney
Radical nephrectomy

Stage 3
Tumor extends into the major veins or adrenal gland with intact Gerota’s fascia or regional lymph nodes involved.
Radical nephrectomy

Stage 4
Tumor invades beyond Gerota fascia (including contiguous extension into the ipsilateral adrenal gland)

• Debulking surgery
• mTOR inhibitors such as everolimus, sirolimus
• Tyrosine kinase inhibitors: sunitinib, sorafenib

Radical nephrectomy consists of the removal of the kidney, perirenal fat, adrenal gland, and regional lymph nodes. The adrenal gland is no longer removed except in cases of obvious tumor involvement. Lymphadenectomy is indicated only in high-risk patients with large primary tumors and enlarged lymph nodes.

Cryoablation is indicated in the T1a stage of RCC if surgery cannot be performed. It is also indicated in advanced/metastatic tumors.

Note: Sunitinib and sorafenib are also used in GIST and hepatocellular carcinoma.

Pearl PF0896: Histologic subtypes of renal cell carcinoma

Clear-cell Type

* Most common type

* Originate from proximal tubule

* Associated with von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease

Papillary Type

* Psammoma bodies are seen in histology

* Originates from distal convoluted tubules, can be multifocal and bilateral.

Chromophobe type

* Are unique in having multiple losses of entire chromosomes

* Originates from intercalated cells of collecting duct

* Good prognosis

Collecting (Bellini) duct type

* Poor prognosis

Renal medullary carcinoma

* Rare

* Associated with sickle cell trait

* Originates from collecting duct

Note:

Sarcomatoid change can occur infrequently in all types of renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and is an ominous feature.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with mental retardation, bone pain, and inability to walk. On funduscopy examination, a cherry red spot is seen. There is no organomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tay-Sachs disease

The given clinical scenario, along with the fundoscopy image showing a macular cherry-red spot, indicates that the most likely diagnosis is Tay-Sachs disease.

Tay-Sachs disease is a lysosomal storage disease caused by the deficiency of β-hexosaminidase. It can present during infancy with macrocephaly, increased startle reaction, gradual loss of motor skills, and a macular cherry-red spot. Affected children usually die by the age of 10–15 years.

It is of two types—juvenile-onset and adult-onset. The symptoms of the juvenile-onset form include ataxia and dementia. Dysarthria, lower motor neuron signs, and psychiatric disorders are common in the adult-onset type.

Other options:

Options B - Niemann-Pick disease is an autosomal recessive inborn error of lipid metabolism. It results due to the deficiency of the sphingomyelinase enzyme. This results in the accumulation of sphingomyelin in the brain, lungs, liver, and spleen. The clinical features include a combination of hepatosplenomegaly, developmental delay, failure to thrive, severe psychomotor regression, interstitial lung disease, and a cherry-red spot in the macula.

Option C - Hurler syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis I) is an autosomal recessive condition that affects multiple organs. Presentation is usually at 6–24 months with corneal clouding, coarse facial features, joint stiffness, and skeletal dysplasia. Glaucoma, retinal degeneration, and nasal discharge are the other features. The condition is generally fatal.

Option D - Gaucher disease is a glycolipid storage disorder that can present with hepatosplenomegaly, mental retardation, and erosion of long bones. It is caused by the deficiency of β-glucosidase. The Gaucher cell has a wrinkled-paper appearance due to intracytoplasmic inclusions, which is a characteristic feature.
questions.learning: Tay-Sachs disease — The given clinical scenario, along with the fundoscopy image showing a macular cherry-red spot, indicates that the most likely diagnosis is Tay-Sachs disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with nasal obstruction, diminished sense of smell, and greenish, dry crusted nasal discharge. Examination shows abnormally wide nasal cavities with atrophied turbinates. Which surgical procedure is most appropriate for managing this condition?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with Atrophic Rhinitis (Ozaena), characterized by mucosal atrophy, shriveled turbinates, and foul-smelling greenish crusts within unnaturally spacious nasal cavities . The aim of surgery is to reduce the volume of the nasal cavity and allow the mucosa to rest and heal. Young’s operation (Option B) involves surgically closing the nostrils (nares) with skin flaps for 6 to 12 months. This stops the drying airflow, preventing crust formation and allowing mucosal regeneration. Submucous resection (Option A) and Septoplasty (Option C) are used to correct a deviated nasal septum, which would not address mucosal atrophy. Vidian neurectomy (Option D) is used for vasomotor rhinitis to reduce excessive secretion, the opposite of the dry state seen here. Modified Young’s operation (partial closure) is also common. Given the pathognomonic finding of shriveled turbinates in spacious passages, Young’s operation is the definitive surgical management
questions.learning: The patient presents with Atrophic Rhinitis (Ozaena), characterized by mucosal atrophy, shriveled turbinates, and foul-smelling greenish crusts within unnaturally spacious nasal cavities .

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In iron deficiency anemia, all of the following is increased except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Transferrin saturation

Transferrin saturation is decreased in iron deficiency anemia.

Clinical presentation may include fatigue, pallor, reduced exercise capacity. Cheilosis (fissures at the corners of the mouth) and koilonychia (spooning of the fingernails) are signs of advanced tissue iron deficiency.

Laboratory findings are:

• Reduced hemoglobin and hematocrit values.
• hypochromia, microcytosis, and poikilocytosis.
• serum iron and ferritin levels are low.
• The total plasma iron-binding capacity that reflects the elevated transferrin levels is high.
• Low serum iron with increased iron-binding capacity results in a reduction of transferrin saturation to below 15%.
• RBC protoporphyrin levels are increased. Protoporphyrin is an intermediate in the heme synthesis pathway. Under conditions in which heme synthesis is impaired, protoporphyrin accumulates within the red cell.
• Bone marrow reveals a mild to moderate increase in erythroid progenitors. The absence of stainable iron in macrophages is a diagnostically significant finding.

Peripheral smear of microcytic hypochromic anemia:
questions.learning: Transferrin saturation Transferrin saturation is decreased in iron deficiency anemia. Clinical presentation may include fatigue, pallor, reduced exercise capacity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Common carotid artery pulse is taken at the level of?
questions.explanation: The common carotid artery pulse is typically palpated in the neck, lateral to the larynx. Specifically, it is assessed at the level of the cricoid cartilage, which corresponds to the C6 vertebrae level. At this point, the artery can be compressed against the prominent carotid tubercle (Chassaignac's tubercle) of the C6 transverse process. The bifurcation of the common carotid into internal and external branches usually occurs higher, at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4 level), which corresponds to the laryngeal prominence (Option B). The suprasternal notch (Option C) is too low for a reliable carotid pulse, and the angle of the mandible (Option D) is the site for the facial artery or the termination of the external carotid. Clinically, the carotid pulse is the most reliable peripheral pulse to check during cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Understanding these surface landmarks is essential for rapid clinical assessment and procedures such as carotid endarterectomy or central line placement
questions.learning: The common carotid artery pulse is typically palpated in the neck, lateral to the larynx. Specifically, it is assessed at the level of the cricoid cartilage, which corresponds to the C6 vertebrae level.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A woman is found dead in a locked room, and during autopsy it is noted that a heat stove was still running inside the room. What is the most likely cause of death?
questions.explanation: A running stove in a confined, locked space is the classic environment for carbon monoxide (CO) accumulation due to incomplete combustion. CO has an affinity for hemoglobin roughly 250 times that of oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin and preventing oxygen transport, which leads to fatal tissue hypoxia. Autopsy typically reveals a characteristic cherry-red post-mortem staining. Cyanide poisoning (Option B) usually results from industrial accidents and shows brick-red staining. H2S poisoning (Option C) occurs in industrial settings or sewers and is identified by a rotten-egg odor and bluish-green staining. Aluminium phosphide (Option D) is common in agricultural suicide cases and releases phosphine gas, which causes cardiac toxicity rather than enclosed-room asphyxiation. Based on the household heating scenario and the high risk of CO buildup, carbon monoxide poisoning is the most probable cause of death

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the cause of death in smoke inhalation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anemic hypoxia

Victims of smoke inhalation are affected by carbon monoxide poisoning. In carbon monoxide poisoning, the cause of death is anemic hypoxia.

Carbon monoxide has a higher affinity to hemoglobin compared to oxygen and hence the amount of hemoglobin available for oxygen transport is markedly reduced. It displaces oxygen from its combination with hemoglobin and forms a relatively stable compound known as carboxyhemoglobin. It thus reduces the oxygen content of the blood, and hence, that of the tissues. It acts as a chemical asphyxiant and produces death due to anemic anoxia.

It is important to note that in the case of anemic hypoxia, O2 content is low but dissolved O2 is within normal limits so it does not stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors.

Note: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes both anemic (due to CO-Hb) and histotoxic (due to inhibition of cytochrome C oxidase) hypoxia. But the main cause of death is due to anemic hypoxia.

Option A - Histotoxic hypoxia- The most common example is cyanide poisoning. Cyanide inhibits important enzymes in the oxidative phosphorylation process, which is essential to the survival of our cells. Additional oxygen supplementation will not be able to overcome this inhibition, so it will have limited benefit. Hyperbaric oxygen may be helpful to some extent.

Option B - Stagnant hypoxia refers to ischemic hypoxia that results from inadequate circulation due to conditions such as heart failure and hypoxia in the setting of shock. In such conditions, administering intravenous fluids can improve the patient's condition because it is the circulation that is affected. If the shock is prolonged it can result in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), which can be treated with positive pressure ventilation and not simply by increasing oxygen administration.
questions.learning: Anemic hypoxia Victims of smoke inhalation are affected by carbon monoxide poisoning. In carbon monoxide poisoning, the cause of death is anemic hypoxia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the standard treatment for empyema thoracis?
questions.explanation: Empyema thoracis is defined as the presence of pus in the pleural cavity, usually as a complication of pneumonia. The standard of care for managing empyema requires a two-pronged approach: "chest tube drainage" (intercostal drain) to evacuate the infected fluid and "systemic antibiotics" to treat the underlying infection. Antibiotics alone (Option A) are insufficient because they cannot penetrate the thick, acidic, and often loculated pus in the pleural space effectively. An ICD alone (Option C) removes the fluid but does not address the bacterial source. "Wait and watch" (Option D) is dangerous, as untreated empyema can lead to fibrothorax and lung entrapment, necessitating more invasive surgery like decortication. Management may also include intrapleural fibrinolytics or Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS) if the empyema is complex or loculated. Early and aggressive drainage combined with appropriate antimicrobial therapy is essential to ensure resolution and prevent long-term respiratory impairment in these patients

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the area marked in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rectovesical pouch

The arrow in the image points to the rectovesical pouch.

The peritoneum covering the anterior surface of the rectum is reflected anteriorly to cover the posterosuperior surface of the bladder in males, forming a rectovesical pouch. This is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in males and an important site for pelvic fluid collection.

Other options:

Option B: Rectouterine pouch- The peritoneum which covers the anterior surface of the rectum is reflected anteriorly to cover the posterior surface of the posterior fornix of the vagina and the uterus, forming a rectouterine pouch.

Option C: Vesicouterine pouch- The peritoneum covering the fundus and body of the uterus, is reflected anteriorly to cover the posterosuperior surface of the bladder forming a vesico uterine pouch

Option D: Pouch of Morrison (hepatorenal recess) - The peritoneum covering the posterior surface of the right lobe of the liver is reflected posteriorly to cover the anterior surface of the right kidney and right suprarenal gland, forming a deep, vertical groove. This is the deepest peritoneal recess in the supine position and an important site for fluid collection.
questions.learning: Rectovesical pouch — The arrow in the image points to the rectovesical pouch. The peritoneum covering the anterior surface of the rectum is reflected anteriorly to cover the posterosuperior surface of the bladder in males, forming a rectovesical pouch.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not a boundary of hepatocystic triangle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cystic artery

Hepatocystic triangle boundaries: cystic duct (lateral), common hepatic duct (medial), inferior liver border (superior). The cystic artery lies within the triangle as content, not as a boundary.
questions.learning: Cystic artery Hepatocystic triangle boundaries: cystic duct (lateral), common hepatic duct (medial), inferior liver border (superior). The cystic artery lies within the triangle as content, not as a boundary.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A gutter fracture of the skull is usually produced by which type of impact or force?
questions.explanation: A "gutter fracture" is a specific type of depressed skull fracture characteristically caused by a bullet or projectile that strikes the skull at a tangential angle. This creates a furrow or "gutter" in the outer table of the skull, often with comminution of the inner table. Sharp objects (Option A) typically cause incised or "cut" fractures. Blunt objects (Option B) or falls from a height (Option C) usually result in linear, stellate, or generalized depressed fractures depending on the force and surface area of the impact. Projectile-related fractures are distinct because the high velocity and energy lead to specific fragmentation patterns. Forensic identification of a gutter fracture is vital for determining the trajectory of a gunshot wound. These injuries are often associated with underlying dural tears and cortical contusions. Management requires neurosurgical evaluation to address intracranial pressure, remove fragments, and repair any underlying dural or brain injury
questions.learning: A "gutter fracture" is a specific type of depressed skull fracture characteristically caused by a bullet or projectile that strikes the skull at a tangential angle.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A woman who had undergone total knee replacement surgery comes with complaints of knee pain with the loosening of implants. The following histopathological slide was obtained which showed foreign body giant cells along with the appearance highlighted in the image below. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Metallosis

The given clinical scenario and image with the said foreign body giant cell point towards a diagnosis of metallosis.

Metallosis is an uncommon complication following total joint replacements of high wear joints like hip and knees. The metal from the prosthesis infiltrates the bone and soft tissue surrounding it. It presents with pain or squeaking on weight bearing or loosening of implant. Sometimes it may be asymptomatic with imaging findings (cloud sign or bubble sign). Aspiration reveals dark fluid consisting of metallic debris.
questions.learning: Metallosis — The given clinical scenario and image with the said foreign body giant cell point towards a diagnosis of metallosis. Metallosis is an uncommon complication following total joint replacements of high wear joints like hip and knees.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most common cause of perforation of the oesophagus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Iatrogenic infection

Oesophageal perforation is a life-threatening surgical emergency associated with high morbidity and mortality due to rapid development of mediastinitis and sepsis. The most common cause is iatrogenic injury, usually occurring during upper gastrointestinal endoscopy or oesophageal dilatation.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Barotrauma: Barotrauma can cause spontaneous oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave syndrome) after forceful vomiting, but it is less common than iatrogenic injury.
• B. Mediastinitis: Mediastinitis is a complication, not a cause, of oesophageal perforation.
• D. Malignancy: Oesophageal cancer may perforate, especially after radiotherapy or stenting, but it is not the most common cause.
questions.learning: Iatrogenic infection Oesophageal perforation is a life-threatening surgical emergency associated with high morbidity and mortality due to rapid development of mediastinitis and sepsis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In which color-coded disposal bag should cytotoxic drugs be discarded?
questions.explanation: According to the latest Biomedical Waste Management guidelines, cytotoxic drugs and contaminated items (such as vials, ampoules, and expired medicines) must be disposed of in a yellow bag or container. These items are specifically labeled as "cytotoxic" and are destined for high-temperature incineration at a common waste treatment facility. Red bags (Option B) are used for recyclable contaminated waste like plastics. Blue bags or cardboard boxes (Option C) are used for broken glassware and metallic implants. Black bags (Option D) were historically used for general municipal waste but are no longer the standard for biomedical segregation in many protocols. Cytotoxic drugs are highly hazardous and require specialized destruction to prevent environmental contamination and health risks to waste handlers. Therefore, the yellow bag is the designated disposal route for chemotherapy-related medications in an oncology unit
questions.learning: According to the latest Biomedical Waste Management guidelines, cytotoxic drugs and contaminated items (such as vials, ampoules, and expired medicines) must be disposed of in a yellow bag or container.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which variety of cartilage generally does not show calcification as a normal age-related change?
questions.explanation: This question reinforces the histological distinction between laryngeal cartilage types and their reaction to the aging process. The thyroid, cricoid, and the base of the arytenoid are hyaline cartilages. Hyaline cartilage is prone to endochondral ossification and calcification beginning in the third decade of life. By contrast, the epiglottis is composed of elastic cartilage, characterized by an abundance of elastic fibers in its matrix. Elastic cartilage is designed for high flexibility and resilience; it does not calcify with age. This property ensures that the epiglottis remains pliable enough to fold over the laryngeal inlet during deglutition throughout a person's lifespan. Options A, B, and D are all hyaline structures that will progressively harden and become more radiopaque over time. Clinically, the calcification of hyaline laryngeal cartilages can sometimes interfere with surgical procedures or be misinterpreted on computed tomography scans of the neck, whereas the epiglottis consistently retains its cartilaginous, non-calcified density
questions.learning: This question reinforces the histological distinction between laryngeal cartilage types and their reaction to the aging process. The thyroid, cricoid, and the base of the arytenoid are hyaline cartilages.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are risk factors for the development of pancreatic cancer? 1. Cigarette smoking 2. Diabetes mellitus 3. Caucasian ethnicity 4. Male gender Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis because it is often diagnosed at an advanced stage. Several modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors increase the likelihood of developing pancreatic cancer, with cigarette smoking being the most important modifiable risk factor.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Cigarette smoking ✅

• Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor, increasing the risk of pancreatic cancer by 2–3 times.

• 2. Diabetes mellitus ✅

• Long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus is an established risk factor. Conversely, new-onset diabetes in older adults may be an early manifestation of pancreatic cancer.

• 3. Caucasian ethnicity ❌

• Pancreatic cancer is more common in African Americans than in Caucasians; therefore, Caucasian ethnicity is not considered a risk factor.

• 4. Male gender ✅

• The incidence is slightly higher in males, partly due to greater exposure to smoking and occupational carcinogens.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis because it is often diagnosed at an advanced stage.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During an autopsy, what is commonly used to preserve blood?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NaF

10 mg/ml of sodium or potassium fluoride and potassium oxalate (anti-coagulant) is used to preserve blood.

Other preservatives used in toxicology postmortem include:

* Saturated NaCl solution: Avoided in poisoning from corrosive acids, alkalis, corrosive sublimate, and aconite.

* Fluoride should be added to urine, CSF, and vitreous humor if alcohol estimation is required and if analysis for cocaine, cyanide, and CO is being done.

A preservative is not necessary if :

* The viscera can be analyzed in 24 hours

* If the sample can be stored in a refrigerator or icebox

* Bone, hair, nails specimens

* Lung for inhaled poisons

* The viscera should not be preserved in formaldehyde because extraction of non-volatile poisons becomes difficult.

In cases of chronic poisoning with heavy metals such as lead, arsenic, mercury, antimony, copper, etc., the shaft of a long bone, strands of scalp hair, fingernails or toenails, and a wedge of the quadriceps muscle should also be taken for sampling.
questions.learning: NaF 10 mg/ml of sodium or potassium fluoride and potassium oxalate (anti-coagulant) is used to preserve blood. Other preservatives used in toxicology postmortem include: * Saturated NaCl solution: Avoided in poisoning from corrosive acids, alkalis,…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old man presents with 15 days of fever and altered sensorium for 1 day. Rapid diagnostic test was done and Plasmodium falciparum was diagnosed. Which of the following is not a complication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arterial pH >7.2

The clinical scenario of a patient presenting with prolonged fever, altered sensorium, and test showing Plasmodium falciparum positive is suggestive of severe falciparum malaria, Arterial pH >7.2 is not a complication of falciparum malaria.

Malaria is a protozoal disease transmitted by the bite of a female anopheles mosquito that has been infected. Five different species of Plasmodium are responsible for disease in humans. They are P. falciparum, P.vivax, P.ovale, P.malariae, and P.knowlesi.

Features of severe falciparum malaria are as follows:

• Unarousable coma or cerebral malaria
• Acidosis is characterized by pH <7.25, base deficit >8 meq/L or plasma bicarbonate <15 mmol/L, venous lactate >5 mmol/L, and labored deep breathing.
• Anemia is severe with a normocytic and normochromic picture with hemoglobin <5g/dL or hematocrit <15%
• Renal failure is characterized by serum creatinine >3 mg/dL, urine output <400 mL, and there is no improvement with rehydration.
• Pulmonary edema or adult respiratory distress syndrome
• Hypoglycemia with plasma glucose <40 mg/dL
• Hypotension or shock is characterized by systolic blood pressure < 50 mmHg in children and < 80 mm Hg in adults, and a prolonged capillary refilling time of >2s
• Bleeding or disseminated intravascular coagulation
• Convulsions, weakness
• Hemoglobinuria
• Jaundice
questions.learning: Arterial pH >7.2 The clinical scenario of a patient presenting with prolonged fever, altered sensorium, and test showing Plasmodium falciparum positive is suggestive of severe falciparum malaria, Arterial pH >7.2 is not a complication of falciparum malaria.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which element plays a key role in the activation of the complement system via the alternative pathway?
questions.explanation: The alternative complement pathway is a key component of innate immunity and is unique because it is antibody-independent. It is continuously active at a low level through a process known as “C3 tick-over.” In this pathway, C3 undergoes spontaneous hydrolysis, generating C3b, which can bind directly to the surfaces of pathogens. This binding initiates the formation of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb), which cleaves additional C3 molecules and creates a powerful amplification loop of complement activation. Why the other options are incorrect: 1. C1 (Option A), C4 (Option D), and C2 (Option B) are components of the classical and lectin pathways, not the alternative pathway. In those pathways, they form the C3 convertase C4b2a after antibody or lectin binding. 2. Because C3 is the central component where all complement pathways converge, deficiency of C3 leads to severe, recurrent pyogenic infections due to impaired opsonization and complement activation. Thus, C3 is the crucial element involved in activation of the complement through the alternative pathway

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which one of the following is related to the release of bicarbonate in exchange for chloride in the RBC to maintain electrical neutrality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chloride shift

The release of bicarbonate in exchange for chloride in the RBC to maintain electrical neutrality is known as the chloride shift or Hamburger phenomenon.

Chloride shift:

* Upon entering the red blood cell, CO2 is rapidly hydrated to H2CO3 by carbonic anhydrase.

* H2CO3 is in equilibrium with H+ and its conjugate base, HCO3-. H+ can interact with deoxyhemoglobin.

* whereas HCO3- can be transported outside of the cell via anion exchanger 1 (AE1 or Band 3).

* To prevent an imbalance in charge, HCO₃⁻ exits the RBC into plasma, and Cl⁻ enters the RBC via the Band 3 transporter, maintaining electrical neutrality. This is called the chloride shift.

* Because of this chloride shift, the Cl – content of the red cells in venous blood is significantly greater than that in arterial blood.

* Note that for each CO2 molecule added to a red cell, there is an increase of one osmotically active particles in the cell - either a HCO 3 – or a Cl – ion. Consequently, the red cells take up water and increase in size.

Other options:

Option A: The Haldane effect is the phenomenon where the binding of oxygen promotes the release of carbon dioxide from hemoglobin, facilitating its removal. This effect allows for efficient gas exchange in the lungs and plays a crucial role in maintaining the balance of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood.

Option B: A right shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve in response to an increase in blood CO2 and hydrogen ions, enhances the release of O2 from the blood in the tissues. This enhances the oxygenation of the blood in the lungs. This is known as the Bohr effect.

Option D: Haber–Weiss reaction is a chemical reaction that generates hydroxyl radicals (•OH), which are highly reactive and contribute to oxidative stress in biological systems. It occurs in the presence of superoxide (O₂⁻) and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) and is catalyzed by iron (Fe³⁺ or Fe²⁺).

Reaction Steps:

* Superoxide reacts with ferric iron (Fe³⁺) to form ferrous iron (Fe²⁺): O2− + Fe3+→O2 + Fe2+

* Ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) reacts with hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) in a Fenton-like reaction to produce hydroxyl radicals (•OH): Fe2++H2O2→Fe3++OH−+⋅OH

* Overall Haber-Weiss Reaction:
O2−+H2O2→O2+OH−+⋅OH
questions.learning: Chloride shift — The release of bicarbonate in exchange for chloride in the RBC to maintain electrical neutrality is known as the chloride shift or Hamburger phenomenon.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are included as a “Deficiency” under the Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK)? I. Hypothyroidism II. Vitamin A deficiency III. Anemia IV. Vitamin D deficiency Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. II, III and IV

The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) is a national child health screening and early intervention program launched under the National Health Mission (NHM). It aims for early identification and management of the “4 Ds” in children from birth to 18 years of age:

• Defects at birth
• Deficiencies
• Diseases
• Developmental delays including disabilities ⭐

Under the “Deficiencies” category, common nutritional deficiencies screened include Vitamin A deficiency, Vitamin D deficiency, Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM), and anemia.

Why is D correct?

• I. Hypothyroidism ✘

• Congenital hypothyroidism is classified under Defects at Birth, not Deficiencies.

• II. Vitamin A deficiency ✔

• Included under the Deficiencies component of RBSK.

• III. Anemia ✔

• Nutritional anemia is one of the major deficiencies screened under RBSK.

• IV. Vitamin D deficiency ✔

• Included among nutritional deficiencies screened under the program.
questions.learning: II, III and IV — The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) is a national child health screening and early intervention program launched under the National Health Mission (NHM).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man initially develops paralysis in both legs, which later progresses to involve the upper limbs. Over time, he improves but is left with paralysis affecting only his lower trunk and both legs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient's final neurological status is defined by paralysis of the lower trunk and both legs, which is the clinical definition of paraplegia. Paraplegia typically results from a lesion in the thoracic or lumbar spinal cord. Diplegia (Option A) refers to symmetrical paralysis of any two similar parts (usually both legs more than arms), often associated with cerebral palsy. Quadriplegia (Option B), also known as tetraplegia, involves paralysis of all four limbs and the trunk, typically resulting from a cervical spinal cord injury. Monoplegia (Option D) is the paralysis of a single limb. While the patient initially had symptoms suggesting quadriplegia (as the weakness progressed to the arms), the final outcome after improvement is paraplegia. This sequence of "ascending" and then "descending" recovery is sometimes seen in Guillain-Barré Syndrome or transverse myelitis as the inflammation resolves
questions.learning: This patient's final neurological status is defined by paralysis of the lower trunk and both legs, which is the clinical definition of paraplegia. Paraplegia typically results from a lesion in the thoracic or lumbar spinal cord.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Following a road traffic accident, a 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department with maxillofacial trauma and inability to open the mouth. To establish an airway, an emergency laryngotomy is performed. Where is the opening made?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cricothyroid membrane

In laryngotomy, an opening is made on the cricothyroid membrane.

Laryngotomy is also called cricothyrotomy or mini-tracheostomy. It is done as an emergency life-saving procedure to buy some time to allow a patient to be carried to the operation theatre. Once stable, it is replaced by intubation or tracheostomy.

Most of the laryngeal foreign bodies are arrested above the vocal cords, i.e. above the middle of the thyroid cartilage. Thus, an effective airway can be provided by piercing the cricothyroid membrane.
questions.learning: Cricothyroid membrane — In laryngotomy, an opening is made on the cricothyroid membrane. Laryngotomy is also called cricothyrotomy or mini-tracheostomy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient came to the hospital with complaints of breathlessness and is diagnosed with a Pancoast tumor. Which of the following findings is not typically associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Exophthalmus

Pancoast syndrome is associated with Horner's syndrome, resulting in ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis. It is not associated with exophthalmus.

Horner syndrome occurs when the sympathetic nerves serving the head, eye, or neck are damaged at any point along their pathway. It is also referred to as oculosympathetic paresis.

Clinical features include:

* Ptosis - usually due to weakness of Muller’s muscle (Option D).

* Miosis - due to unopposed action of sphincter pupillae leading to anisocoria (Option C).

* Anhidrosis - reduced ipsilateral sweating (Option B).

* Heterochromia iridis- seen in congenital and long-standing disease. The affected eye is lighter in color.

* Anisocoria that is accentuated in dim light

* Enophthalmus

Pancoast syndrome  is also called a superior sulcus tumor. It develops when a tumor located at the apex of the lung extends locally. Local extension involves the C8 - T2 nerve roots.

It presents with pain that radiates to the ulnar distribution of the arm, often with the destruction of the 1st and 2nd ribs. Patients with the central or endobronchial growth of the primary tumor may present with a cough, hemoptysis, wheeze, stridor, dyspnea, or post-obstructive pneumonitis.

Regional spread of the tumor can cause:

* Tracheal obstruction, esophageal compression with dysphagia

* Recurrent laryngeal paralysis with hoarseness

* Phrenic nerve palsy with the elevation of the hemidiaphragm and dyspnea

* Sympathetic nerve paralysis with Horner’s syndrome (enophthalmos, ptosis, miosis, and anhydrosis).

The below images show chest X-ray and management of the Pancoast tumor.

Pearl PF1717: Horner's syndrome

Horner's Syndrome:

Horner's syndrome occurring due to occulo-sympathetic paresis is characterized by the classic triad of:

* Mild ptosis (due to paralysis of Muller's muscle).

* Miosis (due to paralysis of dilator pupillae).

* Reduced ipsilateral sweating (anhydrosis).

Other features include:

* Mild enophthalmos,

* Loss of cilio-spinal reflex,

* Heterochromia, i.e., the ipsilateral iris is lighter in colour,

* Pupil is slow to dilate, and there occurs slight elevation of lower eyelid.

Cocaine test (2% to 4%): Small pupils fail to dilate in Horner's syndrome.

In congenital Horner's syndrome, the additional features seen are heterochromia iridis and unilateral straight hair.
questions.learning: Exophthalmus Pancoast syndrome is associated with Horner's syndrome, resulting in ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis. It is not associated with exophthalmus.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In Sanger sequencing, ddNTP is used because:
options: It is used to increase DNA polymerase activity
They exhibit higher affinity for DNA polymerases
It doesn't allow further elongation of DNA
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It doesn't allow further elongation of DNA

In Sanger sequencing, dideoxynucleotides triphosphates (ddNTP) are used because it doesn't allow further elongation of DNA.

The Sanger method is used for DNA sequencing. This method uses the mechanism of synthesis of DNA by DNA polymerases. In the process of synthesis of DNA, the 3'-hydroxyl group of primer reacts with an incoming dNTP to form a new phosphodiester bond. This reaction is catalyzed by DNA polymerase.

In the Sanger sequencing method, ddNTP is used because it halts the DNA synthesis. ddNTPs can bind to the template strand but lack the 3'-hydroxyl group which is required to add the next nucleotide. The products of this reaction are a mixture of DNA strands of varying lengths. This mixture is then separated using polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and autoradiography. This produces a pattern of bands from which the DNA sequence can be read.

The image given below shows the steps involved in Sanger's method.

Sanger’s technique was the first technique used to determine the sequence of proteins. The first protein to be sequenced by this method was insulin. Sanger’s reagent is 1- fluoro 2,4 dinitro benzene.
questions.learning: It doesn't allow further elongation of DNA — In Sanger sequencing, dideoxynucleotides triphosphates (ddNTP) are used because it doesn't allow further elongation of DNA.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Every pregnant woman receives a free antenatal check-up on the 9th of each month, along with free medicines and delivery services, including cesarean sections, under the JSSK program. What does JSSK stand for?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram

JSSK stands for Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram. It is an initiative by the Indian government aimed at reducing maternal and infant mortality.

The provisions of JSSK include:

• Free transport
• Free treatment
• Free drugs and consumables
• Free diagnostics and diet
• Free and cashless delivery
• Free C-Section
• Free provision of blood

Note: Previously under JSSK, the free entitlements were provided only for sick newborns till 30 days after birth. Now it is expanded to cover infants also.
questions.learning: Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram JSSK stands for Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram. It is an initiative by the Indian government aimed at reducing maternal and infant mortality.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are correct about endocrine changes in normal pregnancy? 1. Increase in levels of maternal serum iodine. 2. Increase in serum levels of Corticotropin-Releasing Hormone (CRH). 3. Increase in serum levels of aldosterone. 4. Increase in serum levels of ACTH. Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

• 1. Increase in levels of maternal serum iodine. ✗

• Maternal serum iodine levels do not increase. In fact, iodine requirement increases during pregnancy due to increased renal clearance and fetal thyroid hormone production, making pregnant women more prone to iodine deficiency if intake is inadequate.

• 2. Increase in serum levels of Corticotropin-Releasing Hormone (CRH). ✓

• The placenta secretes CRH, and maternal CRH levels rise progressively throughout pregnancy, especially in the third trimester.

• 3. Increase in serum levels of aldosterone. ✓

• Activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) leads to increased aldosterone, promoting sodium and water retention and expansion of plasma volume.

• 4. Increase in serum levels of ACTH. ✓

• Placental CRH stimulates increased maternal ACTH secretion, leading to elevated cortisol levels during pregnancy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which enzyme is shared between the pathways for cholesterol and ketone body synthesis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HMG-CoA Synthase

HMG-CoA Synthase is an enzyme shared between both cholesterol biosynthesis and ketone body formation. In both pathways, HMG-CoA synthase catalyzes the condensation of acetoacetyl-CoA with another molecule of acetyl-CoA to form 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA). However, there are two different isoforms of this enzyme: a cytosolic form involved in cholesterol synthesis and a mitochondrial form involved in ketogenesis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old primigravida presents with painful vaginal bleeding during the first trimester. Ultrasonography shows a well-defined gestational sac with central embryonic echoes and detectable fetal cardiac activity, indicating a viable fetus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Threatened abortion is defined by vaginal bleeding occurring before 20 weeks of gestation while the cervical os remains closed. The crucial diagnostic finding on ultrasound (USG) in this case is the presence of fetal cardiac motion and a healthy-appearing embryo, which confirms that the pregnancy is still viable despite the bleeding. In an Inevitable abortion (Option A), the cervical os would be dilated, and fetal cardiac activity might be absent or the gestational sac would be low-lying. An Incomplete abortion (Option C) would show retained products of conception on USG with an open cervix. A Complete abortion (Option D) would show an empty uterine cavity on USG. Because the fetus is currently alive and the pregnancy continues, the clinical state is one of "threat" only. Management involves bed rest and observation, as many threatened abortions proceed to a normal full-term delivery. Therefore, Threatened abortion is the most accurate clinical diagnosis

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with abdominal distension and hepatomegaly, with the liver palpable 8 cm below the costal margin and smooth on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Massive, smooth hepatomegaly in a child often points to metabolic disorders like Glycogen Storage Disease (GSD). In GSD subtypes such as Von Gierke disease, the liver becomes uniformly enlarged due to the excessive accumulation of glycogen within hepatocytes. The lack of nodularity or focal masses on palpation suggests a diffuse, infiltrative process rather than a tumor. Lysosomal Storage Diseases (LSD) like Gaucher or Niemann-Pick also cause hepatomegaly but are typically accompanied by massive splenomegaly and developmental regression, which are not described here. Hepatocellular Carcinoma (Option C) is rare in children and would present as a firm, irregular, nodular liver. Autoimmune hepatitis (Option D) usually causes milder enlargement associated with jaundice and fatigue. Thus, smooth, massive hepatic enlargement in early childhood is highly characteristic of a storage-related metabolic defect like GSD
questions.learning: Massive, smooth hepatomegaly in a child often points to metabolic disorders like Glycogen Storage Disease (GSD). In GSD subtypes such as Von Gierke disease, the liver becomes uniformly enlarged due to the excessive accumulation of glycogen within hepatocytes.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department soon after a road traffic accident with intense superficial pain due to injuries. Which nerve fibre is responsible for the conduction of this pain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A delta

The clinical history of acute superficial pain refers to fast pain or first pain. It is transmitted by A delta (δ) fibers.

Pain can be carried by either Aδ fiber (fast pain/ epicritic pain) or by C fiber (slow pain/protopathic pain)

Fast pain is a rapid response and mediates the ability to localize the site and intensity of the noxious stimulus. it occurs when glutamate is released following the stimulation of A delta fibers.

Slow pain on the other hand can also be burning, dull and poorly localized. It is transmitted by C nociceptor fibers which release substance P.

Option B: Aβ is associated with touch and pressure conduction and is seen in conjunction with flower-spray ending. In numerical classification, they correspond to II fibres.

Option D: C fibres (dorsal root) are associated with pain and temperature with a conduction velocity of 0.5-2 m/s while C fibres (sympathetic) carry the postganglionic sympathetic function and conduct at a velocity of 0.7-2.3 m/s.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman presented with complaints of passing grape-like vesicles vaginally. A USG scan was done and is shown below. Which of the following hormonal levels need to be checked in this patient? hCG - Human Chorionic Gonadotropin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. hCG

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of molar pregnancy and beta hCG levels need to be measured.

Molar pregnancy may present with bleeding per vaginum or an acute discharge of vesicular mass per vaginum. On examination, the uterine size is more than the corresponding period of amenorrhea. It shows a characteristic snowstorm appearance on USG.

Suction and evacuation is the treatment of choice. The patient is followed up every week till the hCG levels normalize, after which follow-up is done monthly for 6 months.

Post-evacuation recommendations:

* Anti-D immune globulin if Rh D-negative

* Initiate effective contraception (IUD contraindicated)

* Review pathology report

* Serum hCG levels: within 48 h of evacuation, weekly until undetectable, then monthly for 6 months.

Pregnancy is allowed after 6 months following a negative hCG titer. However, it is advised to avoid pregnancy for 1 year, preferably 2 years, as a fresh pregnancy will interfere with the hCG titers.
questions.learning: hCG The given clinical scenario is suggestive of molar pregnancy and beta hCG levels need to be measured. Molar pregnancy may present with bleeding per vaginum or an acute discharge of vesicular mass per vaginum.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient came to OPD with a complaint of dilated and tortuous veins in the left leg and mild pain while walking. On palpation, the vein is pulsatile. He had a history of road traffic accident, including a left leg fracture 10 years ago. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arteriovenous (AV) fistula

This patient with a history of trauma and a recently developed pulsatile swelling of the same side has a traumatic arteriovenous fistula.
An arteriovenous fistula is an abnormal communication between an artery and a vein and tends to occur when two structures are in proximity. Traumatic AVF can occur secondary to penetrating and blunt trauma. The most common traumatic AV fistula is a carotid-cavernous fistula secondary to the base of the skull fracture.
Clinical features: pulsatile swelling and in chronic cases- limb lengthening, arterialisation of veins and heart failure. Large extremity fistula may present with skin warmth in contrast to cool extremity and signs of venous hypertension which is usually seen in varicosities.

Diagnosis: Ultrasonography can detect flow anomalies. CT angiography can provide anatomic delineation.

Other options

Option A: Varicose veins can present with dilated tortuous veins. However, they are not pulsatile and with a history of trauma AV fistula is more likely.

Option B: Pseudoaneurysms do not present with dilated and tortuous veins.

Option D: Atherosclerosis doesn't present with dilated veins and pulsatile swellings.
questions.learning: Arteriovenous (AV) fistula — This patient with a history of trauma and a recently developed pulsatile swelling of the same side has a traumatic arteriovenous fistula.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text:
Which of the statements given below regarding the muscle shown in the image are correct?

1. They retract the scapula along with the middle fibres of Trapezius
2. They elevate the scapula along with fibres of Trapezius
3. They rotate the scapula tilting the glenoid cavity inferiorly
4. They rotate the scapula tilting the glenoid cavity superiorly
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3

The muscles marked in the above image are rhomboids minor and major. These muscles cause retraction and elevation of the scapula and they rotate the scapula tilting the glenoid cavity inferiorly.

Rhomboids minor and major are innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve. They are supplied by the dorsal scapular artery or the deep branch of the transverse cervical artery.

Muscles involved in movements of the scapula are:

• Protraction (forward movement): Serratus anterior and pectoralis minor are prime movers. Rhomboid muscles control the rate and range of movements. The upper part of the latissimus dorsi acts like a strap across the inferior scapular angle in protraction.
• Retraction (backward movement): Middle trapezius and rhomboids.
• Elevation: Trapezius, Levator scapulae and rhomboids.
• Depression: Usually gravity alone is sufficient for the depression of the scapula. When required, a part of the serratus anterior, pectoralis minor, and trapezius are used.
