questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the type of connective tissue present in the area marked by the arrow in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dense irregular

The area marked is the reticular dermis. It is made up of dense irregular connective tissue.

It is found in the regions that are under considerable mechanical stress and where protection is given to ensheathed organs. It is usually present in:

• Reticular dermis
• Superficial connective tissue sheaths of the muscle and nerves
• Adventitia of large vessels
• Capsules of various organs and glands (e.g., testis, sclera, periosteum, perichondrium)

On the other hand, dense regular collagen fibers are found in tendons.
questions.learning: Dense irregular — The area marked is the reticular dermis. It is made up of dense irregular connective tissue.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: In a neuron, an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) is generated following activation of inhibitory synapses. This hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic membrane occurs due to movement of which of the following ions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Potassium (K⁺) efflux

Inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs) cause hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic membrane, making it less likely to generate an action potential. This occurs primarily due to potassium efflux or chloride influx.

Key points:

• Opening of K⁺ channels → K⁺ moves out → hyperpolarization
• Opening of Cl⁻ channels → Cl⁻ moves in → hyperpolarization
• Both mechanisms increase negativity inside the cell
• Common inhibitory neurotransmitters: GABA, glycine

Why options are incorrect:

• A. Na⁺ influx and B. Ca²⁺ influx cause depolarization (excitatory)
• D. Cl⁻ efflux would depolarize, not hyperpolarize
questions.learning: Potassium (K⁺) efflux Inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs) cause hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic membrane, making it less likely to generate an action potential.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman who underwent dilatation and curettage previously, now presents with amenorrhea. The urine pregnancy test is negative. HSG revealed a honeycomb appearance in the uterine cavity.What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Asherman syndrome

The given clinical features, history and hysteroscopy are suggestive of Asherman syndrome.

Asherman syndrome refers to the presence of adhesion within the endometrial cavity. It is also called uterine synechiae and can be asymptomatic tiny bands or can completely or almost completely obliterate the endometrial cavity. It can occur as a result of trauma to the endometrium following vigorous uterine curettage, tuberculous endometritis, pelvic radiation, or endometrial ablation.

It causes secondary amenorrhoea, oligomenorrhoea, dysmenorrhoea, habitual abortion and infertility depending upon the extent of uterine cavity obliteration.

Asherman syndrome (uterine synechiae) is classified as follows:

* Mild: <25% adhesion involves the uterine cavity, flimsy adhesions involving the fundus and tubal ostia.

* Moderate: 25–70% adhesion of the endometrial surfaces, but no agglutination of the uterine wall.

* Severe: 75% adhesions with agglutination and thick adhesions.

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) may show honeycomb or moth-eaten appearance. Definitive diagnosis requires hysteroscopy as polyps, leiomyomas, air bubbles and blood clots may masquerade as adhesions.

Treatment involves hysteroscopic lysis of the adhesions.

The image below shows a moth-eaten appearance on hysterosalpingography
questions.learning: Asherman syndrome — The given clinical features, history and hysteroscopy are suggestive of Asherman syndrome. Asherman syndrome refers to the presence of adhesion within the endometrial cavity.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs act on sodium channels and potentiate slow sodium inactivation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lacosamide

Lacosamide is a drug acting on sodium channel and potentiating slow sodium inactivation.

Lacosamide acts by blocking the voltage-gated sodium channels. It is used as adjunctive therapy for focal-onset seizures in patients older than 17 years.

It is the first anti-seizure medication that limits persistent repetitive firing, the neuronal firing pattern typical of focal seizures, and prolongs the gradual inactivation of voltage-gated Na+ channels. Additionally, lacosamide binds to the phosphoprotein collapsing response mediator protein-2 (CRMP-2), which is mostly expressed in the nervous system and has a role in controlling axonal outgrowth and neuronal differentiation.

The role of CRMP-2 binding in seizure control is unknown.

Therapeutic Uses:

• It is used for both monotherapy and add-on therapy for focal-onset seizures in patients 17 years and older.
• It is mostly beneficial in hospitalized patients because it is available in an intravenous formulation, has minimal hepatic metabolism, and has no adverse respiratory effects.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct arrangement for the levels of Health Care?
options: 1→ Medical colleges and Hospitals, 2→CHC, 3 → subcentre and PHC
1 → CHC, 2→ Subcentre, PHC , 3→ Medical colleges and Hospitals
1→Subcentre and PHC, 2→ CHC, 3→Medical colleges and Hospitals

Correct answer: D. 1→Subcentre and PHC, 2→ CHC, 3→Medical colleges and Hospitals

The correct arrangement for the levels of Health Care is as follows, Primary, Subcentre and PHC → Secondary, CHC→ Tertiary, Medical colleges and Hospitals.

The NPHCE was established for geriatric care and includes provisions at primary, secondary, and tertiary levels.

Centres
Services according to NPHCE

PHCs (primary)

• Weekly geriatric clinics at PHC.
• Treatment of minor ailments.
• Referral services to higher centres.

Sub-centres (primary)

questions.text: The duration for which copper T 380 A remains effective is referred to as its shelf life.
questions.explanation: The Copper T 380 A (CuT 380A) is one of the most effective and widely used long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARC). The question asks for its effective duration, often clinically termed its lifespan rather than just "shelf life" (which technically refers to storage time). The Copper T 380 A is FDA-approved for 10 years of continuous protection against pregnancy. Option A (3 years) corresponds to older CuT 200 models. Option B (5 years) is the typical duration for the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) like Mirena or the CuT 375. Option C (7 years) is not a standard duration for most commonly available IUDs. The CuT 380 A contains a larger amount of copper (380 ) than previous models, allowing for its significantly extended duration of action. Therefore, it is a highly cost-effective option for long-term birth control, requiring replacement only once every decade

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is considered the treatment of choice for managing central diabetes insipidus?
questions.explanation: Central Diabetes Insipidus (DI) is caused by a deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH/Vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary, leading to polyuria and polydipsia. Desmopressin (dDAVP) is the preferred treatment because it is a synthetic analog of vasopressin with high selectivity for V2 receptors in the collecting ducts of the kidney. It has a longer duration of action than natural ADH and can be administered intranasally, orally, or parenterally. Insulin (Option A) is used for Diabetes Mellitus, not DI. Diazoxide (Option C) is used for hypertensive emergencies or insulinomas. Chlorpropamide (Option D) is a sulfonylurea that can sensitize the kidney to ADH in partial central DI, but it is not the first-line "preferred" treatment due to the risk of hypoglycemia. Desmopressin provides effective control of water excretion with minimal V1-mediated vasoconstrictive side effects. Therefore, Desmopressin is the gold standard for hormone replacement therapy in patients with a confirmed diagnosis of central diabetes insipidus
questions.learning: Central Diabetes Insipidus (DI) is caused by a deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH/Vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary, leading to polyuria and polydipsia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the fluid of choice in pediatric patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. DNS

In pediatric patients, maintenance fluid therapy should provide both water and glucose to prevent hypoglycemia and ketosis; hence dextrose-containing fluids are commonly used.

• DNS (dextrose normal saline) provides glucose along with sodium, making it suitable for many pediatric maintenance needs
• Children have limited glycogen stores and are prone to hypoglycemia during illness or fasting
• Pure crystalloids like normal saline or Ringer lactate do not provide glucose
• 5% dextrose alone lacks electrolytes and is not appropriate for routine use
• In emergency resuscitation (e.g., shock), isotonic fluids like normal saline are preferred initially

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: All of the following statements are true for descriptors of central tendency except:
options: Mode is affected by extreme values
Mean is affected by extreme values
Median is calculated by overall observation
Mode can be used as a qualitative data descriptor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mode is affected by extreme values

Mode is not affected by extreme values in a given set of data.

The mean of a given set of data is responsive to each and every value in the distribution. Thus, the mean is the measure of central tendency which is maximally affected by extreme values (option B). It is usually an inappropriate measure for describing skewed distributions. However, repeated samples from the same population will always tend to have similar means. Mean is able to resist fluctuations between different samples drawn from the same population better than mode or median.

To obtain the median of a given set of data, the values are first arranged in ascending or descending order of magnitude, and then the value of the middle observation is noted. Since the data has to be first arranged in order before the median can be determined, an overall observation is necessary for its calculation (option C).

Mode is the observed value in the frequency distribution that occurs with the greatest frequency. It is completely uninfluenced by extreme values in the distribution. The mode can be used to describe qualitative data (option D).
questions.learning: Mode is affected by extreme values Mode is not affected by extreme values in a given set of data. The mean of a given set of data is responsive to each and every value in the distribution.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A mother complains that her child is reluctant when it comes to taking feeds appropriately. Her 15-month-old boy has a length-for-age ≤ –2 SD below the median. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Moderate stunting

This child with a length-for-age ≤ –2 SD below the median is having moderate stunting.

The anthropometric measures used are weight for age, height for age, weight for height, BMI, and mid-upper arm circumference.

* Low weight for height, or wasting, indicates acute malnutrition. It is also called as wasting as a result of a recent food deficit or an acute illness such as diarrhea.

* High weight-for-height indicates overweight.

* Low height-for-age, or stunting, indicates chronic malnutrition. This is the best indicator of long-term nutritional status in the pediatric population.

* Low weight for age, or underweight indicates acute or chronic malnutrition. It does not differentiate between wasting and stunting. Hence, it has limited clinical significance.

Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is an age-independent parameter used for screening wasting in children. Classification of nutritional status depending on the anthropometry (height/length for age) is given in the pearl below.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25 year old woman comes for her regular antenatal check up. Which arterial gas abnormality is expected to be seen in this woman?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chronic respiratory alkalosis

Chronic respiratory alkalosis is a normal physiologic change seen in pregnancy.

Progesterone directly stimulates central respiratory centers to increase tidal volume and minute ventilation. This leads to increased PaO2 and decreased PaCO2. This paradoxically causes physiological dyspnea. It is an increased awareness of a desire to breathe.

This results in chronic respiratory alkalosis. Bicarbonate level is decreased from 26 to 22 mmol/L(approximately) in metabolic compensation of respiratory alkalosis.
questions.learning: Chronic respiratory alkalosis Chronic respiratory alkalosis is a normal physiologic change seen in pregnancy. Progesterone directly stimulates central respiratory centers to increase tidal volume and minute ventilation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following ions in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is responsible for the resorption of divalent ions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. K+

Potassium (K+) in the thick ascending limb of loop of Henle is responsible for the resorption of divalent ions such as, calcium, magnesium, etc.

This resorption is driven by the lumen-positive potential difference across the cells of the thick ascending limb, created by the potassium leak into the lumen.

Mechanism of resorption in thick ascending limb:

• The luminal membrane contains a Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter.
• There is net resorption of Na+, K+ and Cl- in the thick ascending limb as follows:
• All three ions are transported into the cell on the cotransporter.
• Na+ is extruded from the cell by the Na+-K+ ATPase in the basolateral membrane.
• K+ and Cl- diffuse through channels in the basolateral membrane, down their respective electrochemical gradients.
• Most of the K+ leaves the cell across the basolateral membrane; the remaining portion of K+ however diffuses back into the lumen.
• This K+ leak into the lumen generates a positive electrochemical potential difference in the lumen.
• This lumen-positive potential difference drives the resorption of ions such as sodium(Na+), magnesium (Mg2+), calcium (Ca+),etc.,

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A child has been diagnosed with Turner syndrome. Which of the following findings are characteristic features of this condition?
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome is a chromosomal disorder affecting females. One of its most characteristic physical features is a webbed neck (pterygium colli) resulting from cystic hygromas in utero. Other classic findings include short stature (Option B is incorrect), a broad chest with widely spaced nipples ("shield chest"), and primary amenorrhea due to streak ovaries. Increased carrying angle (cubitus valgus) of the arms is another common feature (Option C is incorrect as it is increased, not decreased). Gynecomastia (Option D) is the enlargement of male breast tissue and is not a feature of Turner syndrome. Patients also have a higher incidence of congenital heart defects, most notably coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve. Turner syndrome is often diagnosed during infancy due to lymphedema or during puberty due to a lack of secondary sexual characteristics and delayed growth. Management involves growth hormone therapy to maximize height and estrogen replacement to induce puberty and maintain bone health
questions.learning: Turner syndrome is a chromosomal disorder affecting females. One of its most characteristic physical features is a webbed neck (pterygium colli) resulting from cystic hygromas in utero.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was undertaken to evaluate the effect of Dietary modification on Serum cholesterol. A group of 100 people were chosen. Their mean cholesterol levels were measured before and after dietary modification. Which statistical test should be applied to test significance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Paired student’s t-test

The variable measured is serum cholesterol, which is:

• Continuous data
• Expressed numerically (mg/dL)

Continuous data → usually analyzed using tests comparing means.

The study compares mean serum cholesterol levels measured before and after intervention in the same group of individuals, producing paired continuous data.

A paired Student’s t-test is appropriate to assess whether the mean difference before and after dietary modification is statistically significant. Chi-square and McNemar tests are used for categorical data, while odds ratio measures association rather than testing mean differences.
questions.learning: Paired student’s t-test — The variable measured is serum cholesterol, which is: • Continuous data • Expressed numerically (mg/dL) Continuous data → usually analyzed using tests comparing means.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During a health education session, people cannot understand your few technical words during the chat, and it’s a miscommunication. This is which type of barrier?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Semantic barrier

A semantic barrier arises when words, symbols, or language used by the communicator are not understood by the audience.

Use of technical or medical jargon during health education can lead to misunderstanding and ineffective communication.

Example:

If a health worker says “hypertension”, people may not understand unless it is explained as “high blood pressure.”

Overcoming semantic barriers requires using simple language, local terms, and culturally appropriate expressions to ensure message clarity.

| Barrier | Main Problem | Medical Example

| ------- | ------------ | ---------------

| Cultural | Difference in beliefs/customs | Refusal of blood transfusion for religious reasons

| Physiological | Physical disability | Deaf patient cannot hear instructions

| Psychological | Emotional/mental factors | Anxiety causing misunderstanding

| Semantic | Language/jargon issue | Patient confused by medical terminology
questions.learning: Semantic barrier — A semantic barrier arises when words, symbols, or language used by the communicator are not understood by the audience. Use of technical or medical jargon during health education can lead to misunderstanding and ineffective communication.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The recombinant form of vaccine to prevent cervical cancer has which of the following proteins?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. L1

The recombinant HPV vaccine use virus-like particles (VLPs) that consists of the HPV L1 major capsid protein. The L1 protein self-assembles into VLPs when expressed in eukaryotic cells.

These VLPs contain the same epitopes as the HPV virion. However they do not contain genetic material and cannot transmit infection. The immunogenicity of the HPV vaccines relies on the development of conformational neutralizing antibodies to epitopes displayed on viral capsids.

The nonavalent HPV vaccine works against strains 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58. It is usually commercialized in the name of Gardasil-9. It has received expanded indication which now includes the prevention of oropharyngeal and other head and neck cancers.

As per the December 2022 WHO updated dose schedules on HPV vaccines, the recommendations for different age groups are as follows:

• 1 or 2 doses schedule for the primary target of girls aged 9–14 years.
• 1 or 2 doses schedule for young women aged 15–20 years.
• 2 doses with a 6-month interval for women older than 21 years.
•

A minimum of 2 doses and when feasible 3 doses remain necessary for those known to be immunocompromised and/or HIV-infected.
questions.learning: L1 The recombinant HPV vaccine use virus-like particles (VLPs) that consists of the HPV L1 major capsid protein. The L1 protein self-assembles into VLPs when expressed in eukaryotic cells.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which one of the following is an abnormal parameter in accordance with WHO Semen Analysis Criteria (Normal reference value)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Viscosity > 4

According to WHO semen analysis criteria, increased semen viscosity is an abnormal finding. Hyperviscous semen impairs sperm motility and may contribute to male infertility.

Why not the other options?

• A. Volume ≥2 mL: Normal (older WHO criteria; current WHO lower reference is ≥1.4–1.5 mL).
• B. Viscosity >4: Abnormal. Normal semen liquefies within 15–60 minutes and should not be excessively viscous.
• C. Progressive forward motility of sperms >50%: Normal (older WHO criteria; current WHO lower reference is ≥32% progressive motility).
• D. Normal morphology of sperms >14%: Normal (older WHO strict criteria; current WHO lower reference is ≥4% normal forms using Kruger strict criteria).
questions.learning: Viscosity > 4 According to WHO semen analysis criteria, increased semen viscosity is an abnormal finding. Hyperviscous semen impairs sperm motility and may contribute to male infertility.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following neurons predominantly fire during forceful expiration?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ventral group of neurons

Ventral groups of neurons fire, when forceful expiration is needed like during heavy exercise.

Dorsal group of neurons control the normal inspiration and expiration.

Pneumotaxic center limits the duration of inspiration.
questions.learning: Ventral group of neurons Ventral groups of neurons fire, when forceful expiration is needed like during heavy exercise. Dorsal group of neurons control the normal inspiration and expiration.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An adult man presents to the outpatient department with painful scrotal swelling and fever. The swelling involves the tunica vaginalis and is associated with fluid accumulation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A hydrocele is defined as an abnormal collection of serous fluid within the layers of the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. While often painless, an acute or infected hydrocele (pyocele) can present with pain and fever. The characteristic "fluid accumulation" within the tunica vaginalis is the hallmark of this condition. A varicocele (Option A) involves the dilation of the pampiniform plexus of veins, often described as a "bag of worms," and does not typically involve fluid accumulation in the tunica. A cystocele (Option B) is the herniation of the bladder into the vagina, which is anatomically impossible in this male patient. Torsion of the testis (Option D) is a surgical emergency presenting with sudden, severe pain and a high-riding testis, but it is primarily a vascular compromise rather than a fluid collection in the tunica vaginalis. Given the specific description of fluid within the tunica vaginalis, hydrocele is the most accurate diagnosis
questions.learning: A hydrocele is defined as an abnormal collection of serous fluid within the layers of the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. While often painless, an acute or infected hydrocele (pyocele) can present with pain and fever.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with hypertriglyceridemia is considered for niacin therapy. She is a known diabetic managed adequately with sugars well under control. Why should niacin be used cautiously in this patient?
options: It can cause scleroderma which makes injecting insulin difficult.
It can increase the metabolism of oral hypoglyemic drugs.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It can cause hyperglycemia.

Niacin should be used cautiously in diabetics as it can cause hyperglycemia.

Niacin induces insulin resistance and also decreases glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, which may result in severe hyperglycemia. When niacin is prescribed for patients with known or suspected diabetes, blood glucose levels should be monitored at least once a week.
questions.learning: Niacin should be used cautiously in diabetics as it can cause hyperglycemia. Niacin induces insulin resistance and also decreases glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, which may result in severe hyperglycemia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following helps manage nausea and vomiting during pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Taking small and frequent meals

Taking small and frequent meals during pregnancy can help alleviate nausea and vomiting, commonly known as morning sickness.

Pregnancy can affect glucose metabolism, causing fluctuations in blood sugar levels, which may trigger nausea. Eating small, frequent meals helps maintain more stable blood sugar levels, reducing the likelihood of nausea associated with hypoglycemia.

The growing uterus exerts pressure on the stomach, reducing its capacity and increasing the sensation of fullness. Large meals can cause significant gastric distension, which may exacerbate nausea and discomfort. Smaller meals are easier to digest and are less likely to cause these symptoms.

During pregnancy, the hormone progesterone relaxes smooth muscle, including the gastrointestinal tract, which can slow gastric emptying and contribute to nausea. Smaller, more frequent meals may help by ensuring that food moves more consistently through the digestive system, reducing the likelihood of stomach contents lingering and causing nausea.

Pregnancy hormones, such as human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and estrogen, are associated with nausea and vomiting. While the exact mechanism is not fully understood, frequent, small meals may help modulate the body's response to these hormones by preventing an empty stomach, which can sometimes worsen nausea.
questions.learning: Taking small and frequent meals Taking small and frequent meals during pregnancy can help alleviate nausea and vomiting, commonly known as morning sickness.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A baby was brought in with complaints of intermittent feculent discharge from the umbilicus. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ileal diverticulum

The presence of feculent discharge at the umbilicus with the persistence of the vitellointestinal duct is suggestive of vitelline fistula which occurs due to an ileal diverticulum.

The given clinical image is that of a congenital umbilical anomaly such as patent urachus, urachal cyst, and vitelline cyst (resulting from the persistence of omphalomesenteric duct). The next best step is the USG abdomen to diagnose if the anomaly is cystic, fibrous or fistula and its connections.

Vitello intestinal duct or omphalomesenteric duct is the connection between the yolk sac and the midgut during embryonic life, which eventually gets obliterated. The persistence of the vitellointestinal duct leads to various abnormalities depending on which part of the duct remains patent.

• Persistence of the proximal intestinal end of the duct leads to the Ileal diverticula/Meckel’s diverticula.
• Persistence of the distal end near the umbilicus leads to the umbilical polyp or sinus.
• Persistence of the distal end with mucus retention leads to the cyst, which may be associated with the intestine or the umbilicus by a fibrous band.
• A fully patent vitellointestinal duct can lead to an enterocutaneous fistula.

Patent urachus occurs due to the failure of urachus to obliterate, resulting in a connection between the bladder and the umbilicus.

Urachal cyst occurs when the urachus fails to obliterate but there is no connection between the bladder and the umbilicus.

The image below shows a urachal cyst (UC) attached to Meckel’s diverticulum (MD) on one side and a urinary bladder (UB) on the other side with a patent tract- urachus (U).
questions.learning: Ileal diverticulum — The presence of feculent discharge at the umbilicus with the persistence of the vitellointestinal duct is suggestive of vitelline fistula which occurs due to an ileal diverticulum.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with repetitive episodes of heartburn and chest pain. What is the most common condition that causes these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Esophagitis

This patient is most likely suffering from dyspepsia and the most common cause of dyspepsia among the given options is esophagitis.

Dyspepsia refers to symptoms of epigastric pain, burning, postprandial fullness or early satiety, sometimes with heartburn condition based on the symptoms is esophagitis. Gastroesophageal reflux which causes esophagitis is the common cause of dyspepsia.

Esophagitis is the most common cause of heartburn and non-cardiac chest pain. The reflux of gastric acid into the lower oesophagus is the most frequent cause of esophagitis. The most common cause of gastroesophageal reflux is transient lower oesophagal sphincter relaxation.

Clinical significance: Reflux esophagitis → chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) → Barrett oesophagus → adenocarcinoma

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old female with a history of severe persistent asthma is currently on inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) and long-acting beta-agonists (LABA). Despite adherence to therapy, she continues to have seasonal exacerbations. Her FEV1 is within normal limits. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated serum IgE levels. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Subcutaneous omalizumab

Severe persistent asthma with elevated IgE and ongoing exacerbations despite ICS + LABA indicates allergic asthma.

Omalizumab is an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody used as add-on therapy in such patients with normal baseline lung function.

Systemic steroids or IV bronchodilators are reserved for acute severe exacerbations, not long-term control.

| C. Omalizumab ✅ | Anti-IgE biologic | ✔ Severe allergic asthma | ✔ Correct | IgE-targeted therapy

| D. IV corticosteroids | Acute inflammation control | Severe exacerbation | ❌ Chronic control needed | Short-term use only

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the appropriate next step in management for a primigravida at 26 weeks of gestation who presents with a blood pressure of 150/90 mm Hg?
questions.explanation: The presentation of a blood pressure of 150/90 mmHg at 26 weeks of gestation in a primigravida suggests a potential diagnosis of pre-eclampsia. Pre-eclampsia is defined by new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks of pregnancy accompanied by proteinuria or organ dysfunction. The immediate and most essential next step to differentiate simple gestational hypertension from pre-eclampsia is a urine dipstick to screen for proteinuria. Uric acid levels (Option A), liver function tests (Option B), and a complete blood count (Option C) are important follow-up investigations to assess the severity of pre-eclampsia or the development of HELLP syndrome, but they are not the primary screening step. If the urine dipstick is positive (1+ or more), further quantification via a 24-hour urine protein or protein-creatinine ratio is warranted. Therefore, checking for proteinuria via dipstick is the critical initial management step in a pregnant woman with elevated blood pressure

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A student went on a trip to Jaisalmer, where the temp is 40 degrees, and the relative humidity is 20%. What will the mechanism of heat loss be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Evaporation

Evaporation is the mechanism of heat loss in this student.

Evaporation happens when perspiration evaporates from the skin. This is a significant source of heat loss during activity but not at rest in normal temperature settings.

When the temperature of the surroundings is more than that of the skin, the body gains heat by both radiation and conduction. Under these conditions, the heat can be lost from the body only by evaporation or sweating.

Different methods of heat loss:

• Radiation is heat loss in the form of infrared rays. (Option B)
• Conduction is heat loss that occurs by direct contact with an object. (Option C and D)
• Convection is heat loss resulting from air movement
questions.learning: Evaporation Evaporation is the mechanism of heat loss in this student. Evaporation happens when perspiration evaporates from the skin.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Oral contraceptives act by all of the following mechanisms except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increase GnRH release

Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) do not cause an increase in GnRH, they inhibit the release of GnRH.

OCPs act via the following mechanisms:

• Inhibiting ovulation - Both estrogen and progesterone act on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis to inhibit the release of GnRH (and thus subsequently LH and FSH). Seen in combined oral pills.
• Preventing implantation - Under the effect of OCPs, endometrial stroma undergoes hypoplasia, with atrophy of glands. This makes it unfavorable for implantation of the embryo. Seen primarily with mifepristone, but is a secondary mechanism of action with progesterone-only pills as well.
• Cervical mucus becomes thick and scanty under the effect of progesterone. This makes it difficult for sperm to enter. Seen in progesterone-only pills.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the condition associated with the murmur depicted in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mitral regurgitation

The given image shows pansystolic murmur, and it is associated with mitral regurgitation.

Mitral regurgitation may result from an abnormality or disease process that affects functional components of the mitral valve apparatus.

Causes of mitral regurgitation include

• Acute: Blunt trauma, papillary muscle rupture, infective endocarditis
• Chronic: Mitral valve prolapse, rheumatic fever, healed infective endocarditis, ischemic cardiomyopathy, HOCM, etc.

A pansystolic murmur of at least grade III/VI intensity can be auscultated in chronic severe mitral regurgitation. It is heard best at the apex and radiates to the axilla. Ruptured chordae tendineae may produce a murmur with a cooing or “seagull” quality, whereas a flail leaflet may produce a murmur with a musical quality.

S1 is generally absent or soft. Wide splitting of S2 may occur due to premature closure of the aortic valve. A low-pitched third heart sound (S3) may occur following A2. S4 can also be audible in patients with acute severe MR.

The image below depicts the pansystolic murmur in mitral regurgitation.

Other options:

Option B: An early diastolic murmur can be auscultated in chronic aortic regurgitation. It is high-pitched and blowing in character. It is best heard in the third intercostal space along the left sternal edge. It may be accompanied by a mid-systolic ejection murmur in isolated AR or the Austin Flint murmur in severe AR. The latter is a soft, low-pitched, rumbling, mid-to-late diastolic murmur produced by the displacement of the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve by the AR stream.

A2 is usually absent, and occasionally, S4 also may be heard.

Option C:  In aortic stenosis, an ejection mid-systolic murmur can be auscultated. It begins after the first heart sound (S1), increases in intensity toward the middle of the ejection, and ends just before aortic valve closure. It is low-pitched, rough, and rasping in character. It is best heard at the base of the heart, most commonly in the second right intercostal space.

A systolic ejection click can be heard in young patients with a bicuspid aortic valve, but disappears as the valves become calcified. A2 and P2 may be heard at the same time, or A2 may follow P2, resulting in the paradoxical splitting of the second heart sound (S2). The fourth heart sound (S4) is often heard at the apex, indicating the presence of left ventricular hypertrophy.

Option D: In mitral stenosis, a diastolic murmur can be heard during auscultation.
questions.learning: Mitral regurgitation — The given image shows pansystolic murmur, and it is associated with mitral regurgitation. Mitral regurgitation may result from an abnormality or disease process that affects functional components of the mitral valve apparatus.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Shifting fluid sign is seen in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Exudative RD

The presence of shifting fluid is a hallmark feature of serous or exudative retinal detachment.

In serous retinal detachment, there is a subretinal accumulation of the serous fluid mostly due to the breakdown in the blood-retinal barrier. When the position of the head is altered, the fluid shifts to the dependent portion. Serous retinal detachment has a smooth convex configuration. A retinal tear or preretinal traction is absent.

Other options:
Option B: Traction RD has a concave configuration and breaks are absent. Retinal mobility is severely reduced and shifting fluid is absent.
Option C: Rhegmatogenous RD presents with tobacco dust in anterior vitreous with substantial vitreous blood or inflammatory cells. Retinal breaks are also seen.
questions.learning: Exudative RD — The presence of shifting fluid is a hallmark feature of serous or exudative retinal detachment. In serous retinal detachment, there is a subretinal accumulation of the serous fluid mostly due to the breakdown in the blood-retinal barrier.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with weight gain, hair thinning, and dry skin and is diagnosed with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Which autoantibody is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is a chronic autoimmune condition and the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions. It is characterized by the presence of anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies, which target the TPO enzyme essential for thyroid hormone synthesis. These antibodies mediate the autoimmune destruction of the gland, leading to the patient's symptoms of weight gain, hair thinning, and dry skin. Anti-TSH antibodies (Option B) are not a diagnostic marker for this condition. Anti-TBG antibodies (Option C) are rare and lack clinical relevance for Hashimoto’s diagnosis. Long-acting thyroid-stimulating antibodies (LATS) (Option D) are pathognomonic for Graves' disease, which causes hyperthyroidism rather than the hypothyroidism seen in Hashimoto's. Laboratory confirmation of Hashimoto's typically relies on elevated TSH, low free T4, and positive anti-TPO titers. Therefore, anti-TPO is the most relevant diagnostic antibody

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the dye and filter used to diagnose corneal ulcers?
options: Fluorescein dye - visualized under green filter
Fluorescein dye - visualized under cobalt blue filter
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fluorescein dye - visualized under cobalt blue filter

The image given is of a dendritic ulcer seen in recurrent herpetic keratitis. Corneal ulcers can be detected with the help of fluorescein sodium dye and a cobalt-blue filter. The epithelial defect of the cornea appears opaque green with a cobalt blue filter.

Fluorescein staining of the cornea is carried out with a disposable autoclaved filter paper strip impregnated with the dye. The denuded epithelial area seen in corneal abrasions or ulcers appears brilliant green when stained with fluorescein. Under a cobalt blue light, the stained area appears opaque green.

Other options:

Lissamine green dye is used to stain devitalized cells of the cornea and conjunctiva. It is used to diagnose ocular surface disorders, like dry eye.
questions.learning: Fluorescein dye - visualized under cobalt blue filter The image given is of a dendritic ulcer seen in recurrent herpetic keratitis. Corneal ulcers can be detected with the help of fluorescein sodium dye and a cobalt-blue filter.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presents with cervical lymphadenopathy, a dull tympanic membrane, hearing loss, and tinnitus in the left ear. Tympanometry shows a type B curve. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In an elderly patient, the triad of a unilateral serous otitis media (evidenced by the dull tympanic membrane and type B tympanogram), unilateral hearing loss/tinnitus, and neck nodes (cervical lymphadenopathy) is highly suggestive of nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). The tumor originates in the nasopharynx (often the Rosenmüller fossa) and obstructs the eustachian tube opening, leading to fluid accumulation in the middle ear. Chronic suppurative otitis media (Option A) would show a perforated eardrum and discharge. A Glomus tumor (Option B) classically causes pulsatile tinnitus and a "red reflex" behind the drum. Sensorineural hearing loss (Option D) would not explain the fluid-related type B tympanogram curve . Any elderly adult presenting with new-onset unilateral middle ear effusion must undergo a nasopharyngoscopy to rule out NPC. Therefore, given the specific combination of otological symptoms and nodal involvement, nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the prioritized diagnosis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
Match the following disorders causing secondary amenorrhoea with their respective lab findings.

Condition
Lab markers

1. Sheehan's syndrome
A. Normal FSH, Normal LH, Normal estradiol

2. Premature Ovarian failure
B. High LH, Low FSH, Low estradiol

3. PCOS
C. Low LH, Low FSH, Low estradiol

4. Asherman's syndrome
D. High LH, High FSH, Low estradiol
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1-C, 2-D, 3-B, 4-A

The correct answer is 1-C, 2-D, 3-B, 4-A.

Condition
Lab markers

1. Sheehan's syndrome
C. Low LH, Low FSH, Low estradiol

2. Premature Ovarian failure
D. High LH, High FSH, Low estradiol

3. PCOS
B. High LH, Low FSH, Low estradiol

4. Asherman's syndrome
A. Normal FSH, Normal LH, Normal estradiol

Secondary amenorrhoea is the absence of menses for more than three months in girls or women who previously had regular menstrual cycles or six months in girls or women who had irregular menses.

Premature Ovarian failure or premature menopause is the development of menopause before the age of 40 years. It is diagnosed when at least 2 serum FSH levels are elevated (>40 mIU/l) when measured at least 1 month apart in a woman <40 years. The other findings consistent with POF include low estradiol and an elevated FSH/LH ratio.

Asherman's syndrome is the presence of uterine synechiae, due to the destruction of large areas of the endometrium, most commonly as a result of trauma to the endometrium following pregnancy-related curettages. Oligomenorrhoea, amenorrhoea, dysmenorrhoea, abortion, and infertility are seen with uterine synechiae. The laboratory investigations and hormonal assays are generally normal in isolated cases of uterine synechiae. Diagnosis is generally established using hysteroscopy. Moth-eaten appearance on hysterosalpingography suggests a diagnosis of Asherman syndrome. Treatment is by hysteroscopic adhesiolysis.

PCOS is a multisystem, metabolic, endocrine dysfunction that commonly occurs among women in the reproductive age group. The endocrinological changes reflecting in the assays are summarized in the pearl attached below.

Sheehan's syndrome/ pituitary apoplexy is hemorrhagic infarction of large pituitary adenomas or pituitary infarction due to traumatic major blood loss. If this blood loss occurs during delivery, it's called Sheehan's syndrome. Affected women may present with panhypopituitarism and may have persistent hypotension, tachycardia, hypoglycemia, and lactation failure. The most prominent among symptoms are lactation failure (due to deficiency of prolactin) and postpartum amenorrhea (due to deficiency of gonadotropins).

Note: Estradiol level in PCOS is low in comparison to Estrone (E1).

The common differentials for the presentation for secondary amenorrhea and the lab evaluation is summarized in the flowchart shown below.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 10-year- old child with a two-year history of recurrent fractures, blue sclera, dental abnormalities, and a positive family history?
questions.explanation: Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI), often called "brittle bone disease," is a genetic disorder of Type I collagen synthesis. The clinical presentation is classic: frequent fractures from minimal trauma, blue sclera (due to thinning of the scleral collagen allowing the underlying choroid to show through), and dentinogenesis imperfecta (dental abnormalities). The positive family history supports its autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Scurvy (Option A) involves Vitamin C deficiency and causes bleeding gums and subperiosteal hemorrhages. Rickets (Option B) is due to Vitamin D deficiency and presents with bony deformities like bowing of legs and "rachitic rosary". Osteomalacia (Option D) is the adult form of rickets, involving defective bone mineralization rather than a primary collagen defect. OI is diagnosed clinically and confirmed by genetic testing. There is no cure, so management focuses on preventing fractures and using bisphosphonates to increase bone density. Therefore, the ocular and dental findings confirm the diagnosis

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient develops Achilles tendonitis along with swelling of the leg after taking an antibiotic. What is the most likely mechanism of action of the drug responsible for these adverse effects?
options: Inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
Inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis at 50S subunit
Inhibition of bacterial folic acid synthesis
Inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis
questions.explanation: The development of Achilles tendonitis and swelling is a well-documented adverse effect of fluoroquinolones (e.g., Ciprofloxacin, Levofloxacin). These antibiotics work by inhibiting two essential bacterial enzymes: DNA gyrase (Topoisomerase II) and Topoisomerase IV. This inhibition interferes with negative DNA recoiling and strand separation, leading to the failure of DNA replication and transcription, which ultimately causes bacterial cell death. Option B (50S protein synthesis inhibition) describes the mechanism of macrolides. Option C (folic acid inhibition) describes sulfonamides. Option D (cell wall inhibition) is the mechanism for beta-lactams like penicillins. Fluoroquinolones are associated with a significantly increased risk of tendon rupture, particularly in the elderly or those also taking corticosteroids

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presented with knee pain. The x-ray of his knee joint is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osteoclastoma

The given clinical scenario and the x-ray showing a lytic lesion at the end of a long bone with a soap-bubble appearance suggest a giant cell tumor (GCT)/ osteoclastoma.

Osteoclastoma is a benign but locally aggressive tumor that usually affects young adults of age 20 to 40 years with slight female predominance. It affects the ends of long bones, involving metaphysis/epiphysis of long bones. GCT is most commonly seen in the distal femur, proximal tibia, proximal humerus, and distal radius. Common presenting complaints are swelling and vague pain. Sometimes, the patient presents for the first time with a pathological fracture through the lesion.

Important X-ray features of a GCT:

• A solitary, possibly loculated, lytic lesion in the epiphysis.
• Eccentric location, most often subchondral.
• Expansion of the overlying cortex.
• Soap bubble appearance - The tumor is homogeneously lytic with trabeculae of the remnants of bone traversing it, giving it a loculated appearance called soap bubble appearance.
• No calcification within the tumor.
• No or minimal reactive sclerosis around the tumor.

Histologically, GCTs consist of undifferentiated spindle cells profusely interspersed with multi-nucleated giant cells. The tumor stroma is well-vascularized with bands of cellular or collagenous fibrous tissue.

The image below shows the histopathology of osteoclastoma:

The treatment of choice for GCT is extended curettage and bone grafting.

• GCT in the relatively insignificant bone like the distal ulna, clavicle, and proximal fibula is treated by resection without reconstruction.
• Bisphosphonates have been shown to reduce the proliferation of osteoclasts and hence have been shown to stabilize local and metastatic disease.
• Radiation can be used for spinal or sacral tumors.

Other options:

Option A: Chondroblastoma is a benign tumor that usually appears as well-circumscribed round or oval lytic lesions in the center of the epiphysis of a long bone. It presents as a painful mass that causes effusion or stiffness. It is most commonly seen in ages 10-20 years.

The following is an x-ray image of the knee showing chondroblastoma:

Option B: Osteochondromas are common benign bone tumors commonly present in adolescents. The lesions consist of a bony mass, often in the form of a stalk, produced by endochondral ossification of a growing cartilaginous cap. They are usually painless. The common sites of involvement are the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus.

The following is an x-ray image of the knee showing osteochondroma of the distal knee:

Option D: Fibrous dysplasia is a condition that affects bone development and is characterized by the replacement of the bone with fibrous tissue. The patient presents with a progressive limb deformity or a fracture through a previously asymptomatic lesion which often occurs in the second decade. Other symptoms include nonspecific bone pain, tenderness, and swelling in the affected area. The commonly involved sites are the proximal femur, tibia, pelvis, and foot.

Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia is associated with McCune-Albright syndrome.

Radiological findings include:

• Well-defined, expansile intramedullary lesions
• Hazy ground glass appearance is seen in the majority of cases
• Shepherd's crook deformity - Expansion with marked varus in the proximal femur

The given image shows the common locations of various bone tumors:

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue, easy bruising, and recurrent infections. Peripheral blood smear shows macrocytosis and dysplastic neutrophils with hyposegmented nuclei (pseudo–Pelger-Huët anomaly). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient's age and presentation of pancytopenia (fatigue/anemia, bruising/thrombocytopenia, and infections/leukopenia) suggest a bone marrow disorder. The definitive clue is the presence of dysplastic neutrophils with hyposegmented nuclei (pseudo-Pelger-Huët anomaly) and macrocytosis on the blood smear, which are classic features of Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS). MDS is a group of clonal bone marrow disorders characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis and a high risk of transformation to Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML). Iron Deficiency Anemia (Option A) would show microcytosis and is not associated with neutrophil dysplasia. Aplastic Anemia (Option C) presents with pancytopenia but the cells themselves are typically normal in morphology, not dysplastic. Anemia of Chronic Disease (Option D) is usually normocytic and doesn't explain the dysplasia or thrombocytopenia. MDS is often considered a "pre-leukemic" state. Diagnosis is confirmed with a bone marrow biopsy showing hypercellularity with characteristic dysplastic changes in one or more cell lines
questions.learning: The patient's age and presentation of pancytopenia (fatigue/anemia, bruising/thrombocytopenia, and infections/leukopenia) suggest a bone marrow disorder.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with a history of molar pregnancy six months ago now presents with persistent abdominal pain and distension. Her β-hCG levels remain elevated, and a chest X-ray reveals cannon-ball lesions. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of a prior molar pregnancy combined with persistently elevated beta-hCG levels is highly suggestive of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN), specifically choriocarcinoma. Choriocarcinoma is a malignant form of gestational trophoblastic disease that characteristically metastasizes early via the hematogenous route. The finding of "cannon-ball foci" on a chest X-ray is pathognomonic for pulmonary metastases from this malignancy. Endometriosis (Option B) typically presents with cyclical pelvic pain and does not involve elevated beta-hCG or lung nodules. Ovarian cysts (Option C) may cause distension but do not produce high hCG or metastatic lung patterns. Asherman’s syndrome (Option D) involves intrauterine adhesions leading to amenorrhea but is unrelated to trophoblastic tissue proliferation or hCG elevation. Therefore, given the specific history of molar gestation and the classic "cannon-ball" pulmonary metastases, the diagnosis is gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. Treatment usually involves chemotherapy, often methotrexate or multi-agent regimens, and has a generally good prognosis if identified promptly
questions.learning: The patient’s history of a prior molar pregnancy combined with persistently elevated beta-hCG levels is highly suggestive of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN), specifically choriocarcinoma.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The tip of the uncinate is attached superiorly to which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Middle turbinate

The uncinate process is a key structure in the lateral nasal wall that forms part of the osteomeatal complex, and its superior attachment is most commonly to the middle turbinate.

·         The uncinate process is a thin, curved bone of the ethmoid

·         It helps form the medial wall of the infundibulum (drainage pathway of frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses)

·         Superior attachment variations exist (middle turbinate, lamina papyracea, skull base),

but:

o    Most common attachment = middle turbinate

Clinical significance:

·         Determines the drainage pathway of frontal sinus

·         Important landmark in FESS (Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery)

Why not other options:

·         Middle meatus: Space, not an attachment site

·         Inferior turbinate: Not related to uncinate attachment

·         Ethmoid bulla: Lies posterior to uncinate, not a superior attachment

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions exhibit the given radiological findings?
questions.explanation: The Chest X-ray demonstrates multiple, large, discrete, and well-circumscribed bilateral nodules, a classic finding known as "cannon-ball metastasis". This pattern is highly characteristic of Lung metastasis, most commonly originating from primary tumors such as renal cell carcinoma, testicular seminoma, or choriocarcinoma. Miliary TB (Option A) presents with numerous tiny (1–2 mm), millet-seed-like nodules distributed evenly throughout the lungs. Aspergillosis (Option B) usually presents as a mass within a pre-existing cavity or as areas of consolidation. Consolidation (Option C) appears as a more confluent, ill-defined area of opacity, often within a single lobe, rather than multiple discrete round masses. Cannon-ball metastases typically signify an advanced, disseminated malignancy. Identifying this specific radiological pattern is a high-yield clinical clue that directs the search for a primary malignancy elsewhere in the body
questions.learning: The Chest X-ray demonstrates multiple, large, discrete, and well-circumscribed bilateral nodules, a classic finding known as "cannon-ball metastasis".

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: All the following are used for identification of a dead body except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nail

In forensic identification, biological samples containing rich DNA sources are preferred for establishing identity.

• Commonly used samples:

• Blood: High DNA yield → most reliable
• Muscle/tissues: Useful in decomposed bodies
• Hair (with root): Contains nuclear DNA

• Nails:

• Mainly composed of keratin (dead tissue)
• Poor DNA yield unless nail root is present
• Hence, not routinely used for identification

Forensic significance:

• Proper sample selection improves accuracy of DNA profiling
• Helps in mass disasters, decomposed bodies, and unidentified remains

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following diseases is characterized by destructive lymphoid infiltration of the thyroid gland leading to fibrosis and enlargement of the thyroid gland with an increased risk of developing thyroid lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis

Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas and is an autoimmune thyroid disorder characterized by destructive lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland, leading to progressive fibrosis and thyroid enlargement (goiter). Patients with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis have a significantly increased risk of developing primary thyroid lymphoma, particularly Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma (DLBCL) and MALT lymphoma.

• D. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis:

• Autoimmune destruction of the thyroid by T-lymphocyte-mediated inflammation.
• Associated with anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies.
• Increases the risk of primary thyroid lymphoma.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. de Quervain’s thyroiditis: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, usually post-viral, presents with a painful, tender thyroid and transient thyrotoxicosis.
• B. Multinodular goitre: Non-inflammatory enlargement of the thyroid with multiple nodules; not associated with thyroid lymphoma.
• C. Riedel’s thyroiditis: Rare fibrosing thyroiditis causing a hard, “woody” thyroid, but not associated with lymphoid infiltration or increased lymphoma risk.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which intestinal disorder is commonly associated with dermatitis herpetiformis?
questions.explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is a chronic, intensely pruritic, blistering skin condition that is considered the cutaneous manifestation of Celiac disease. Nearly all patients with DH have some degree of gluten-sensitive enteropathy (celiac disease), even if they do not have overt gastrointestinal symptoms. DH is characterized by symmetric, herpetiform (grouped) vesicles on extensor surfaces like the elbows and knees. Ulcerative colitis (Option A) and Crohn's disease (Option D) are forms of inflammatory bowel disease associated with other skin conditions like pyoderma gangrenosum or erythema nodosum, but not DH. Whipple's disease (Option B) is a rare systemic infection that causes malabsorption but is not associated with this specific skin disorder. The diagnosis of DH is confirmed by skin biopsy showing granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae. The primary treatment for both the skin and intestinal symptoms is a lifelong, strict gluten-free diet
questions.learning: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is a chronic, intensely pruritic, blistering skin condition that is considered the cutaneous manifestation of Celiac disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Ground-glass appearance on HRCT is seen in which of the following condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Silicosis

Silicosis on HRCT shows a ground-glass appearance.

Silicosis is due to the inhalation of crystalline silicon dioxide (silica) seen in individuals employed in sandblasting or rock mining. Macrophages phagocytose inhaled silica particles, thereby activating and releasing inflammatory mediators (IL-1, IL-8) that cause fibroblast recruitment.

Microscopy reveals coalescent nodules of whorled collagen fibers surrounded by a peripheral zone of silica-laden macrophages. HRCT shows a “crazy paving” pattern due to interlobular septal thickening on the background of ground-glass opacity.

Given below is a HRCT image of silicosis:

Option A: Asbestosis - X-ray shows peripheral reticular opacities predominantly in the lower zones. It predominantly affects the lower lobes of the lung, in contrast to other forms of pneumoconiosis, which affect the upper lobes.

Option C: Anthracosis/coal workers' pneumoconiosis is a pulmonary condition seen in coal miners. The inhaled carbon pigment is engulfed by alveolar or interstitial macrophages, which accumulate in the connective tissue. Initially, it causes simple coal workers pneumoconiosis with little or no pulmonary dysfunction. With continued exposure, lung tissue undergoes progressive massive fibrosis which is called complicated coal workers pneumoconiosis. The upper lobes of the lungs are commonly involved.

Simple coal workers' pneumoconiosis appears as small round nodular opacities with an occasional appearance of reticular or reticulonodular opacities. Compared to silicosis, the nodules in CWP tend to have less well-defined margins and a more granular appearance.

Option D: Cotton dust causes byssinosis and can induce occupational asthma. It is characterized clinically as occasional (early-stage) and then regular (late-stage) chest tightness toward the end of the first day of the workweek-Monday chest tightness.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the diagnosis based on the image given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bronchiectasis

The diagnosis in this patient is bronchiectasis. The CT scan shows the signet ring sign is specific for bronchiectasis where the internal diameter of the bronchi is greater than the adjacent pulmonary artery.

The clinical scenario observed in bronchiectasis is:

* Repeated chest infections

* Presence of large amounts of yellow sputum

* Non-smoker

Bronchiectasis refers to the irreversible dilatation of one or more bronchi, which occurs due to recurrent cycles of infection, inflammation, and tissue damage. Development of the disease requires an infectious insult in combination with impaired bacterial clearance (eg, impaired immune defences, structural airway defect).

Bronchiectasis is commonly associated with

* Kartagener syndrome

* Cystic fibrosis

* Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.

Radiological findings - Chest X-ray shows tram track appearance due to the dilated airways.

CT findings include:

* Signet ring sign

* Lack of bronchial tapering

* Tree-in-bud pattern - It occurs due to the thickening of the dilated airways along with the inspissated secretions.

* Cysts originating from the bronchial wall (pronounced in cystic bronchiectasis)

Note: High-Resolution CT (HRCT) is the best method for the diagnosis of bronchiectasis.

Other options:

Option A: Pulmonary tuberculosis is an infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Patients often present with chronic cough and hemoptysis. Low-grade fever, anorexia, and weight loss are the commonly associated symptoms. CT findings of pulmonary tuberculosis are Ghon focus, Ranke complex, nodal calcifications, cavities, and hilar/paratracheal lymphadenopathy.

Option B: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease[COPD], is inflammation-induced destruction of lung parenchyma resulting from cigarette smoke or other pollutants. Patients typically will be smokers with exertional dyspnea, and cough with productive sputum. Lung hyperinflation (emphysema) and airflow obstruction are characteristic of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

Option C: Bronchial asthma is an airway hyperresponsiveness disease characterized by reversible airway narrowing and obstruction by mucus plugging. Patients typically present with symptoms such as wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and cough usually on exposure to triggering agents. CT findings in bronchial asthma are bronchial wall thickening, mucus plugging, decreased lung attenuation, and gas trapping.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In the given barium swallow image, which of the following shows the left atrium impression on the esophagus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3

In the given barium swallow image, the arrow marking with the number 3 shows the left atrium impression on the esophagus.

The esophagus is a fibromuscular tube that connects the pharynx of the neck to the stomach, passing through the thorax through the superior and posterior mediastinum. It starts below the cricopharyngeus muscle, at the level of C6- the cricoid cartilage's bottom margin. The esophagus is located behind the trachea in the neck. It passes posterior to the left main bronchus, the left atrium, and the aortic arch as it descends through the mediastinum, each of which leaves an impression.

The vagus nerves accompany the esophagus as it travels through the diaphragmatic gap at T10 and finishes at the gastric cardia at T11. The left lobe of the liver is located anterior to the abdominal esophagus. Thus, the esophagus is composed of a short cervical, a long thoracic, and a short abdominal segment.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In which condition is popcorn calcification seen ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pulmonary hamartoma

Popcorn calcification is seen in pulmonary hamartoma.

Popcorn calcification is defined as a pattern of calcification in rings and arcs that resembles popped corn kernels.

The presence of fat in a well-circumscribed solitary pulmonary nodule which does not demonstrate significant growth is pathognomonic of a pulmonary hamartoma.

Chest x-ray showing pulmonary hamartoma:

Amorphous calcifications with rings and arcs which resemble popped corn kernels in appearance are known as pop-corn calcification.

It may be seen in

* Chondroid lesions like chondrosarcoma

* Fibrous dysplasia

* Pulmonary hamartomas

* Fibroadenoma breast

* Calcified uterine fibroid

* Metaphyses and epiphyses of long bones of children with osteogenesis imperfecta.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In a 100-m dash, most of the energy consumed by skeletal muscles to replenish ATP is derived from _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phosphocreatine

In a 100-m dash that takes 10 s, 85% of the energy consumed is derived anaerobically by phosphocreatine, which is hydrolyzed to creatine and phosphate groups with the release of considerable energy.
The ATP concentration in a muscle is low enough (4 millimolar) to sustain contractions for 1-2 seconds after which ATP is dephosphorylated into ADP. The ADP is re-phosphorylated by phosphocreatine for the next 5 to 8 seconds.

ADP is re-phosphorylated by 3 sources.

• Phosphocreatine after 2 seconds upto 10 seconds.
• Glycolysis (anaerobic) after 10 seconds upto a minute
• Oxidative metabolism - after a minute upto 2-4 hours.
questions.learning: Phosphocreatine — In a 100-m dash that takes 10 s, 85% of the energy consumed is derived anaerobically by phosphocreatine, which is hydrolyzed to creatine and phosphate groups with the release of considerable energy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents to you with features of anemia, fever, and recurrent nosebleeds. On examination there is hepatosplenomegaly, Lab investigations revealed: Hb = 6 g/dL, TLC count = 40,000/ cu.mm with 10% blasts and platelet count = 12,000/cu.mm. On further investigation, t(8;21) was detected in the blasts. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute myeloblastic leukemia (AML)

The given clinical picture suggests leukemia.

For the diagnosis of acute myeloblastic leukemia (AML), the blast cell count should be ≥20% either in the peripheral blood or bone marrow, as per WHO criteria.

However, there are three important exceptions. For cases with lower blast count (<20%), a diagnosis of AML can be made if there is the presence of any one of the following three cytogenetic abnormalities:

* t(15;17)

* t(8;21)

* Inversion 16 or t(16;16)
questions.learning: Acute myeloblastic leukemia (AML) — The given clinical picture suggests leukemia. For the diagnosis of acute myeloblastic leukemia (AML), the blast cell count should be ≥20% either in the peripheral blood or bone marrow, as per WHO criteria.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following diseases affects predominantly large arteries?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Giant cell arteritis

Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis) is a large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, especially the extracranial branches of the carotid artery (e.g., temporal artery). It commonly occurs in patients >50 years and presents with headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms, and is often associated with polymyalgia rheumatica.

Why not the other options?

• A. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA): Small-vessel vasculitis involving the upper/lower respiratory tract and kidneys.
• B. Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN): Medium-vessel vasculitis affecting renal, mesenteric, and other medium-sized arteries.
• D. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA): Small-vessel vasculitis associated with asthma and eosinophilia.
questions.learning: Giant cell arteritis Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis) is a large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, especially the extracranial branches of the carotid artery (e.g., temporal artery).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following organisms is the causative agent most commonly associated with acne fulminans?
questions.explanation: Acne fulminans is a rare and severe immunological reaction that represents the most extreme form of acne vulgaris. It is triggered by an abnormal systemic immune response to the antigens of Propionibacterium acnes (now renamed Cutibacterium acnes) (Option B). This bacterium is a normal inhabitant of the pilosebaceous unit. In acne fulminans, the body reacts with high levels of inflammation, leading to painful, ulcerated acne lesions and systemic symptoms like fever and bone pain. Actinomyces (Option A) causes actinomycosis, typically presenting with sulfur granules in jaw abscesses. Mobiluncus (Option C) is associated with bacterial vaginosis. Bifidobacterium (Option D) is a common gut probiotic and not a primary skin pathogen. Therefore, the hypersensitivity reaction to P. acnes is the definitive underlying cause of this severe dermatological condition. Management usually requires systemic corticosteroids and isotretinoin
questions.learning: Acne fulminans is a rare and severe immunological reaction that represents the most extreme form of acne vulgaris. It is triggered by an abnormal systemic immune response to the antigens of Propionibacterium acnes (now renamed Cutibacterium acnes) (Option B).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which is not an obvious advantage of high pressure oxygen through nasal cannula:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreases need of intubation

High flow nasal cannula (HFNC), which delivers oxygen at high flow, and pressure through the nasal cannula.

Advantages of high-flow nasal cannula:

• Soft and pliable nasal prongs provide comfort to the patient.
• Warming and humidification of secretions: The heating of air to core temperature and humidification of the inspired air is better at high-flow. The humidification causes increased water content in the secretions, which facilitates the removal of secretions. It also decreases the work of breathing and avoids airway dessication and epithelial injury.
• Reduces dead space: The high flow of the oxygen delivered clears the upper airway of the expired air, which reduces dead space by a decrease of rebreathing and allows a higher fraction of minute ventilation to participate in alveolar gas exchange.
• Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP): HFNC increases the positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), and reduces the work of breathing.
• High flow rate causes decreased entrainment of room air, allowing more accurate delivery of oxygen.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A child presents with nocturnal perianal itching severe enough to disturb sleep. On examination, eggs of the causative organism are seen in the provided image. Which organism is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of perianal itching at night is the classic symptom of Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm or threadworm). The itching is caused by the female worm migrating out of the anus at night to lay eggs in the perianal folds. The provided image confirms this, showing the pathognomonic D-shaped egg (planoconvex) with a translucent, double-layered shell. Trichuris trichiura (Option B) eggs are barrel-shaped with bipolar plugs. Trichinella spiralis (Option C) is usually diagnosed by finding larvae in muscle biopsies. Strongyloides stercoralis (Option D) is typically diagnosed by finding larvae in the stool, as eggs hatch within the intestinal mucosa. Pinworm infection is extremely common in children and is diagnosed using the "Scotch tape test" to collect eggs from the perianal area. Given the noctural itching and the characteristic D-shaped eggs, Enterobius is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of perianal itching at night is the classic symptom of Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm or threadworm). The itching is caused by the female worm migrating out of the anus at night to lay eggs in the perianal folds.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Split thickness skin graft for wound closure on thigh includes:
options: Epidermis and variable parts of dermis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epidermis and variable parts of dermis

Split-thickness skin graft for wound closure on the thigh includes epidermis and variable parts of the dermis.

Split-thickness skin graft (Thiersch graft ) consists of the whole of the epidermis and only a portion of the dermis.

Full-thickness skin grafts (Wolfe graft): include the epidermis and entire dermis, with portions of the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles.

Advantages of split skin graft over full-thickness skin graft:

* Large grafts can be harvested.

* In the case of thinner split-thickness grafts, the donor site heals more rapidly and can be reused in severe cases such as burns.

* Uptake is good. Meshing can be done, i.e. small splits are made in graft and any exudates collected can come out through this and this improves graft take-up.

* Meshing also allows the graft to expand.

Advantages of a full-thickness skin graft over split skin graft:

* It has a lesser degree of post-graft contraction

* Best cosmetic appearance as they include the highest number of skin appendage elements.

The most preferable donor site is buttocks in cosmetically sensitive individuals and children. The most commonly used donor site is the thigh.

* The graft is taken from the donor site with a handheld Humby knife or electric dermatome.

* Grafts are perforated to allow exudates to escape and improve ‘take’. It can further be meshed to allow expansion.

* Grafts will take up only on the beds which are vascularized, hence preparation of wound bed is an essential step.

* Skin grafts are completely dependent on nutrition on the tissue over which they are placed and can heal well over muscle, perichondrium, and periosteum. They do not take well over bone or cartilage or on tissue that has been irradiated or infected or is hypovascular.

* A clean healthy wound bed with a meshed graft tied in place to stop movement will encourage take.

* The presence of group A beta-hemolytic streptococci is a contraindication in grafting as it can destroy split grafts completely and also convert donors to full-thickness defects.

* The donor area is dressed appropriately and the dressing is opened after 10 days and not earlier.

The given image shows Humby's knife. The average thickness of the graft obtained from a Humbys knife is 0.3 mm.

Pearl PF1917: Skin graft : phases of uptake of the graft

The take of skin graft occurs in three phases:

* Imbibition (Plasmatic circulation): during the first 48 hours, the graft is nourished with plasma exudate from host bed capillaries.

* Inosculation, in which cut vessels from the host bed line up with the cut ends of the vessels of the graft to form anastomoses

* Neovascularization, in which blood vessels grow from the recipient bed into the graft

Sensibility returns to the graft over time, with reinnervation beginning at approximately 4 to 5 weeks and being completed by 12 to 24 months. Pain returns first, with light touch and temperature returning later.

Note: some books give that the 3 phases are imbibition,revascularisation (inosculation+neovascularisation) and organisation (fibrin layer holds the graft in place and this is replaced by postgraft day 7 with fibroblasts)
