questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-month-old infant is noted to have an increased respiratory rate, without chest indrawing and no associated danger signs. According to IMNCI guidelines, what is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation: According to the IMNCI classification for a sick child aged 2 months to 5 years, the diagnosis of pneumonia is based on fast breathing in the absence of severe signs. For an infant aged 2 months up to 12 months, "fast breathing" is defined as 50 breaths per minute or more. This 3-month-old's rate of meets the criteria. Since there is no chest indrawing and no general danger signs (such as inability to feed or lethargy), the child is classified as having pneumonia (Option A) rather than severe pneumonia (Option C). A diagnosis of "no pneumonia: cough or cold" (Option B) is only applied if no fast breathing or danger signs are present. Allergy (Option D) is not a standard IMNCI classification category for acute respiratory assessment. Treatment for pneumonia in this setting typically involves oral amoxicillin and home care advice
questions.learning: According to the IMNCI classification for a sick child aged 2 months to 5 years, the diagnosis of pneumonia is based on fast breathing in the absence of severe signs.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presented with failure to thrive and recurrent infections. On examination, tonsils are absent. Further evaluation confirms the deficiency of adenosine deaminase. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Severe Combined Immuno Deficiency

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) due to a deficiency of adenosine deaminase.

Affected children present with prominent thrush (oral candidiasis), extensive diaper rash, and failure to thrive. Some patients develop a morbilliform rash shortly after birth because maternal T cells are transferred across the placenta and attack the fetus, causing graft-versus-host disease (GVHD).

Persons with SCID are extremely susceptible to recurrent, severe infections by a wide range of pathogens, including:

• Candida albicans
• Pneumocystis jiroveci
• Pseudomonas
• Cytomegalovirus
• Varicella

The thymus biopsy shows remnants of Hassall's corpuscles, indicating severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) due to adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency. SCID affects both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses, primarily impacting T cells and resulting in the absence or severe underdevelopment of lymphoid tissues like lymph nodes and tonsils.

There are two main types of SCID:

• X-linked SCID: The most common form, caused by a mutation in the common γ-chain (γc) subunit of cytokine receptors. This leads to reduced T-cell numbers and impaired antibody synthesis despite normal B-cell counts. The thymus shows undifferentiated epithelial cells.
• Autosomal recessive SCID: Often due to ADA deficiency, causing toxic metabolite accumulation that damages T cells, resulting in greater T-cell reduction.

In both forms, the thymus is small and lacks lymphoid cells, but ADA deficiency uniquely features remnants of Hassall’s corpuscles.

Note: X-linked SCID is the first human disease in which gene therapy has been successful.

Other options:

Option A: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is due to a deficiency of the enzyme Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase(HGPRT). It is an X-linked recessive disease. The clinical features include intellectual disability, self-mutilation, aggression, hyperuricemia, and gout.

Option B: Ataxia Telangiectasia is a progressive neurodegenerative genetic disease causing poor coordination and small dilated blood vessels. It is autosomal recessive in inheritance due to ATM gene mutation on Ch 11q22-23.

Option D: Friedrich's ataxia involves the posterior column, pyramidal, and spinocerebellar tracts. Clinical features include cardiomyopathy, optic atrophy, and diabetes mellitus. It should be differentiated from other forms of ataxia as Tabes dorsalis and SACD(Subacute Combined Degeneration).
questions.learning: Severe Combined Immuno Deficiency — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) due to a deficiency of adenosine deaminase.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which microorganism is most likely responsible for causing bilateral pulmonary infiltrates in an HIV-positive patient?
questions.explanation: In an HIV-positive patient with a low CD4 count, the classic cause of pneumonia presenting with bilateral, diffuse interstitial infiltrates (often described as "ground-glass" opacities) on a chest X-ray is Pneumocystis jirovecii. As discussed in Questions 54 and 100, this fungal pathogen causes an opportunistic infection that characteristically spreads through the alveolar spaces of both lungs simultaneously. Cryptococcus (Option A) more commonly causes meningitis or focal lung nodules. Histoplasmosis (Option B) can cause diffuse disease but often presents with hilar lymphadenopathy or miliary-style patterns. Aspergillus (Option D) typically causes focal consolidation or cavities in immuno compromised hosts. Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) remains a leading cause of hospitalization and death in patients who are unaware of their HIV status or who are not consistently on antiretroviral therapy. Diagnosis is confirmed by visualizing the organism in sputum or BAL fluid using specialized stains like Silver stain or by PCR testing
questions.learning: In an HIV-positive patient with a low CD4 count, the classic cause of pneumonia presenting with bilateral, diffuse interstitial infiltrates (often described as "ground-glass" opacities) on a chest X-ray is Pneumocystis jirovecii.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Ansa cervicalis supplies all of the following muscles, except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thyrohyoid

The ansa cervicalis (C1–C3) is a loop of the cervical plexus that supplies most of the infrahyoid (strap) muscles, including the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and both bellies of the omohyoid.

The thyrohyoid is the exception, as it is supplied by C1 fibers traveling with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), not by the ansa cervicalis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sternothyroid: Supplied by the ansa cervicalis.
• B. Omohyoid: Supplied by the ansa cervicalis.
• C. Sternohyoid: Supplied by the ansa cervicalis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child is being assessed for developmental milestones. At what age of life can the child transfer objects from one hand to another?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 6 months

Transferring objects from one hand to another is seen at 6 months.

The developmental milestones at the age of six months are:

* Fine motor and adaptive: reaches out for objects with one hand - unidextrous reach and transfers objects from one hand to another

* Gross motor: Independently sits with arms forward for support - "tripod" fashion

* Social and adaptive milestones: Recognises strangers, stranger anxiety

* Language milestones: Monosyllables like ba, da, pa

Other options:

* A child attains a mature pincer grasp around 12 months of age.

* A child can build a tower of two blocks and imitate scribbling around 15 months of age.

* A child can build a tower of three blocks and scribble around 18 months of age.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a history of chronic liver disease presents with abdominal distension, jaundice, and pruritis. Ascitic fluid analysis revealed neutrophil count > 650 per cubic mm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

In the given scenario and image of a patient with abdominal distension, jaundice, pruritus, and neutrophil count >650 per mm3, the likely diagnosis is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is an acute bacterial infection of the ascitic fluid. It is commonly seen in adults in association with liver cirrhosis. The pathogens involved are Escherichia coli, streptococci, enterococci, and pneumococci.

In a patient with ascites, SBP presents with fever, and acute abdominal pain. On examination, tachycardia, tachypnea, and signs of peritonitis are seen. Hepatic encephalopathy and gastrointestinal bleeding may also occur.

Diagnosis is by paracentesis, and an ascitic fluid neutrophil count of >250/mm3 is suggestive of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Ascitic fluid culture may reveal the pathogenic organisms.

Management is mainly by third-generation cephalosporins such as cefotaxime. Albumin infusion can be given as it decreases the risk of renal failure and improves patient survival. Early diagnosis and treatment improve the prognosis.

Other options:

Option B: Malignant ascites occurs as a complication of intrabdominal and extraabdominal malignancies. Patients can present with increasing abdominal girth, generalized abdominal pain, and shortness of breath. Weight loss may be more common. Ascitic fluid analysis reveals a milky or bloody appearance with elevated levels of tumor markers and VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor). Treatment is by paracentesis and peritoneovenous shunt.

Option C: Ascites are often seen in patients with tubercular peritonitis. Multiple tubercles are seen on the peritoneum. Ascitic fluid analysis reveals a straw-colored fluid with a white blood cell count >500/mm3. Laparoscopy and peritoneal biopsy may be helpful in diagnosis. Management is by supportive and anti-tubercular therapy.

Option D: Intestinal obstruction can present as pain, abdominal distension, vomiting, and absolute constipation. Abdominal radiographs taken in a supine position are useful in diagnosis. Abdominal radiograph in erect posture shows fluid levels. Management is mainly by insertion of a nasogastric tube, replacement of fluid and electrolytes, and surgery.
questions.learning: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis — In the given scenario and image of a patient with abdominal distension, jaundice, pruritus, and neutrophil count >650 per mm3, the likely diagnosis is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman is set to undergo a complete laparoscopic hysterectomy. She wants to know if there are any disadvantages to this procedure. What are the disadvantages of laparoscopic over open surgery?
options: Not knowing the extent of thermal burns
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Not knowing the extent of thermal burns

The disadvantage of laparoscopic over open surgery is not knowing the extent of the thermal burns.

Diathermy burns are a particular hazard in laparoscopic surgery due to the following reasons:

• Relative lack of visibility of the entire instrument.
• Faulty insulation of laparoscopic instruments
• Intraperitoneal contact of the diathermy with another metal instrument while activating the pedal.
• Inadvertent activation of the pedal while the diathermy tip is out of the vision of the camera.
• Retained heat in the diathermy tip touching susceptible structures, such as the bowel.

The advantages of laparoscopic over open surgery are as follows:

• Less postoperative pain (Option D)
• Less blood loss (Option C)
• Cosmetically better
• Earlier recovery and shorter postoperative stay at the hospital (Option A)
• Fewer intraoperative adhesions
• Better perception of anatomy intraoperatively

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 12 week old child presented with fever, cyanosis and fatigue. His chest X ray is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation

The given X-ray shows figure of 8 or snowman appearance characteristic of total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation (TAPVC).

TAPVC refers to a condition in which pulmonary veins instead of draining into the left atrium drain into the right atrium directly or indirectly. This results in anomalous drainage of pulmonary venous blood flow into the systemic venous circulation. It is a cyanotic heart disease with features of congestive heart failure. The patients are irritable and have failure to thrive.

The following types are seen:

• Supracardiac (most common): Common pulmonary vein drains into superior vena cava or the left innominate vein
• Cardiac: Pulmonary veins drain into the right atrium or coronary sinus.
• Infracardiac (always obstructive and most dangerous): Pulmonary veins drain into portal vein or inferior vena cava.

Snowman appearance is classically seen in supracardiac variant of TAPVC. The dilated vertical vein on the left, brachiocephalic vein on top, and the superior vena cava on the right form the head of the snowman; the body of the snowman is formed by the enlarged right atrium. It is shown in the image below.

Other options:

Option B: Tetrology of Fallot comprises pulmonary stenosis, ventricular septal defect, overriding of the aorta over the ventricular septum, and right ventricular hypertrophy. On chest X-Ray, the cardiac silhouette appears like a boot ("coeur en sabot”).

Option C: In the transposition of great arteries, the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk from the left ventricle. The X-ray shows cardiomegaly with cardiac contours which appear like an egg on a string.

Option D: Pericardial effusions occur when excessive fluid gets collected in the pericardial space. The X-ray shows globular enlargement of the cardiac shadow giving a water bottle configuration.
questions.learning: Total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation — The given X-ray shows figure of 8 or snowman appearance characteristic of total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation (TAPVC).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about Cuthbertson's metabolic ebb and flow responses to trauma?
options: The "ebb" phase is associated with a decline in body temperature and oxygen consumption.
The "flow" phase occurs after resuscitation from a state of shock.
The "ebb" phase is aimed at reducing posttraumatic energy depletion.
The "ebb" phase leads to activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic acute-phase response.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. The "ebb" phase leads to activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic acute-phase response.

The "flow" phase (not "ebb") leads to activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic acute-phase response.

Cuthbertson's ebb and flow response to trauma:

The "ebb" phase lasts for a brief duration and is associated with a decline in body temperature and oxygen consumption, aimed at reducing post traumatic energy depletion.

The "flow" phase occurs after resuscitation from a state of shock, which leads to an increased metabolic turnover, activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic acute-phase response. This hypercatabolic condition leads to a significantly increased oxygen consumption and energy expenditure.
questions.learning: The "ebb" phase leads to activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic acute-phase response. The "flow" phase (not "ebb") leads to activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic acute-phase response.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The minimum requirements of a health worker job are given: should be a woman, a resident of the village, 25 to 45 years old, and have a formal education till 10th standard. What is this health worker called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. ASHA worker

The requirements of being a woman, a resident of the village, 25 to 45 years old, and having a formal education till 10th standard is for an ASHA(Accredited Social Health Activist) worker.

An ASHA is a trained female community health activist and a resident woman of the village with a formal education of at least up to 10th grade. . This may be relaxed upto 8th standard only if no suitable person with this qualification is available. She should preferably be in the age group of 25 to 45 years (married/divorced/widow) and have qualities such as good communication skills and leadership skills. The general norm of selection recommends having one ASHA for 1000 population, but in tribal, hilly, and desert areas, the norm could be relaxed to one ASHA per habitation.

Roles of ASHA:

* To create awareness and provide information to the community on determinants of health such as nutrition, basic sanitation, and hygienic practices.

* To counsel women on birth preparedness, the importance of safe delivery, breastfeeding and complementary feeding, immunization, and contraception.

* To counsel women on the prevention of common infections including reproductive tract infections/sexually transmitted infections.

* To mobilize the community and help them in accessing health and health-related services.

* To arrange and escort pregnant women and children requiring treatment/admission to the nearest pre-identified health facility.

* To inform the sub-centre/primary health centre about the births and deaths in her village and any unusual health problems/disease outbreaks in the community.

* To promote the construction of household toilets under the total sanitation campaign.

Other options:

Option A: An Anganwadi worker is a community-based health worker in India, primarily responsible for providing maternal and child health services, nutrition, and education. They work under the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) program to support the well-being of children and mothers.

Option B: A nurse is a healthcare professional responsible for providing patient care, administering medications, and assisting with treatment plans. They play a crucial role in promoting health, preventing illness, and supporting recovery across various healthcare settings.

Option C: A midwife is a trained professional who specializes in assisting women during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period. They provide prenatal care, support during labour, and postnatal care for both the mother and newborn.

Pearl PF0294: ASHA

ASHA is an Accredited Social Health Activist.

An ASHA must be a woman, a resident of the village, 25 to 45 years old and have a formal education till 10th standard preferably if they are in good numbers. This may be relaxed upto 8th standard only if no suitable person with this qualification is available. She is part of the primary health care at the village level.

National norm: In rural areas, a population of 1000 should have at least 1 ASHA, but in remote areas, one ASHA per habitation is the norm. In urban areas, 1 ASHA worker is assigned to a population of 1000-2500. This norm is also mandated by each state, differently, according to their requirements.

Responsibilities of ASHA:

* Health education and awareness

* Reproductive and child health and family planning

* Facilitate the access to health services

* Promotion of sanitation and household toilet construction

* Provision of primary medical care for minor ailments

* Provider of DOTS

* Depot holder of essentials like ORS, iron and folic acid tablets, condoms, disposable delivery kits, etc.

* Dispersal of health information on her community to higher centres

* Some responsibilities are integrated with Anganwadi workers and Auxiliary Nurse Midwife
questions.learning: ASHA worker — The requirements of being a woman, a resident of the village, 25 to 45 years old, and having a formal education till 10th standard is for an ASHA(Accredited Social Health Activist) worker.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Windkessel effect is shown by all except ____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Radial artery

Windkessel effect is shown by all except the radial artery.

The windkessel effect is seen in the large elastic arteries like the aorta, carotid, and renal artery. The elasticity or windkessel effect is the exclusive property of large and elastic vessels. These vessels when stretched undergo elastic recoil.

The aorta is stretched during systole. This expansion causes temporary storage of blood, allowing more blood to enter the aorta. This buffer stock of blood is released during diastole, to maintain organ perfusion even during diastole.

The image given below shows the windkessel effect seen in the aorta.

Several methods can be used to evaluate the elastic properties of the aortic Windkessel in living humans. One simple approach is to measure the pulse wave velocity along the aorta, where a higher velocity indicates increased stiffness and elastic resistance. Alternative methods involve assessing the ratio between pulse pressure and changes in aortic volume (delta P/delta V). These methods can be noninvasively performed using ultrasound or tomographic techniques.
questions.learning: Radial artery Windkessel effect is shown by all except the radial artery. The windkessel effect is seen in the large elastic arteries like the aorta, carotid, and renal artery.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Arrange the following steps of Karyotyping in the correct order :

1. Collect cells by peripheral vein using a heparin syringe.
2. Culture in phytohaemoagglutinin.
3. Incubation at 37 degrees C for 3 days.
4. Harvest with colchicine.
5. Routine staining with Giemsa
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5

The correct order of steps of Karyotyping is as follows:

1. Collect cells by peripheral vein using a heparin syringe.
2. Culture in phytohaemoagglutinin.
3. Incubation at 37 degrees C for 3 days.
4. Harvest with colchicine.
5. Routine staining with Giemsa

Karyotyping is the process by which chromosomes are isolated, stained, and examined to find chromosomal anomalies. It is used in prenatal diagnosis, investigation of repeat pregnancy loss, investigation of children and adults suspected of having a chromosomal disorder, and subtyping of lymphomas and leukemias for the purpose of exact diagnosis, giving a prognosis, and treatment.

Various techniques are used in karyotyping to study chromosomes. Staining with various compounds produces various results and helps us to understand the chromosomes better.

Common techniques used are:

• Q banding - fluorescence staining with quinacrine mustard
• G banding - Giemsa staining after partial denaturation of chromatin
• R banding - reverse Giemsa staining. In this, the light and dark areas are reversed
• C banding - staining of heterochromatin with silver salts
• T banding - staining the telomeres of chromosomes

The karyotyping of a normal human male is given below.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 The correct order of steps of Karyotyping is as follows: 1. Collect cells by peripheral vein using a heparin syringe.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A neonate was brought with features of lethargy, and poor oral intake. On examination, a cataract was seen. Urine Benedict's test was positive but negative for Glucose. What will be the enzyme deficiency in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase

The given clinical scenario of a neonate presenting with lethargy, and poor oral intake, with examination revealing a cataract and urine benedict's test was positive but negative for glucose, is suggestive of classical galactosemia and enzyme deficient is galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase.

Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency leads to classical galactosemia. It is an autosomal recessive disorder. Normally, newborns receive up to 40% of their intake as lactose (glucose + galactose). The deficiency of this enzyme leads to an inability to convert galactose-1-phosphate to uridine diphosphate galactose. This leads to the accumulation of galactose 1-phosphate and causes injury to the kidney, liver, and brain.

Clinical features:

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the liver causes liver damage & leads to hepatomegaly, vomiting, and convulsions.

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate depletes the liver of inorganic phosphate leading to diminished ATP synthesis which affects gluconeogenesis resulting in hypoglycemia.

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the nerves causes intellectual disability.

* Accumulation of galactitol in the lens causes oil-drop cataracts.

* Patients with galactosemia are at an increased risk of developing Escherichia coli neonatal sepsis.

In uridyl transferase deficiency, the epimerase is present in adequate amounts, so that the galactosemic individual can still form UDPGal from glucose. This explains how normal growth and development of affected children can occur despite the galactose-free diets.

Urinary reducing sugar (Benedict's test) and mucic acid test are positive. Direct enzyme assay using erythrocytes establishes the diagnosis.

Treatment is a galactose-free diet.

Other options:

Option A: Hexokinase is a glycolytic enzyme, involved in maintaining intracellular glucose concentration by catalysing the first step in glucose metabolism, i.e., phosphorylation of intracellular glucose.  Its deficiency leads to hemolytic anaemia. Splenomegaly may be another presenting feature.

Option B: Galactokinase is the enzyme responsible for the conversion of galactose to galactose 1-phosphate. Only cataract is seen in the deficiency of this enzyme because galactose-1-phosphate is not formed. Hence no toxic effects of this compound are manifested.

Option D: Phosphofructokinase is a key regulatory enzyme of glycolysis and is necessary for the ATP-dependent conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-diphosphate. Tauri's disease is type VII glycogen storage disorder that results due to the deficiency of phosphofructokinase.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A man is brought to the hospital with bizarre behavior and an inability to recall his personal identity or the events surrounding his travel over a distance of 100 km. Collateral history reveals that he experienced a traumatic earthquake a few months earlier. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s inability to recall his identity combined with purposeful travel (100 km) and no memory of the journey constitutes dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue. This condition is directly linked to a recent severe traumatic stressor, such as the earthquake mentioned in the history. Dissociative identity disorder (Option B) involves two or more distinct personality states, which is not described here. Schizophrenia (Option C) is a psychotic disorder characterized by hallucinations and disorganized thought rather than isolated identity loss. Global amnesia (Option D) is typically caused by organic conditions like stroke and does not specifically follow trauma. Since the amnesia is localized to personal information following an identifiable psychological trauma, dissociative amnesia is the most specific diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient’s inability to recall his identity combined with purposeful travel (100 km) and no memory of the journey constitutes dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following micronutrients are associated with decreased sexual maturation and hypogonadism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Zinc

Zinc deficiency is associated with decreased sexual maturation and hypogonadism.

Zinc is the second most common trace element in the body after iron. As a component of zinc finger proteins, zinc regulates gene transcription and participates in nucleic acid metabolism, protein synthesis and thereby cell growth. Zinc is a major antioxidant being part of the enzyme superoxide dismutase.

Zinc is derived mainly from animal protein. Diets based on cereals, plants and legumes are associated with zinc deficiency due to dietary phytic acid decreasing the bioavailability of zinc.

Zinc is absorbed throughout the small intestine by a process of facilitated diffusion. Almost 90% of the total body zinc is localized in bone and skeletal muscle.

Deficiency -

• Poor physical growth is an important feature of zinc depletion in preschool and school-age children. Delayed sexual maturation and hypogonadism are prominent features of zinc deficiency in adolescents. Other features include anemia, anorexia, diarrhea, alopecia, impaired immune function and poor wound healing.
• Acrodermatitis enteropathica is an autosomal recessive disorder of severe zinc deficiency, caused by impaired intestinal absorption due to a defect in intestinal zinc transporter protein. It presents in early infancy with vesiculobullous, dry, scaly, or eczematous skin lesions chiefly in the periorificial and acral areas.

Normal requirements for children range between 3.5 and 5.0 mg/day. Acquired zinc deficiency stats can be treated with 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg/day for several weeks. Malnourished children have much higher requirements of 2-4mg/kg/day.

Other options :

Option B - Copper deficiency results in microcytic, hypochromic anemia unresponsive to iron therapy, depigmentation of hair, neutropenia, neurological problems and osteoporosis. Disruption in copper transport is linked to Wilson's disease and Menke's disease.

Option C - Selenium deficiency is a cause of Keshan disease, a form of cardiomyopathy in young children seen in some regions of China. In combination with iodine deficiency, lack of selenium can result in myxedematous endemic cretinism.

Option D - Iron deficiency causes anemia, irritability, anorexia, pica, angular stomatitis, leg cramps and congestive heart failure.
questions.learning: Zinc Zinc deficiency is associated with decreased sexual maturation and hypogonadism. Zinc is the second most common trace element in the body after iron.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is not seen in heat exhaustion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Loss of thermoregulatory mechanism

Loss of the thermoregulatory mechanism is not seen in heat exhaustion. It is seen in heat stroke.

Heat exhaustion is caused by excessive exposure to heat, leading to nausea, vomiting, dizziness, altered sensorium(option B), thirst, fatigue, headache, sweating, and decreased urine output. Increases in sweating and dehydration can cause orthostatic hypotension(option C). Body temperature may rise but does not exceed 40.5°C (105°F). In heat exhaustion, the body maintains thermoregulation and no CNS dysfunction occurs. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent the progression of life-threatening heat stroke.
questions.learning: Loss of thermoregulatory mechanism Loss of the thermoregulatory mechanism is not seen in heat exhaustion. Heat exhaustion is caused by excessive exposure to heat, leading to nausea, vomiting, dizziness, altered sensorium(option B), thirst, fatigue,…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding the cause for onset of labour: Statement 1: Alteration in estrogen-progesterone ratio results in prostaglandin synthesis and onset of labour. Statement 2: Decreased fetal production of dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S) and cortisol inhibits the conversion of fetal pregnenolone to progesterone. Which one of the following is correct with respect to the above statements?
options: Both Statements 1 and 2 are true and Statement 2 is the correct explanation of Statement 1
Both Statements 1 and 2 are true but Statement 2 is not the correct explanation of Statement 1
Statement 1 is true but Statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false but Statement 2 is true
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Statement 1 is true but Statement 2 is false

Statement 1: True

• Near term, there is a functional increase in the estrogen-to-progesterone ratio.
• Estrogen promotes:

• Prostaglandin synthesis
• Increased oxytocin receptors
• Formation of gap junctions between myometrial cells
• Increased myometrial contractility

• These changes contribute to the onset of labour.

Statement 2: False

• It is increased fetal cortisol and DHEA-S, not decreased production, that contributes to the hormonal changes preceding labour.
• Fetal adrenal DHEA-S is converted by the placenta into estrogens, while fetal cortisol promotes placental estrogen production.
• Thus, decreased fetal DHEA-S and cortisol would not explain the onset of labour.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which paraphilia is characterized by a male obtaining sexual gratification from cross-dressing?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Eonism

Understand that eonism (transvestic fetishism) is a paraphilia in which a heterosexual male derives sexual arousal or gratification from wearing clothing traditionally associated with females. It should be distinguished from gender dysphoria, where cross-dressing is related to gender identity rather than sexual arousal.

Why not the other options?

• A. Fetishism: Sexual arousal is obtained from inanimate objects or specific non-genital body parts, not from cross-dressing itself.
• C. Frotteurism: Sexual gratification is achieved by rubbing or touching a non-consenting person, usually in crowded places.
• D. Exhibitionism: Involves exposing one’s genitals to an unsuspecting stranger for sexual excitement.

High-yield Pearl:

| Paraphilia | Characteristic Feature

| ---------- | ----------------------

| Eonism (Transvestic fetishism) | Sexual gratification from cross-dressing

| Fetishism | Sexual arousal from objects/body parts

| Frotteurism | Touching/rubbing against a non-consenting person

| Exhibitionism | Exposing genitals to strangers
questions.learning: Eonism Understand that eonism (transvestic fetishism) is a paraphilia in which a heterosexual male derives sexual arousal or gratification from wearing clothing traditionally associated with females.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A woman reports a one-month history of greenish, frothy vaginal discharge with associated vulvovaginal erythema. Saline wet mount examination reveals motile organisms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a greenish-frothy vaginal discharge coupled with vulvovaginal erythema (often described as a "strawberry cervix") is highly characteristic of Trichomoniasis, a sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis. The definitive diagnostic clue provided is the presence of motile organisms on saline wet mount microscopy, which identifies the pear-shaped, flagellated trophozoites. Bacterial vaginosis (Option B) typically presents with a thin, greyish-white discharge with a "fishy" odor and "clue cells" but lacks motile protozoa. Chlamydial cervicitis (Option C) often presents with mucopurulent discharge and cervical friability but is usually diagnosed via molecular testing rather than wet mount. Candidiasis (Option D) is characterized by a thick, "curd-like" white discharge and the presence of pseudohyphae on microscopy, with intense pruritus rather than frothiness. Treatment for Trichomoniasis involves oral metronidazole or tinidazole for both the patient and their sexual partner to prevent reinfection. Early diagnosis is essential as the infection can increase the risk of acquiring other STIs

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy presents with recurrent episodes of urinary tract infection. His mother says that he urinates frequently but has a poor urinary stream along with dribbling of urine. On examination, he has a palpable bladder. What investigation can be used to find out the underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Micturating cystourethrography

The clinical scenario is suggestive of the posterior urethral valve which affects only males and MCU is the investigation of choice.

Posterior urethral valves:

Features:

* Posterior urethral valves are the most common cause of severe obstructive uropathy in children.

* The valves are membranes that have a small posterior slit within them, which typically lie just distal to the verumontanum

* They function as flap valves and are obstructive to antegrade urinary flow. A urethral catheter can be passed retrogradely.

* 15% of boys with posterior urethral valves have unilateral reflux into a nonfunctioning dysplastic kidney, termed the VURD syndrome (valves, unilateral reflux, dysplasia)

* Diagnosis is most commonly made antenatally with ultrasound, which demonstrates bilateral hydronephrosis above a distended bladder

* Antenatal USG would also demonstrate oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia.

* If the diagnosis is not made antenatally, then babies typically present with urinary infection in the neonatal period or with uremia and renal failure

* Clinically a poor urinary stream, dribbling, and palpable bladder (due to diverticula) can be present.

* The investigation of choice is micturating cystourethrography

* The ultrasound shows the typical 'key-hole sign in which the bladder and the proximal urethra is dilated

* Definitive treatment is by urethroscopic destruction of the valves with continuing lifelong supportive treatment of the dilated urinary tract, recurrent urinary infections, and uremia.

The given image below shows the 'key-hole sign seen in USG.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with chronic alcohol use disorder presents in a fasted state with hypoglycemia. Laboratory testing shows a markedly elevated NADH/NAD+ ratio, and despite high fatty acid availability, ketone body production is suboptimal relative to expected starvation physiology. Which biochemical explanation accounts for this finding, tracing the fate of a specific TCA cycle intermediate?
options: High NADH state shifts oxaloacetate toward malate, depleting oxaloacetate available for gluconeogenesis, but this has no effect on ketogenesis since ketogenesis does not require oxaloacetate
High NADH state downregulates the TCA cycle, shunting oxaloacetate to malate; while ketogenesis itself does not require oxaloacetate directly
High NADH directly inhibits HMG-CoA lyase, the rate-limiting enzyme of ketogenesis, fully explaining the suboptimal ketone production
High NADH state has no relationship to oxaloacetate or malate; ketogenesis failure is entirely attributable to alcohol's direct toxic effect on adipose tissue lipolysis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High NADH state downregulates the TCA cycle, shunting oxaloacetate to malate; while ketogenesis itself does not require oxaloacetate directly

Chronic alcohol overuse produces a high NADH state, which downregulates the TCA cycle and shunts oxaloacetate to malate. While ketogenesis (via HMG-CoA lyase) does not directly require oxaloacetate, the broader hepatic metabolic derangement (impaired TCA cycle flux, depleted gluconeogenic capacity) disrupts the liver's overall capacity to coordinate the fasting response, contributing to the clinical picture of hypoglycemia with disrupted, rather than appropriately compensatory, ketone production — distinguishing this from a primary defect in the ketogenic pathway itself.

| Condition | Oxaloacetate fate | Mechanism

| --------- | ----------------- | ---------

| Prolonged starvation/DKA | Depleted for gluconeogenesis | Used in gluconeogenesis itself

| Chronic alcohol overuse | Shunted to malate | High NADH downregulates TCA cycle

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a function of glucagon?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glycolysis

Glycolysis is not a function of glucagon but is a function of insulin.

Role of insulin and glucagon:

When blood glucose falls during fasting, there is increased secretion of glucagon and decreased release of insulin.

Effects of increased glucagon: insulin ratio on enzymes of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis:

* It activates glycogen phosphorylase, the key enzyme of glycogenolysis, and deactivates glycogen synthase. This causes a rapid mobilization of liver glycogen stores to be utilized as fuel.

* It favors the synthesis of glucose-6-phosphatase which converts glucose-6-phosphate to glucose. The resulting glucose is used by red blood cells (lack mitochondria) and the brain as they are largely dependent on glucose in the fasting state.

* Phosphoenol pyruvate carboxykinase and fructose-1, 6-bisphosphatase are induced, leading to increased gluconeogenesis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 45-year-old truck driver with a history of multiple sexual partners presents to the dermatology department with the findings shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The provided image shows a characteristic maculopapular rash on the palms, which is a classic clinical finding for secondary syphilis. The patient's social history (truck driver with multiple sex partners) places him at a significantly higher risk for sexually transmitted infections. Secondary syphilis is the "great imitator" but its presence on palms and soles is a highly specific clue. Lichen planus (Option B) typically presents as itchy, purple papules on the wrists rather than generalized palmar macules. Scabies (Option C) would present with intense itching and burrows, usually visible in the finger webs rather than discrete reddish macules. Psoriasis (Option D) on the palms would show thick, scaly plaques and fissures. Given the risk factors and the pathognomonic palm-involved rash, the diagnosis of secondary syphilis must be suspected and confirmed using non-treponemal (RPR) and treponemal (TPHA) tests

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which of the following clinical conditions is the use of an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) absolutely contraindicated?
questions.explanation: According to WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC), active, untreated HIV infection with symptomatic AIDS is classified as a Category 4 contraindication for the insertion of an IUCD. In these immunosuppressed patients, the risk of ascending pelvic infections and subsequent sepsis is unacceptably high. However, if a patient is clinically stable on antiretroviral therapy (ART), IUCD use may be considered Category 2 (benefits outweigh risks). Hypertension (Option A), hyperlipidemia (Option B), and diabetes mellitus (Option C) are not absolute contraindications; copper IUCDs are generally safe to use in these patients unless other severe complications are present. Other absolute contraindications include current PID, pregnancy, and unexplained vaginal bleeding. Thus, in the context of the provided options, symptomatic HIV infection represents the most significant health risk for initial IUCD placement
questions.learning: According to WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC), active, untreated HIV infection with symptomatic AIDS is classified as a Category 4 contraindication for the insertion of an IUCD.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not an indication of splenectomy?
questions.explanation: Splenectomy is indicated for conditions where the spleen is either damaged beyond repair or is actively contributing to the disease process. In bone marrow failure (Option D), such as aplastic anemia, the primary problem is a lack of blood cell production rather than splenic destruction; thus, removing the spleen does not resolve the underlying cytopenia. In fact, in some marrow disorders, the spleen may provide essential extramedullary hematopoiesis, making its removal counterproductive. Iatrogenic splenic trauma (Option A) during abdominal surgery often requires splenectomy if the hemorrhage cannot be controlled. Thrombocytopenia (Option B), specifically Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP), is a classic indication for splenectomy if medical therapy fails, as the spleen is the site of platelet destruction. Hairy cell leukemia (Option C) was historically treated with splenectomy to manage symptomatic splenomegaly and cytopenias, though targeted medical therapies are now more common. Therefore, bone marrow failure stands out as a non-indication for this surgical procedure
questions.learning: Splenectomy is indicated for conditions where the spleen is either damaged beyond repair or is actively contributing to the disease process. In bone marrow failure (Option D), such as aplastic anemia, the primary problem is a lack of blood cell production…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Which of the following drugs used in this condition act as prostacyclin receptor agonists? 1. Epoprostenol 2. Iloprost 3. Ambrisentan 4. Selexipag
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, and 4

Pulmonary arterial hypertension is a story of:

• Vasoconstriction
• Endothelial dysfunction
• Vascular remodeling

The imbalance:

| Vasodilators ↓ | Vasoconstrictors ↑

| -------------- | ------------------

| Prostacyclin (PGI₂) ↓ | Endothelin-1 ↑

| Nitric oxide ↓ | Thromboxane ↑

Treatment targets these pathways like a three-pronged attack.

| Class | Drugs | Mechanism

| ----- | ----- | ---------

| Prostacyclin analogs / agonists | Epoprostenol, Iloprost, Selexipag | Vasodilation, ↓ proliferation

| Endothelin receptor antagonists | Ambrisentan, Bosentan | Block vasoconstriction

| PDE-5 inhibitors | Sildenafil, Tadalafil | ↑ NO → vasodilation

| Pathway | Drug Example | Mnemonic

| Prostacyclin | Epoprostenol | “PROS-tacyclin = PROS vasodilation”

| Endothelin | Ambrisentan | “Endothelin = enemy constrictor”

| NO pathway | Sildenafil | “Sildenafil = smooth flow”

• Prostacyclin drugs = Epoprostenol, Iloprost, Selexipag
• Ambrisentan = NOT prostacyclin (endothelin blocker)
• PAH = 3 major pathways targeted
• Severe PAH → IV prostacyclin (life-saving)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant lady with a history of recurrent abortions is now diagnosed to have antiphospholipid syndrome. What would be the best mode of treatment for her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aspirin+heparin

The best mode of treatment for a pregnant woman with antiphospholipid syndrome(APS) is aspirin and heparin.

APS is a prothrombotic disorder (autoantibody-mediated thrombophilia) affecting both arterial and venous systems.

Patients present with recurrent pregnancy loss due to thrombosis of uteroplacental vessels, poor placental perfusion, and prevention of normal decidual changes after zygote implantation. They may also present with preterm delivery, pre-eclampsia, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), and fetal death.

Criteria for APS include:

1. at least one otherwise unexplained fetal death at or beyond 10 weeks;
2. at least one preterm birth before 34 weeks gestation because of eclampsia, severe preeclampsia, placental insufficiency; or
3. at least three unexplained consecutive spontaneous abortions before 10 weeks.

Aspirin (60-80mg daily) with heparin (5000-10,000 U subcutaneously every 12h) is the most effective therapy for APS. Treating APS with only aspirin (option A) is not recommended as heparin is crucial in preventing thrombus formation at the decidual-thrombotic interface, Corticosteroids (option C, D) should not be used in primary APS (without an associated connective tissue disorder) but are indicated in patients with pre-existing systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and APS (secondary APS).
questions.learning: Aspirin+heparin — The best mode of treatment for a pregnant woman with antiphospholipid syndrome(APS) is aspirin and heparin. APS is a prothrombotic disorder (autoantibody-mediated thrombophilia) affecting both arterial and venous systems.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 36-year-old woman presents with bleeding per rectum that coincides with her menstrual cycles. On per rectal examination, a nodule is palpated anteriorly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometriosis

Deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE) should be suspected in women with cyclical bleeding per rectum, dyschezia, or painful defecation during menstruation. A tender nodule on the anterior rectal wall on per rectal examination is characteristic of rectovaginal septum or bowel endometriosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Colorectal cancer: Causes persistent, non-cyclical rectal bleeding, often associated with weight loss or altered bowel habits.
• C. Hemorrhoids: Cause painless bright red bleeding during defecation and are not related to the menstrual cycle.
• D. Inflammatory bowel disease: Produces chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, and rectal bleeding independent of menstruation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: When choosing the power of an intraocular lens (IOL) for a child younger than one year, which factors should be taken into account?
questions.explanation: Pediatric cataract surgery requires careful IOL power calculation due to the rapid growth of the eye. A child's eye undergoes significant elongation of the axial length and flattening of the cornea during the first few years of life. This physiological growth results in a predictable myopic shift over time. If a child is corrected to emmetropia (zero power) at infancy, they will become severely myopic (nearsighted) as they grow. Therefore, when selecting an IOL for a child under 1 year old, surgeons typically "under-correct" the eye, leaving the infant with a significant amount of hypermetropia initially to account for the future myopic shift. Option B is the result of the desired under-correction, but Option A is the underlying biological phenomenon that necessitates it. Options C and D relate to the capsule rather than the refractive shift. Thus, myopic shift is the primary factor driving IOL power choice

questions.text: Which of the following muscles is not involved in the overhead abduction of the arm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pectoralis major

Pectoralis major is mainly involved in adduction and medial rotation of the arm and is not involved in the abduction of the arm.

Glenohumeral abduction is about 120° or more. The glenohumeral arthrodesis restricts the abduction at about 45°. Further abduction occurs at the sterno and acromioclavicular articulations, and contralateral vertebral flexion.

Muscles involved in the abduction of the shoulder:

• The first 15° of abduction is initiated by the supraspinatus muscle.
• 15° to 90° of abduction is carried out mainly by the middle fibers of the deltoid muscle.
• Abduction of the arm, beyond 90°, is carried out by the movement of the shoulder girdle caused by the action of trapezius and serratus anterior.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A newborn baby presents with difficulty breathing. It is noted that his symptoms improve when he cries. In which disease does the symptom improve upon crying?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Choanal atresia

The given clinical scenario stridor in an infant that relieves on crying is suggestive of choanal atresia.

Improvement of stridor on crying is seen in gross obstruction like choanal atresia while laryngomalacia presents with worsening of stridor while crying or feeding. Sinusitis presents with stretor rather than stridor and it does not relieve while crying.

Choanal atresia is the persistence of the bucconasal membrane, unilateral is more common and may remain undiagnosed until adult life, bilateral atresia will present as a respiratory obstruction in the newborn. The initial clinical evaluation consists of placing a large laryngeal mirror under each nostril and checking for fogging, this is known as the laryngeal mirror test.

Diagnosis can be made by:

* Presence of mucoid discharge in the nose

* Absence of air bubbles in the nasal discharge

* Failure to pass a catheter from the nose to the pharynx

* Putting methylene blue dye into the nose and checking its passage to the pharynx

* Putting a radio-opaque dye into the nose and taking a lateral radiograph

* CT in the axial plane

Management: In bilateral atresia, emergency treatment is to provide an airway, which is done by McGovern's technique- (a feeding tube with a large hole that provides a good oral airway), this removes the need for tracheostomy. Definitive treatment is correcting the atresia either by trans palatal or transnasal approach, which is usually done at one and a half years of age.

Pearl PF1080: Choanal atresia

* It is due to the persistence of bucconasal membrane which separates primitive oropharynx from the primitive nasopharynx

* Unilateral > bilateral

* 30% of cases are bony and 70% are mixed

* Unilateral cases may be asymptomatic and present in adult life

* Bilateral cases are life-threatening and present with respiratory distress

* Associated with CHARGE syndrome

* C- Coloboma of the eye

* H- Heart defects

* A- Atresia of choana

* R- Retarded growth and development

* G- Genital anomalies

* E- Ear anomalies and hearing loss.

* CT scan is the best investigation

Image: Membranous, bilateral choanal atresia in a newborn

* McGoverns technique- A feeding nipple with a large hole provides a good oral airway

* Definitive treatment consists of correction of atresia by a trans-nasal or trans-palatal approach.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding paediatric cardiopulmonary resuscitation?
options: Chest compression at the rate of 30:2 with 2 rescuers
Adenosine via interosseous is preferred over other methods
In chest compression, depth must be at least 1/3rd of the child's chest AP diameter
Adrenaline given in dose 0.01 mg/kg iv/io in 1:1000 concentration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. In chest compression, depth must be at least 1/3rd of the child's chest AP diameter

The depth of compressions in infants should be at least 1.5 inches or 1/3 the depth of the infant’s chest.

Effective chest compressions in infants and pediatric population:

• 100 to 120 compressions per minute (30 compressions for every 15-18 sec).
• One provider: Place two fingers, one between the nipple line and the other 1 cm below the first finger
• Two providers: Encircle the infant's torso with both hands, thumbs pointing cephalad and positioned 1cm below the nipples over the sternum.
• Depth of compressions should be at least 1.5 inches or 1/3 the depth of the infant’s chest.
• Press hard and fast
• Allow for full chest recoil after every compression

Other Options:

Option A: Chest compression at the rate of 30:2 with 2 rescuers: For children, the compression-to-ventilation ratio is 15:2 when there are two rescuers. A 30:2 ratio is used only if there is a single rescuer, similar to adult CPR.

Option B: Adenosine via interosseous is preferred over other methods: Adenosine is not used in pediatric cardiopulmonary resuscitation. It is used in PSVT treatment in intravenous routes.

Option D: Adrenaline given in dose 0.01 mg/kg iv/io in 1:1000 concentration: Epinephrine is the drug of choice for treating bradycardia in infants and children. The recommended dose is 0.01 mg/ kg of a 1:10,000 solution.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is most likely to be seen due to rupture of a saccular aneurysm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

Subarachnoid hemorrhage is most likely to be seen due to the rupture of a saccular aneurysm.

Saccular aneurysms are thin-walled outpouchings measuring 2 or 3 cm in diameter with a bright, red, translucent wall. These are mainly seen at the arterial branching points along the circle of Willis.

The absence of smooth muscle and internal elastic lamina is the main pathogenesis in saccular aneurysms. Female sex, smoking, cocaine abuse, and family history are some other risk factors.

Genetic conditions predisposing to subarachnoid hemorrhage are:

• Adult polycystic kidney disease
• Fibromuscular dysplasia
• Neurofibromatosis type 1
• Ehler Danlos syndrome and Marfan's syndrome.

Clinically, subarachnoid hemorrhage presents with a sudden and severe headache commonly referred to as thunderclap headache. It may be associated with seizures, unresponsiveness, and vomiting.

CT scan is the imaging method of choice. It shows blood in basal cisterns and aneurysms appear as round enhancing lesions. Management includes craniotomy and clipping or coiling by endovascular embolization. Medical management includes fluid replacement with normal saline, oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours, and supportive measures.

Hyponatremia can be a frequent complication in subarachnoid hemorrhage. The below image shows a CT of subarachnoid hemorrhage with blood in basal cisterns.

Other options:

Option A: Subdural hemorrhage or subdural hematoma occurs mainly due to rupture of the cortical bridging veins. Symptoms of raised intracranial pressure (ICP)  such as headache, vomiting, blurring of vision, as well as focal deficits are seen.

Option C: Intracerebral hemorrhages may spontaneously occur in patients with hypertension, amyloid angiopathy, coagulation disorders, or as a complication of ischemic stroke. Headache, raised ICP, and focal neurological deficits can be present.

Option D: Hydrocephalus is a condition where the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulation is obstructed or there is a failure to resorb thereby leading to an increase in CSF volume with enlargement of the ventricles. Symptoms of raised ICP are seen.
questions.learning: Subarachnoid hemorrhage Subarachnoid hemorrhage is most likely to be seen due to the rupture of a saccular aneurysm. Saccular aneurysms are thin-walled outpouchings measuring 2 or 3 cm in diameter with a bright, red, translucent wall.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is the afferent limb of the corneal reflex?
questions.explanation: The corneal reflex is an important protective reflex of the eye that involves both a sensory (afferent) and a motor (efferent) component. The afferent limb is carried by the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V), specifically its ophthalmic division (V₁). This division supplies sensory innervation to the cornea and detects tactile or noxious stimuli applied to it, transmitting the impulse to the brainstem. The efferent limb of the corneal reflex is mediated by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), which innervates the orbicularis oculi muscle, producing bilateral blinking in response to corneal stimulation. The optic nerve (Option A) is involved in visual pathways and serves as the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex, not the corneal reflex. The trochlear nerve (Option D) innervates the superior oblique muscle and has no role in corneal sensation or blinking. Therefore, the trigeminal nerve is the correct answer, as it provides the sensory input necessary to initiate the corneal reflex
questions.learning: The corneal reflex is an important protective reflex of the eye that involves both a sensory (afferent) and a motor (efferent) component. The afferent limb is carried by the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V), specifically its ophthalmic division (V₁).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Does Von Gierke's disease involve a deficiency of which enzyme?
questions.explanation: Von Gierke's disease, also known as Glycogen Storage Disease Type I (GSD I), is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme glucose 6-phosphatase. This enzyme is essential for the final step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, as it converts glucose 6-phosphate into free glucose in the liver and kidneys. Without it, patients experience severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly (due to glycogen accumulation), hyperuricemia, and lactic acidosis. Liver phosphorylase deficiency (Option A) causes GSD Type VI (Hers disease), which is generally milder. Lysosomal alpha-glucosidase deficiency (Option B) causes GSD Type II (Pompe disease), characterized by cardiomegaly and muscle weakness. Hepatic glycogen synthase deficiency (Option C) is known as GSD Type 0, which results in decreased glycogen stores rather than accumulation. Understanding these enzymatic defects is fundamental for metabolic biochemistry and pediatrics. Von Gierke's requires frequent feedings with uncooked cornstarch to maintain stable blood glucose levels and prevent life-threatening hypoglycemic episodes and metabolic derangements

questions.text: Myxoedema Madness most frequently presents as:

Correct answer: A. Auditory Hallucination and Paranoia

• In its most severe form, myxedema madness a term describing the psychiatric manifestation of severe hypothyroidism can present with a range of symptoms, including paranoia, depression, hypomania, and hallucinations.
• Auditory hallucinations are the most common form in psychiatric conditions generally, making auditory hallucination plus paranoia the most characteristic presentation in this context.
• This combination can closely mimic paranoid psychosis or schizophrenia, particularly in elderly women with undiagnosed hypothyroidism.
• The pathophysiology involves thyroid hormone deficiency leading to widespread alterations in neurotransmitter balance, cerebral metabolism, and cognitive function, producing a full spectrum of mood and psychotic symptoms.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented to the OPD with complaints of abdominal pain and diarrhea. On further evaluation, the patient was found to have cutaneous flushing, extensive wheeze, and tricuspid insufficiency. Contrast enhanced-MRI revealed the presence of endocardial fibrosis. Which of the following substances will be excreted excessively in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5-Hydroxy indole acetic acid

5-hydroxy indole acetic acid (5-HIAA) will be excreted excessively in the above given clinical scenario, as this is a case of carcinoid syndrome.

Carcinoid syndrome is due to excessive production of serotonin, a specialized product of tryptophan metabolism. It is then metabolized and excreted in urine as 5-HIAA. It is characterized by cutaneous flushing, abdominal cramps, and diarrhoea.

Note:

5-HIAA testing is a 24-hour urine test that is specific to carcinoid tumours. This test is the most common biochemical test for carcinoid tumours associated with carcinoid syndrome.

Pearl PF0663: Carcinoid syndrome

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A newborn presents with photophobia and excessive lacrimation. Examination reveals a patent tear drainage system, a clear but enlarged cornea, and the presence of Haab’s striae on ocular evaluation. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Buphthalmos, derived from the Greek for "ox eye," is the classic presentation of primary congenital glaucoma. In infants, the tissues of the eye are highly elastic; therefore, increased intraocular pressure (IOP) causes the entire globe and cornea to enlarge (megalocornea). The neonate’s symptoms—photophobia, lacrimation, and blepharospasm—form the classic symptomatic triad. "Haab's striae" are horizontal or curvilinear breaks in Descemet's membrane caused by the corneal stretching. Option B (Keratoconus) and Option D (Keratoglobus) are corneal ectasias that usually present later in life and are not associated with increased globe size or congenital glaucoma symptoms. Option C (Trachoma) is an infectious conjunctivitis that causes scarring, not globe enlargement. Congenital glaucoma is a surgical emergency caused by the maldevelopment of the trabecular meshwork (dysgenesis). Management typically involves goniotomy or trabeculotomy to lower the IOP and prevent permanent optic nerve damage and vision loss

questions.text: Which of the following would help in explaining the mechanism of action of ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. cGMP

Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) increases intracellular cGMP by activating the enzyme guanylyl cyclase.

ANP is secreted by the heart from atrial storage granules in response to an increase in intravascular volume. It decreases aldosterone secretion and decreases blood pressure.

Option A: cAMP is increased by activation of adenyl cyclase. Norepinephrine is a hormone that acts on intracellular adenylyl cyclase.

Option C: Gi of G-protein coupled receptors (GPCR) act via the IP3-DAG (phospholipase C) pathway.

Option D: Tyrosine kinase receptors act via the JAK/STAT pathway.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the preferred treatment for a benign tumor of the superficial parathyroid gland?
questions.explanation: (Note: The question likely refers to the parotid gland, not the parathyroid, given the options.) For a benign tumor (like a pleomorphic adenoma) located in the superficial lobe of the parotid gland, the preferred and standard treatment is a superficial parotidectomy. This procedure involves removing the entire superficial lobe along with the tumor, which allows the surgeon to definitively identify and preserve the facial nerve. Simple enucleation (Option A)—just "shelling out" the tumor—is strictly avoided because it leads to a very high rate of recurrence (up to 25%) due to microscopic extensions of the tumor through its capsule. Chemotherapy (Option C) and Radiation therapy (Option D) have no role in the primary treatment of benign parotid neoplasms. During a superficial parotidectomy, the facial nerve acts as the anatomical plane dividing the gland. Preserving this nerve while ensuring an adequate margin around the tumor is the primary goal. Accurate surgical technique is critical to prevent complications like facial palsy or Frey's syndrome

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with a foreign body (chuna) in his eyes and complains of irritability and lacrimation. What is the first step of management in this patient?
options: Irrigation of eye with normal saline
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Irrigation of eye with normal saline

Chemical injury to the eye (e.g., chuna/lime = alkali burn) is an ocular emergency, and the first and most important step is immediate copious irrigation.

• Alkali substances penetrate rapidly and cause liquefactive necrosis
• Immediate dilution/removal of the chemical limits depth of damage and improves prognosis

Management priority:

• Start irrigation immediately (do not wait for history or examination)
• Use normal saline, Ringer lactate, or even clean water if saline unavailable
• Continue until ocular pH normalizes (\~7–7.4)
• Evert eyelids to remove retained particles

Why not others:

• Antibiotic drops: Given later to prevent infection
• Tarsorrhaphy: For healing in severe cases, not initial step
• Scraping: Not indicated initially and may worsen injury

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 72-year-old male presents with complaints of a weak urinary stream and frequent urination in small amounts and is on prazosin. He also mentions that he frequently feels lightheaded and has low blood pressure. Which of the following alpha-blockers will you prefer to give him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tamsulosin

The given scenario is suggestive of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and tamsulosin should be given as it has the least effect on blood pressure.

It is an α-blocker that has more selectivity towards α1A/1D when compared to α1B receptors. The vasodilatory effects are mainly attributed to blockade of α1B receptors present on blood vessels.

The relief of BPH symptoms is mainly due to the blockade of α1A receptors present predominantly in the prostatic stroma. It lacks apoptotic effect on prostatic cells that is seen with terazosin and doxazosin.

α1 receptor antagonists can be classified as:

* Selective antagonists

* Silodosin (α1A)

* Tamsulosin (α1A + α1D)

* Non-selective

* Prazosin

* Terazosin

* Doxazosin

* Alfuzosin

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 80 year old male presented with diminution of vision since 2 years. The right eye was red and painful. On examination, the IOP was 50 mmHg in left eye and 16 mmHg in right eye. The right eye had deep anterior chamber with some cells and flare. What could be the possibility?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phacolytic glaucoma

Phacolytic glaucoma is a lens-induced secondary open-angle glaucoma seen in elderly patients with long-standing hypermature cataract.

• Elderly patient with gradual visual loss (cataract history)
• Painful red eye
• Very high IOP (e.g., \~50 mmHg)
• Deep anterior chamber (open angle)
• Cells and flare in anterior chamber due to inflammatory response

Pathophysiology:

• Leakage of lens proteins from hypermature cataract
• Macrophages ingest proteins → block trabecular meshwork
• Leads to acute rise in IOP

Why not others:

• Phacomorphic glaucoma:

• Due to intumescent lens → shallow anterior chamber (angle closure)

• Malignant glaucoma:

• Shallow/flat anterior chamber, usually post-surgery

• Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis:

• Chronic, mild uveitis with low-grade inflammation, not markedly raised IOP

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines, what is the minimum number of antenatal visits recommended for a pregnant woman to achieve optimal maternal and fetal health outcomes?
questions.explanation: In 2016, the World Health Organization (WHO) updated its antenatal care (ANC) guidelines, increasing the recommended minimum number of visits from four to eight. This change was based on evidence showing that a higher frequency of contacts between a pregnant woman and healthcare providers is associated with a lower probability of stillbirths and improved overall maternal and neonatal health outcomes. The older "focused" ANC model, which recommended only four visits (Option B), is now considered the absolute baseline but no longer the ideal standard for comprehensive care. Options C (12 visits) and D (14 visits) represent even higher frequencies that may be utilized in high-risk pregnancies but are not the general WHO minimum recommendation. These eight contacts are strategically timed to screen for complications like pre-eclampsia, provide essential nutrition counseling, and prepare the mother for a safe birth. Adhering to the eight-visit model is a critical global health strategy for reducing preventable maternal and newborn morbidity and mortality
questions.learning: In 2016, the World Health Organization (WHO) updated its antenatal care (ANC) guidelines, increasing the recommended minimum number of visits from four to eight.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A smoker presents with long-standing complaints of copious, yellow, foul-smelling sputum that markedly increases with changes in posture. Based on this history, what is the most likely initial differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The chronic history of yellow, copious, foul-smelling sputum (purulent expectoration) that increases with postural change is the classic clinical description of Bronchiectasis. Bronchiectasis involves the permanent dilation of the bronchi due to chronic infection and inflammation, leading to "pools" of mucus that drain when the patient shifts position. Asthma (Option A) presents with wheezing and episodic breathlessness, not chronic foul sputum. Pneumonia (Option B) is an acute infection with a shorter duration and focal lung findings. Lung cancer (Option D) usually presents with hemoptysis and weight loss in an older smoker but not the specific postural drainage pattern of mucus. While smoking contributes to chronic bronchitis, the postural change and "foul-smelling" nature strongly favor bronchiectasis. Diagnosis is confirmed using High-Resolution CT (HRCT) showing the "signet-ring" sign. Management focuses on chest physiotherapy, postural drainage, and treating acute infectious exacerbations with targeted antibiotics
questions.learning: The chronic history of yellow, copious, foul-smelling sputum (purulent expectoration) that increases with postural change is the classic clinical description of Bronchiectasis.

questions.text: A female presents to OPD with 6 weeks of amenorrhea complaints of bleeding per vagina and mild abdominal pain. The urine pregnancy test is positive and hCG level is 2800 IU/L. Correct answer: B. Single-dose methotrexate injection

Methotrexate- It stops trophoblastic growth, leading to resolution of the ectopic pregnancy. Medical treatment can be given if:

| -------- | -----------

| Hemodynamically stable | No rupture

| Mass size <3.5–4 cm | Small ectopic

| β-hCG <5000 IU/L | Lower success failure risk

| No fetal cardiac activity | Non-viable ectopic

This patient fulfills all criteria. She has a stable, unruptured ectopic with mass <3.5 cm and β-hCG <5000 IU/L, fulfilling criteria for medical management. Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate is preferred. Surgery (e.g., salpingectomy) is reserved for hemodynamic instability, larger mass or fetal cardiac activity.

questions.text: During post-mortem examination, cherry-red hypostasis is observed in a patient. Which type of poisoning is most likely responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation: During a post-mortem examination, the appearance of a bright, cherry-red hypostasis (post-mortem staining) is a classic and pathognomonic indicator of Carbon Monoxide (CO) Poisoning. This distinct color results from the formation of carboxyhemoglobin in the blood, which has a much higher affinity than oxygen and is bright red. Hydrogen cyanide poisoning (Option D) also results in bright red hypostasis, but it is typically described as "bright pink" or "cherry pink," and the body may have a characteristic bitter almond odor. Hydrogen sulfide (Option B) results in a green or dark-colored staining. Yellow phosphorus (Option C) can lead to jaundice and purpuric patches but not primary cherry-red hypostasis. CO poisoning is common in victims of house fires or those inhaling exhaust fumes in closed spaces. Recognizing this specific "cherry-red" color is an essential first step for forensic pathologists to establish the cause of death. Definitive confirmation involves measuring the carboxyhemoglobin concentration in the blood

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which receptor contributes to static 2 point discrimination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Merkel cell

Merkel cell contributes to static 2 point discrimination.

Merkel cells are responsible for static two-point discrimination. These cells are specialized for detecting pressure and texture and are involved in the detection of fine touch. They provide information about the spatial resolution of tactile stimuli, which is essential for static two-point discrimination, where the ability to differentiate between two distinct points of touch is tested.

Merkel cells are expanded dendritic endings in the epidermis of glabrous (non-hairy) skin. They respond to sustained pressure and touch. They are slowly adapting receptors.

Static vs. Dynamic Two-Point Discrimination
Static: Measures the ability to distinguish stationary points; mediated by Merkel cells (slow-adapting receptors).
Dynamic: Measures the ability to distinguish moving points; mediated by Meissner corpuscles (fast-adapting receptors).

Other options:

Option B: Meissner corpuscle: Meissner corpuscles are dendrites encapsulated in the connective tissue beneath the epidermis of glabrous (non-hairy) skin. They respond to tap and flutter (low-frequency vibration - 5-40Hz). They are rapidly adapting receptors.

Option C: Pacinian corpuscle: Pacinian corpuscles are the largest cutaneous mechanoreceptor. They are present in the dermis of glabrous (non-hairy) and hairy skin. A Pacinian corpuscle consists of a nerve ending encapsulated by concentric layers of connective tissue, giving it an onion-like appearance. They respond to fast vibration (60-500Hz) and deep pressure. They are rapidly adapting receptors.
